Title: Testimony at the 10th International Colloquium on Public Finance
text: It is a real pleasure for me to respond to the invitation of the Ministry of Finance and the Association for the International Public Finance Foundation (FONDAFIP). I would like to thank Professor Michel Bouvier and Noureddine for offering me the opportunity to participate in this forum, which is now celebrating its tenth anniversary. Ten years is certainly a small amount, but as the testimony attests, the record in terms of debates, participation and outreach is more than commendable. The importance of this conference is first and foremost the interest of the topics discussed. Public finances are at the crossroads of several areas that are equally essential for economic and social development. In any case, for us as a Central Bank, we follow very closely the direction of fiscal policy and the state of public finances because they are important data in the preparation of monetary policy decisions and to a large extent condition its effectiveness. Secondly, this symposium has become over the years, due to the number and quality of participants, one of the main forums for debate and reflection researchers and experts in public finance. For a country in modernization like ours, this regular debate offers an opportunity both for a critical look at its public finance system and for the identification of avenues for reform and improvement. Thirdly, FONDAFIP, through its expertise and its wide network woven in several countries both developed and emerging, gives an international opening to this conference. Similarly, the support of the French journal of public finances allows a wide sharing and dissemination of the conclusions of this conference and therefore contributes to its international influence. I am pleased to extend my sincere congratulations to the promoters of this forum for the work accomplished over the past ten years and I am delighted, after having participated in the 2009 and 2010 editions, to be associated again with this edition. Ladies and gentlemen I am invited today for a testimony that I see as an opportunity to share with you the facts and lessons of a career path that began in the mid-1960s. Of the different responsibilities that I had to assume, I will stop in particular at those related to public finances, an area where I plunged in the 80s, admits, one of those that have marked me the most professionally but also personal. A simple look at the evolution of our public finances and our economy in general, shows that we have come back from very far compared to our situation at the end of the 70s and the beginning of the 80s. This is obviously not the result of chance, but of a continuous desire for consolidation, recovery and reform. Those who have followed this symposium since its inception in 2007, have had the opportunity to see the debates come back from time to time on the different stages of this evolution, on what has been done and of course, on what remains to be undertaken. While it is true that significant progress has been made, we have all witnessed how an unfavourable international environment, and I am referring here to the last economic and financial crisis in 2008 and its consequences as well as oil price shocks, can impact our economy in general and destabilize our macroeconomic balances in particular. The 2008 crisis was generally well managed by the authorities and the economy was generally resilient. However, external risks to our economy led us to seek the support of the moreover, it was the only member country of this institution to benefit from this instrument. It should be recalled in this regard that the LPL as designed, and I quote the IMF, "makes it possible to provide financing to meet the real or potential balance of payments needs of countries with good economic policies; it has been designed to serve as insurance or help resolve crises in a wide range of situations. ..... The admission of a country to benefit from the LPL testifies to the fundamental strength of its economy and the economic policy pursued by the authorities, which helps to strengthen the confidence of the markets in the measures they are considering." Our experience with the LPL is in my eyes a good success. It has made it possible to maintain the mobilization for the safeguarding of macroeconomic balances and the pursuit of structural reforms, to strengthen the confidence of rating agencies and investors, ensuring better external financing conditions and greater attractiveness of our country. The gradual decline in the level of access to the line, the fact that we have never pulled it and the prospect of no longer using it in the future, testify to the success of this agreement and the solidity of the fundamentals of the Moroccan economy. Why did I start with these episodes? It is by what quite simply, they are rich in teachings. Our experience during the 80s Certainly redress, do better without a doubt, but also reduce vulnerabilities and build resilience to shocks, especially since, as we all see, the world is increasingly volatile and uncertain. This is the only way to ensure the long-term sustainability of our public finances and the efficiency of budgetary spending and to free up more room for economic and social investment. Ladies and gentlemen, today, the progress made, in particular with the recent adoption of the new Organic Finance Law, allows us to be relatively optimistic about the future of our public finances. This reform was in fact necessary, first for its conformity with the new Constitution of 2011, and then as an action to consolidate all the progress made in terms of budgetary reform, to strengthen the credibility, transparency and legibility of public policy and action. I would like to recall that historically in Morocco, the reform of laws Has always been articulated with the constitutional revision process. Indeed, the Constitution of 1962 was followed by the adoption of the first Organic Finance Law in November 1963, which independent and enshrined the autonomy of budgetary and financial rules and principles from those governing public accounting and public procurement. The Organic Finance Laws of 1970 and 1972, which resulted from the constitutional revisions of the same years, essentially introduced the possibility of suspending the execution of certain investment expenditure in order to meet the constraints of the economic situation which characterized that period. The 1996 Constitution was also followed by the adoption of the 1998 Organic Finance Law, which abolished ancillary budgets, reduced the number of categories of special Treasury accounts and strengthened the prerogatives of the executive in budgetary management in particular. Most recently, the Constitution adopted in 2011 gave pride of place to public finances by laying down principles and rules to govern this area. It explicitly empowers both Parliament and the Government for the need to ensure that the balance of the State's finances is preserved. Parliament, for its part, finds itself greatly strengthened in its prerogatives of legislation, control of the action of the executive, evaluation of public policies and animation of the debate representatives in matters of public finances. The right to information has also been strengthened and the right to amend draft finance laws is better regulated, even if the Government has additional mechanisms compared to Parliament, in particular through article 77 of the Constitution. It also introduced multi-annual budgetary status and elevated the settlement law to constitutional status in order to meet the requirements of accountability. In line with the provisions of this new Constitution, the Organic Law, adopted in 2015, reinforces the role of the Finance Law as an indispensable tool for implementing public policies, taking into account the imperatives of efficiency, transparency and performance. It introduced a fiscal rule limiting net new borrowing to investment financing and broadened the range of information to be produced. This improvement in information on budget management and the availability of public finance data is also one of the areas in which Morocco has come a long way. Let us remember that in the 80s the presentation of the finance law to Parliament was based only on the body of the law, while today we are at 13 documents with the beginning of publication in 2016, as provided for in the investment law and a report on public land mobilized for investment. These documents are equally interesting. Take the case of the report on tax expenditures prepared since 2005. This was the first time that Morocco was able to know precisely, and since then continuously improved, the loss of revenue resulting from the derogations granted. This has naturally sparked and continues to raise a lot of debate around the relevance and performance of these waivers. The latest debate is the one organized on the 8th of this month by the Finance Section of the Union of Moroccan Engineers under the theme "Tax expenditures: balance sheet and prospects". In the coming years, this documentation will be enriched from 2018 by the general accounting of the State which will make it possible to establish its assets and financial situation and, from 2020, the draft regulation law will be accompanied by the general account of the State, the annual performance report and the performance audit report. This enrichment of information makes it possible to put the controls of Parliament and the Court of Auditors on an even more solid footing. It should contribute to strengthening the dialogue between the Government and expectations and a better adherence to public policy. On the tax side, the Moroccan system has undergone a profound reform since the mid-80s, the main objective being the establishment of a modern, coherent, efficient and more universalist regime. Moroccan taxation has therefore come closer in its overall architecture to the best tax systems known at the time. The principles of the reform of the 80s were set out in the 1984 framework law on tax reform. Its main objectives were to set up a system which would ensure, on the one hand, a better distribution of the tax burden, a broadening of the tax base and a reduction in the number of taxes and, on the other hand, a strengthening of the guarantees that the law grants to taxpayers. In particular, it introduced VAT in 1986 as a substitute for the tax on products and services, the SI in 1988 and the IGR in 1990 replacing several categorical taxes. The first national conference on taxation held in November 1999 was a new step in the tax reform process. This resulted in several changes aimed at simplifying the system by reducing schedule fees, some of which were repealed and others incorporated into the SI or IGR. In addition, many measures have been introduced by the simplification, rationalization and harmonization laws. They concerned in particular the reform of registration fees in 2004 and the start of the VAT reform in 2005. Subsequently, taking into account economic and social changes, as reflected in the recommendations of the National Conference on Taxation of April 2013, efforts focused on the integration of the informal sector, the broadening of the tax base, the limitation of exemptions, the generalization of refunds and convergence towards two tax rates for VAT. In this respect, the great success of the status of auto-entrepreneur set up in 2015 and which aims at the integration of a segment of the working population in the formal sector is more than encouraging. The latest available figures indicate more than 20 thousand members at the end of May 2016, a pace that suggests, if maintained, that the target of 100 thousand members targeted by 2020 would probably be achieved. These various reforms and revisions of Moroccan taxation, however, resulted in an abundance of tax texts that made their follow-up by both practitioners and researchers quite difficult. The grouping since 2007 of all the tax texts in a single volume, in this case the General Tax Code, has been a great achievement in this sense. This document is now a complete reference that has greatly facilitated the task for users. As a testimony, I have the opportunity to congratulate Noureddine who was the bearer and pillar of this major advance. Ladies and gentlemen, As you know, despite their negative impacts on economies and societies, crises are often opportunities to challenge and launch reforms. structural. The case of the worsening of the compensation burden, which reached 54.9 billion dirhams or 6.5% of GDP in 2012, led to a worrying budgetary slippage with a deficit of 7.2% of GDP. The reform of the compensation system was then a matter of survival for our public finances. The Government has therefore decided to initiate the gradual dismantling of the fuel price subsidy system. This important reform is in fact a reactivation of the application of the system of indexation of the prices of petroleum products which prevailed since 1995 and which was frozen from 2000, the State therefore bearing the difference between the cost of production and the consumer price. often cited as an example by international institutions and rating agencies. The drop in oil prices from June 2014 onwards greatly contributed to this success, which was facilitated by the implementation of appropriate communication. However, the asymmetry that we have observed since the liberalisation of the fuel sector in December 2015, in the repercussions of international prices on prices at the pump to the detriment of the consumer, rightly calls on the authorities concerned to be more vigilant in this regard. Ladies and gentlemen Another testimony I would like to share with you is that of the evolution of the sector of companies and public institutions. The development of this sector dates back to the 1970s. The Economic and Social Development Plan 1973-1977, which His Majesty Hassan II, in his speech in Erfoud of March 1974, had asked to be revised, grants public enterprises and establishments a privileged role in the Economic and Financial Policy of the Government. This period also saw the creation of 157 entities, or more than thirty companies per year. The recommendations of the McKinsey reports in 1974 and that of the team public action in this sector, aimed at a programme of reforms that affects the institutional, organizational, financial and policy aspects of State intervention in the economic field. This reform program was supported from 1987 by a loan from the World Bank aimed at the restructuring of public enterprises (PERL) and which came to support Law No. 39-89 promulgated in April 1990. The latter initiated the process of privatization of public enterprises and institutions, which began in 1993. At the end of 2015, it resulted in 117 transactions of disposals to the private sector for total revenues of around 110 billion dirhams. This is one of the major reforms of modern Morocco that are part of its policy of gradual opening and orientation towards the market economy. Unfortunately, and so far, no comprehensive evaluation has been made of this experience. I believe that such an evaluation is an obligation and a necessity for public authorities and researchers to better understand this experience and draw lessons for the future. Beyond the economic and social balance sheet of these privatization operations, it would be particularly useful to evaluate the process itself. Recent developments concerning certain privatized enterprises confirm the need for this exercise in order to draw all the useful lessons. According to the data of the 2016 finance law, companies and public institutions should invest 108 billion dirhams, which represents 57% of the overall volume of public investment which would reach 189 billion dirhams (108 MM of the EEP; 67.5 MM of the general budget and special accounts and SEGMA; and 13.5 MM of local authorities). In view of these figures, it seems to us today more than in the past that the good management of public finances calls for placing the governance of these companies to the best international standards in order to ensure an optimization of their resources and an efficiency of their expenses. Ladies and gentlemen When we talk about testimony, we often tend to think about the past. In fact, recounting and evaluating past events is only important if it contributes to a better future success. It is in this sense that I would like to look to the future in order to draw attention to some challenges in the field of public finances that I consider important. Obviously, there is first of all the implementation of the organic law of finance that will have to be successful. In my opinion, this is not an easy bet. This requires a significant effort to adapt the various entities of the State, especially since the level of transparency required in this law requires an example, the evaluation of the State's assets which will be mandatory from 2020, requires detailed and updated information that does not exist in a consolidated way today. This requirement alone gives us an idea of the extent of the work still to be done. The reform of the compensation system also remains incomplete. The big challenge at the moment is to extend it to other commodities, sugar, flour and especially butane gas, which accounted for more than 60% of compensation expenditure in 2015. Due to the social sensitivity of these products, this is a difficult step. We have all witnessed the hesitation surrounding the desire to decompensate the price of sugar. Its entry into force was announced by the authorities for 1 January 2016, but was eventually suspended. The same was true of the tariffs for the water and electricity distribution service. Following social protests in some cities, the increases in the rates of water distribution services scheduled for January 2015 and January 2016 as part of the programme contract between the Government and THE ONEE, have not been implemented. The success of these reforms requires the establishment of an effective targeting mechanism beforehand. Such systems are strictly not Moroccan while going gradually. Even more than when it came to the decompensation of fuel prices, it is necessary to adopt a concerted approach and to communicate around these reforms to minimize the negative perception of the population. In the same sense of rationalization of State spending, it seems essential to us today to conduct a general review of expenditure like the General Review of Public Policies initiated in 2007 by the France and which was an essential phase for the completion of the budgetary reform in this country. FONDAFIP can shed very useful light on this subject. More generally, the question of the efficiency of spending and the return on investment is a problem that arises acutely for our country. It should be remembered in this regard that our economy remains marked by a return on investment as measured by the marginal coefficient of capital (ICOR) which gives the number of investment units to produce an additional unit of GDP. Over the last ten years, it has averaged 7.7 for Morocco against 5.2 for Turkey; 3.5 for Malaysia or 2.9 for South Korea. among those who make the most efforts in education, with annual spending of more than 5% of GDP, well above the global average. However, it continues to be one of the least successful in the world. By way of illustration, in the TIMSS (Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study) program that assesses students' skills in mathematics and science, the 2011 results for mathematics show that Moroccan students in the fourth year of primary school are ranked in the penultimate position ahead of only their counterparts in Yemen. Similarly, in the PIRLS (Progress in International Reading Literacy Study) program that assesses students' reading and comprehension skills, Morocco was ranked last in 2011. Worse still, our country is not only among the last but, regresses if we compare its scores to those obtained in the 2007 evaluations for TIMSS and 2006 for PIRLS. In addition, Morocco has alarming dropout rates at all school levels. Between 1999 and 2012 nearly 400 thousand dropouts annually, all cycles combined were recorded and the cumulative repetition is estimated at nearly 11 million students during the same period, or more than 760 thousand repeating students per year. Based on annual loss of more than 8 billion dirhams. It is these observations that His Majesty the King has highlighted several times in these speeches. In the 2014 Speech from the Throne, our Sovereign called for a study on intangible capital and called for it to be placed at the centre of public policy concerns. The report prepared in this respect by the EESC and BAM does indeed show that capital Intangible, consisting mainly of human capital, is both the main component and the main determinant of the country's wealth. Such observations and our country's commitments in several agendas International projects such as the Sustainable Development Goals or the fight against climate change as well as the many structuring projects underway involving significant financial resource needs remind us of the urgency of optimizing the State's resources and revising the approach adopted for the development and implementation of public policies. It is in this sense that Bank Al-Maghrib has called for the adoption of strategic planning. The latter places a central emphasis on evaluation, results-based management and adjustment of policies as they are implemented, thus ensuring maximum return. Public in our country is that of financial support for advanced regionalization. Having been a member of the Commission on Advanced Regionalisation set up in 2010, I can testify that this project represents a qualitative leap towards an integrated system of territorial governance, based on the consolidation of local democracy as well as on sustainable regional development. The implementation of this structuring project is only in its infancy and it is important to be cautious and to move forward gradually to avoid redundancies in the decision-making centers and especially to prevent this transfer of resources and responsibilities from the central to the local from turning into a financial abyss for the State. In addition, the success of this project requires skills at the local level capable of assuming the responsibility that will be devolved to them, particularly in terms of budget management. Another issue to which I would like to draw attention is related to the participation of women in the development of the country. This is a much more important issue than one might think and is not far from our concerns in terms of public finances. To give you a figure, the McKenzie Institute estimates in a recent study published in women by 2025 would increase global GDP by 25 trillion US dollars, equivalent today to the sum of the GDPs of the United States and China. In Morocco, we have shown a lot of will and we have implemented many institutional and societal reforms in this direction, especially since the early 2000s. The latter have concerned in particular the Family Code, gender equality enshrined in several laws such as the Labour Code, the Nationality Act, the introduction of quotas in elections, the withdrawal of reservations to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women and, of course, there is the 2011 Constitution which enshrines equality and makes it compulsory. We are certainly seeing the emergence of high-level female executives in both the private sector and the public administration. However, women's participation overall is still very low. 75% of women of working age are outside the labour market. According to a June 2015 report by the World Bank (Morocco: mind the gap -empowering women for a more open, inclusive and prosperous society), women's wages in Morocco are on average more than 30% lower than those of men. It therefore seems urgent to us to tackle this problem, which constitutes moreover, a central axis of that of human capital. In this regard, and not only anecdotally, the initiative taken by the Ministry of Finance since 2006 to prepare a gender-sensitive budget report is to be welcomed. The multiplication of such actions would contribute to raising awareness around this issue. Still on the future and with regard directly to Bank Al-Maghrib, I cannot pass without mentioning another structuring project that our country will soon begin, which is that of the transition to more flexibility of the exchange rate regime and inflation targeting. And on this subject, we are not moving away from public finances, because among the prerequisites of this transition are budgetary sustainability and more transparency in the orientation of the State's budgetary policy. The decision to take this step is a sign of confidence in the ability of our economic fabric to overcome its weaknesses and would strengthen its resilience to external shocks. Similarly, the move to explicit inflation targeting will strengthen the Central Bank's credibility, better anchor agents' expectations, and enhance its contribution to economic development. ensure that both financial intermediaries and operators are prepared. We are currently developing a communication strategy to ensure better ownership of this major reform. It is important here to clarify that such reforms, once undertaken, are irreversible. It is therefore necessary that the prerequisites, including budgetary sustainability in particular, be ensured in the long term. Moreover, in the context of the latest assessment of Morocco's eligibility for the IMF's precautionary and liquidity line, out of the 5 criteria selected, it is only in the budgetary area that it appears to be underperforming, although not significantly. Still, in view of the efforts made since 2013 and the recovery observed, I remain optimistic. Moreover, the debt sustainability analyses we carry out at Bank Al-Maghrib indicate that the Treasury's indebtedness should begin to decline gradually from 2017 onwards. Ladies and gentlemen I think I have exhausted my time, so now is the time for me to give the floor. It is true that I have mentioned only a few themes that seemed important to me. Others are as much and what is still certain is that new ones will arise naturally in connection with the mutations. economic and financial to come both internally and externally. I remain convinced that for the coming decade, this forum will continue to gain influence and will establish itself in the landscape as an essential platform contributing to debates and reflection on public finances. When he has to celebrate his 20th birthday with an even brighter record, it will certainly be other actors who will come to testify in this place. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Closing remarks at the 11th international colloquium on public finance
text: 11th International Symposium on Public Finance Public finances and state sovereignty Closing address by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 16 September 2017 Dear friends, dear colleagues, Ladies and gentlemen First of all, I would like to express my sincere regret that I cannot be with you for this 11th edition of the International Symposium on Public Finance, because of commitments outside Morocco made long before the invitation addressed to me by Noureddine. Not having attended the debates, my task is not simple, especially since the theme chosen by the organizers "Public finances and sovereignty of States" does not lack complexity. I have therefore opted, if I may, to share with you some ideas on this issue, while extending the debate on sovereignty to other macroeconomic policies, in particular those falling within the remit of central banks. That said, I know that for you it is the end of two days of intense work and in addition it is a Saturday afternoon, so I will try to be brief. Ladies and gentlemen The developments and changes in the global economic landscape are not without consequences for the sovereignty of States, a question that is increasingly coming up in debates. Indeed, economic liberalization and globalization have not failed to exacerbate tax competition between countries with a view, in particular, to encouraging and attracting investment. Incentives granted in this context by aligning at least with competitors' practices reduce the authorities' own margins of appreciation and weaken their sovereignty to some extent. On the other hand, the formation of economic and monetary groupings, because of their requirements in terms of fiscal, monetary and institutional convergence, naturally results in a certain renunciation of economic sovereignty. In this respect, the case of the European Union, which you have certainly touched upon, is instructive. Fiscal convergence in the Union and the issue of the mutualisation of sovereign debt following the 2010 crisis, which severely affected some countries, notably Greece, continue to give rise to rather tense debates between the defenders of national sovereignty and those of supranationalism. Finally, countries using financial markets are required to demonstrate their ability to honour their commitments in order to benefit from the best financing conditions. This pushes them to be more rigorous in the management of macroeconomic balances. These efforts, which are often beneficial to countries in the medium and long term, are generally perceived by public opinion and especially among the layers of the population who suffer the most, such as a grip of the financial markets and international institutions to the detriment of the sovereignty of States. It is this fear of loss of sovereignty, combined with the fallout from globalization and, more recently, the largely unequal international crisis between countries and populations, that partly explains the recent rise in populism and protectionism, which is in fact only the manifestation of a certain desire to recover that sovereignty. Ladies and gentlemen In Morocco, we are not immune to this debate either. As you know, our country went through very difficult periods in the late 70s and early 80s when it found itself in a situation of inability to meet its debt maturities and pay its imports. It had to put in place, under the auspices of international institutions, a structural adjustment plan with binding conditionalities in several areas, in particular budgetary. This situation has put a strain on our country's economic sovereignty. Those responsible who have had to manage it certainly have a better grasp of the concrete meaning of the word sovereignty. I can assure you that there is no worse feeling than the weakness and sometimes the helplessness that one feels when we are faced with negotiators, with significantly reduced margins. If there is one lesson to be learned from this episode in our history, it is that we should always remember that safeguarding macroeconomic balances, contrary to what we sometimes hear and read, is the best bulwark against threats to sovereignty. Today, fortunately, despite the many challenges, Morocco's situation is much better. Moreover, I believe, as evidenced by the recently adopted texts and laws, that there is a strong awareness of the importance of ensuring balance. For example, article 77 of the Constitution explicitly empowers both Parliament and the Government to preserve the balance of State finances. This requirement was partly enshrined in the budgetary rule introduced in the new Organic Finance Law of 2015. Article 20 of the Act stipulates that new net borrowings must be limited to the financing of the investment. That said, the issue of economic sovereignty has not been resolved. Indeed, Morocco, like many countries, remains linked to international markets and financial organizations. As a result, its economic situation is subject to regular assessments by rating and international institutions such as the IMF as part of its annual consultations or in its reviews since 2012 under the Precautionary and Liquidity Line. These assessments are sometimes perceived as interference in the affairs of the country. In reality, these assessments provide an external look at our management of the economy, our achievements and our performance. They are not indisputable truths, but often remain an invitation to greater rigour in the management of macroeconomic balances with the aim of freeing up more margins for economic and social investment. Moreover, we have seen how some of these institutions are trying to improve their assessments, in particular by extending their coverage to other dimensions, such as social and gender inequalities, for some time. Ladies and gentlemen The preservation of sovereignty requires, above all, an appropriate governance framework that meets several fundamental prerequisites. First of all, it is a question of the democratic legitimisation of decision-making, including a central role for Parliament as the representative of the people. On this point, I invite you to refer to Noureddine's excellent introductory report at the previous edition of this conference, which returned to the the role and extent of the control of public finances by the representatives of the people and the interaction between the executive and legislative powers in this area. To further support this legitimacy, management and the decision-making process must be subject to strict criteria of transparency. On this aspect, it should be recalled that the contribution of the new organic law of finance is substantial. It provides for the regular production and publication of a set of documents on public financial management. These include general state accounting and performance reports and audits. This documentation will make it possible to put the controls of Parliament and the Court of Auditors on an even more solid basis. More generally, it will contribute to the entrenchment of the principle of evaluation and accountability inherent in modern democracies. Ladies and gentlemen Beyond public finances, debates on state sovereignty are also topical in other areas, including monetary and financial. With globalization, the external environment has become an increasingly important determinant of domestic monetary and financial conditions. Since the 2008 crisis, emerging economies have suffered the consequences unconventional policies implemented in advanced economies, with significant impacts on their macroeconomic and financial stability. We have seen several times how monetary decisions mainly in the United States impact other countries, both advanced and emerging. Monetary policy conducted by the US Federal Reserve sometimes destabilizes their economies and puts a lot of pressure on their currencies. Under these conditions, in addition to the trend towards the flexibilization of exchange rate regimes with the aim, inter alia, of cushioning external shocks and strengthening the autonomy of monetary policy, many countries have established or strengthened their framework for developing and implementing their macro-prudential policies. However, with the free movement of capital, the effectiveness of this policy in preserving economic and financial stability remains relatively limited, particularly in emerging countries. Indeed, despite apparent sovereignty, economies with an open capital account remain hostage to the financial cycles of the most advanced countries and consequently find themselves in a situation that some authors define as the triangle of financial incompatibility. This one, different from Mundell's famous monetary triangle, states that one cannot have in a systematic and simultaneous: (i) sovereignty of macro-prudential policy; (ii) international financial integration; and (iii) financial stability. In other words, national macro-prudential policy cannot be entirely sovereign in a context of free movement of capital. Regarding our country, while it is true that we are not yet facing volatility in capital flows, we are still subject to the vagaries of the international economy. Fluctuations in commodity prices, activity in partner countries and tourist flows are sources of sometimes violent shocks to our economy and a source of vulnerability and uncertainty. We are called upon today, to capitalize on the opportunities offered by our openness, to preserve the resilience of our economy and strengthen its competitiveness. To ensure financial stability, we have put in place an institutional framework for the conduct of macro-prudential policy. The latter, established in the Banking Law of 2014 as well as in the new statutes of Bank Al-Maghrib currently being adopted, is based on cooperation and coordination between the various regulators of the banking system and financial markets. The underlying analytical framework now makes it possible to produce regular assessments of the risks to financial stability, which are the subject of an annual report. Ladies and gentlemen Another threat that is gradually increasing against the sovereignty of States is that induced by the digital revolution. The edifying illustration in this regard is the emergence of virtual currencies like Bitcoin. The development of the latter is now beyond the control of central banks and risks weakening their sovereignty in some of their areas of intervention. The Blockchain technology underlying these currencies is now a real threat, not only to the power of central banks but also to that of large traditional economic players such as commercial banks and intermediation institutions in the financial, real estate, energy fields... Another consequence of this revolution is the development of big data and mega information hubs, sometimes containing detailed personal data, often exploited in the context of developing communication and marketing strategies. The large multinationals that control this data and "pull the strings" of the technological revolution, especially the so-called GAFA, are gradually establishing themselves as real actors who shape the evolution of our economies and societies. These rapid and obviously irreversible developments lead us to question the role of the State in the face of these profound changes and the meaning and scope of the concept of sovereignty. In view of the universal dimension of the technological revolution, no state, no matter how powerful, can claim to control its development. The answer seems rather collective to us within the framework or under the auspices of international bodies such as the United Nations. The objective would not be to modify or stop the dynamics of the mutation, but rather to accompany and supervise it to avoid possible drifts and minimize their negative impacts. These are some of the ideas I wanted to share with you through this speech. Thank you for your attention and wish you a good weekend.

Dans ces conditions, outre la tendance <88> la flexibilisation des r<8e>gimes de change dans l<d5>objectif notamment d<d5>amortir les chocs externes et de renforcer l<d5>autonomie de la politique mon<8e>taire, de nombreux pays ont mis en place ou renforc<8e> leur cadre dlaboration et de mise en <cf>uvre de leur politique macro-prudentielle. Toutefois, avec la libre circulation des capitaux, l<d5>efficacit<8e> de cette politique <88> pr<8e>server la stabilit<8e> <8e>conomique et financi<8f>re reste relativement limit<8e>e, notamment dans les pays <8e>mergents. En effet, malgr<8e> une souverainet<8e> apparente, les <8e>conomies avec un compte capital ouvert restent otages des cycles financiers des pays les plus avanc<8e>s et se retrouvent en cons<8e>quence dans une situation que certains auteurs d<8e>finissent comme le triangle d<d5>incompatibilit<8e> financi<8f>re. Celui-ci, diff<8e>rent du fameux triangle mon<8e>taire de Mundell, stipule qu<d5>on ne peut avoir de mani<8f>re syst<8e>matique et simultan<8e>e : (i) une souverainet<8e> de la politique macro-prudentielle ; (ii) une int<8e>gration financi<8f>re internationale ; et (iii) la stabilit<8e> financi<8f>re. Autrement dit, la politique macro-prudentielle nationale ne peut pas <90>tre totalement souveraine dans un contexte de libre circulation des capitaux. Concernant notre pays, s<d5>il est vrai que nous ne faisons pas encore face <88> une volatilit<8e> des flux de capitaux, nous sommes tout de m<90>me sujets aux al<8e>as de la conjoncture internationale. Les fluctuations des cours des mati<8f>res premi<8f>res, de l<d5>activit<8e> dans les pays partenaires et des flux touristiques constituent des sources de chocs parfois violents sur notre <8e>conomie et une source de vuln<8e>rabilit<8e> et d<d5>incertitude. Nous sommes appel<8e>s aujourd<d5>hui, pour fructifier les opportunit<8e>s qu<d5>offre notre ouverture, <88> pr<8e>server la r<8e>silience de notre <8e>conomie et <88> renforcer sa comp<8e>titivit<8e>. Le dispositif analytique sous-jacent permet aujourd<d5>hui de produire des <8e>valuations r<8e>guli<8f>res des risques pesant sur la stabilit<8e> financi<8f>re et qui font l<d5>objet d<d5>un rapport publi<8e> annuellement. Mesdames et Messieurs, Une autre menace qui se renforce progressivement contre la souverainet<8e> des Etats est celle induite par la r<8e>volution digitale. Le d<8e>veloppement de ces derni<8f>res <8e>chappe aujourd<d5>hui au contr<99>le des banques centrales et risque d<d5>affaiblir leur souverainet<8e> dans certains de leurs domaines d<d5>intervention. La technologie Blockchain sous-jacente <88> ces monnaies constitue aujourd<d5>hui une v<8e>ritable menace, non seulement pour le pouvoir des banques centrales mais <8e>galement pour celui de grands acteurs <8e>conomiques traditionnels tels que les banques commerciales et les institutions d<d5>interm<8e>diation dans les domaines financier, immobilier, <8e>nerg<8e>tique... Une autre cons<8e>quence de cette r<8e>volution est le d<8e>veloppement des Big data et des m<8e>gas centrales d<d5>informations, contenant parfois des donn<8e>es personnelles d<8e>taill<8e>es, souvent exploit<8e>es dans le cadre dlaboration de strat<8e>gies de communication et de marketing. Les grandes multinationales qui contr<99>lent ces donn<8e>es et <c7> tirent les ficelles<c8> de la r<8e>volution technologique, notamment celles qu<d5>on appelle les GAFA, s<d5>imposent progressivement comme de v<8e>ritables acteurs qui fa<8d>onnent lvolution de nos <8e>conomies et de nos soci<8e>t<8e>s. Ces <8e>volutions rapides et <8e>videmment irr<8e>versibles, nous am<8f>nent <88> nous interroger sur le r<99>le de l<d5>Etat face <88> ces mutations profondes et sur le sens et la port<8e>e du concept de la souverainet<8e>. Au regard de la dimension universelle de la r<8e>volution technologique, aucun Etat aussi puissant soit-il ne saurait pr<8e>tendre en contr<99>ler l<d5>essor. La r<8e>ponse nous parait plut<99>t collective dans le cadre ou sous les auspices d<d5>instances internationales comme les Nations-Unies. L<d5>objectif ne serait pas de modifier ou d<d5>arr<90>ter la dynamique de la mutation, mais plut<99>t de l<d5>accompagner et de l<d5>encadrer pour <8e>viter dventuelles d<8e>rives et en minimiser les impacts n<8e>gatifs. Voil<88> Mesdames et Messieurs quelques-unes des id<8e>es que je voulais partager avec vous <88> travers cette intervention. Title: Third International Meeting on Social Protection
text: Third International Meeting on Social protection: a work in progressMacroeconomic balances and sustainability of the financing of the project Speech by Mr. Abdellatif JouahriWali of Bank Al-Maghrib Skhirat, 26 July 2022 Mr. Head of Government, Ladies and Gentlemen Ministers, Heads of Diplomatic Missions and Representatives of International Organizations, Ladies and Gentlemen Heads of Constitutional Institutions, Ladies and Gentlemen Members of Parliament, Secretaries General and Directors General, Ladies and Gentlemen Representatives of Civil Society, Members of the General Inspectorate of Finance, Distinguished panelists, Ladies and gentlemen It is an honor and a pleasure for me to take part in this international meeting dedicated to the project launched by His Majesty the King for the generalization of social protection in our country. I would like to take this opportunity to thank, for their invitation, the organizers, both the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the Association of Members of the General Inspectorate of Finance, in particular its dynamic president, Si Fouzi Lekjaa. I would also like to congratulate them on these initiatives, which provide an opportunity to discuss and reflect together on the best way to make this project a reality and to maximize its chances of success. Indeed, given the challenge it represents and its economic and social implications, great caution and very close monitoring of its implementation are required. That said, the diversity and quality of the speakers scheduled for this meeting attest to a level of mobilization capable of allowing the apprehension of the different dimensions of this project and hoping for its successful outcome. Ladies and gentlemen In the time allotted to me, I would like to start by briefly addressing social development in general in our country before focusing on the challenge of macroeconomic balances. I know that I do not need to go back over the importance of social protection, which has been sufficiently emphasised since the beginning of this session and in previous meetings devoted to it. As we all know, the social development of our country continues to suffer from a deficit despite a strong will at the highest level of the State. Significant progress has certainly been made on certain aspects such as poverty reduction and the generalization of schooling, but it remains overall below the objectives targeted, particularly in the context of the Sustainable Development Goals Agenda. His Majesty had already drawn attention to this deficit since the early 2000s, which led him to launch the National Initiative for Human Development in 2005 and to recurrently address social issues in his speeches and messages. Long before the pandemic. He had called for social protection reform, notably in his 2018 Speech from the Throne, but the crisis has highlighted the urgency of the project and the need for a holistic approach. This should constitute a break with previous policies characterized by the multiplicity of actors and programs, sometimes resulting in inconsistencies and weaknesses in terms of efficiency and performance. The 2020 Speech from the Throne illustrates the Royal determination to transform this crisis into an opportunity and to initiate a real revolution in social policy. Today, the authorities are called upon to give concrete content to this project and to comply with the requirements and deadlines set by His Majesty, particularly in his speech of October 2020. For this, it would take exceptional mobilization on all levels to live up to its expectations. One need only look at the data of the International Labour Organization to realize that a large number of countries, including the most advanced, still find it difficult to achieve widespread coverage of social protection. There are many reasons for this, particularly related to its high cost and the inability of healthcare supply in particular to meet demand. Unfortunately, this gap is even widening, due in particular to demographic factors linked to the ageing of the population and the increase in life expectancy, phenomena that are not specific to advanced countries but also to countries that are experiencing an accelerated demographic transition such as ours. Ladies and gentlemen The number of major reforms launched in recent years in Morocco is impressive and consecrates its reputation as a reform-minded country. The challenges today are to mobilize the necessary human and financial resources, but also to ensure coherence and synergies that will enable them to succeed and succeed. As far as financial resources are concerned, a problem that has been set for me by the organisers, I would first like to remind you of a fact that seems important to me. Morocco, according to the World Bank's classification, is a country in the lower-middle-income category, with a gross per capita income of 3350 in 2021. This figure must be taken into account if we want to assess the overall potential in terms of resource mobilization and draw the limits of what is feasible in the short and medium term. In addition, and in addition to the level of GDP, the potential of resources that can be mobilized is diminished by several structural characteristics of our economy. These include the narrowness of the tax base, the size of the informal sector and tax advantages that cost around 2.5% of GDP annually. In addition, there are other problems such as tax evasion or corruption,... While it is difficult to accurately estimate the size of the gap between actual tax revenue collection and potential, it is possible to obtain approximate estimates. For example, in a study published on the 6th of the current month, the IMF estimates this gap for Morocco at around 12.1% of GDP. This is equivalent, taking into account the GDP forecast for this year, to more than 160 billion dirhams annually, i.e. more than three times the annual cost of generalizing social protection. On another front, the mobilization of resources to finance social protection faces other difficulties related to the population's ability to pay. Indeed, the income figures I have just put forward do not provide information on the inequalities that we can understand from the household income survey carried out by the HCP just before the pandemic. Data from this study indicate that the 20% of the population with the highest incomes account for 53.3% of income, compared with 5.6% for the 20% with the lowest income. This leads to the conclusion that a large part of the population has an income well below the average. These results are corroborated by HCP data from the national employment survey. Indeed, of the 27 million people of working age in 2021, more than half, or 54.7%, were inactive. This rate peaks at nearly 80% for women, one of the highest rates in the world. In addition, and in addition to the 1.5 million people who are unemployed, the 10.8 million people who are employed are mostly employed in informal activities and should not have adequate income. Moreover, three-quarters of them do not have medical coverage. This is to say that the ability to pay of a large part of the population remains low for the moment and consequently, the corollary of the generalization of social protection is, quite clearly, a significant contribution from the State. Ladies and gentlemen Today, Morocco, like the majority of countries in the world, is emerging from a pandemic crisis where the State had to make a very substantial budgetary effort that was not without consequences on public finances. The recovery trend that began in 2013 was suddenly reversed with, between 2019 and 2020, an increase in the budget deficit of 3.3 points of GDP but above all an increase in debt of nearly 12 points of GDP, the equivalent of nearly 140 billion dirhams. Despite this deterioration, the assessments carried out by the various international and national institutions, including Bank Al-Maghrib, show that the public finance situation remains sustainable. In addition, Morocco now has a legal framework that allows it to prevent significant imbalances in its public finances. These are the organic law relating to the finance law adopted in 2015 but also and above all the provisions of the Constitution which, as a reminder, stipulates in its Article 77 that "Parliament and the Government shall ensure the preservation of the balance of the State's finances". What is also reassuring is the permanent desire at the level of our country's governments to watch over these balances. This is what has allowed it, despite a few difficult episodes, to never fail and to benefit from the reputation it enjoys today with international investors and partners. Proof of this is the conclusion of the Precautionary and Liquidity Line agreements with the IMF since 2012 and the conditions under which the Treasury's latest issuance on the international financial market was carried out. The big challenge today is to maintain this credibility and reputation in a context as difficult as the one we are going through. Suffering from the deterioration of the international environment, the growth of the national economy is weakening with an uncertain outlook and remains dependent on climatic conditions, at a time when the sharp rise in prices, mainly of external origin, is increasing the pressure on the State budget and financing conditions on the international markets are tightening significantly. Restoring the State's finances requires a great deal of caution, effort and above all difficult trade-offs, at least in the short and medium term. In addition, the health care offer remains far below the norms and standards in the field. This is what led His Majesty in his speech last October to call for "a real upgrade of the health system", a challenge that he described as major. The government is certainly working to make this project a reality, but it is clear that its completion in all its components requires a certain amount of time. It is therefore important that the generalisation of social protection in its health component takes these delays into account. Ladies and gentlemen To conclude, the crises we are going through remind us of the importance and the challenge of preserving the balance of public finances. Contrary to popular belief, the best way to strengthen sovereignty is to manage your finances well to avoid dependence on international donors. This presupposes a clear definition of priorities, the AMO being "the priority of priorities" after the National Cause. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that it has all the necessary human, financial and logistical resources over time. It is therefore important to continue and accelerate structural reforms to improve potential growth and therefore potential resources and ultimately accelerate the country's development and the improvement of the living conditions of its population. Despite the difficult international situation, it should be remembered that our country's weaknesses are also opportunities to be exploited and gains to be made, provided that mobilization is general and that all stakeholders work together in a spirit of synergy and overall coherence. The resounding success of the vaccination campaign and the management of the crisis are there to remind us of what we can accomplish together with will and determination. Thank you.
