Title: Opening remarks by the Director General during The Regional Workshop on "Cyber Resilience for Central Banks
text: Regional Workshop on Cyber Resilience for Central Banks Organized by Bank Al-Maghrib and the Bank of England November 28-29, 2022 Opening remarks by the Director General His Excellency the British Ambassador of His Majesty To Morocco, Dear Colleagues It is a real pleasure for me to welcome you to this joint workshop organized with the Bank of England on cyber resilience for central banks First, I would like to convey my warmest thanks to His Excellency the Ambassador for honoring us with his presence, testifying to the historical friendship between our two countries and His kind and constant support for the fruitful cooperation between them. I also extend my sincere thanks to the senior staff of the Bank of England who contributed to the organization and facilitation of this seminar, enriching its program with their expertise and feedback. Besides, I would like to welcome our colleagues representing central banks from the African continent and the Middle East region, who have kindly made the trip to attend this seminar and share their experiences. Likewise, I express my sincere gratitude to the Direction Generale de la Securite des Systemes d'Information, our national cyber security authority, for its willingness to take part in the proceedings of this workshop, in the tradition of our mutual cooperation which is continuously strengthening. i Ladies and Gentlemen, The cooperation between the BoE and BAM, which we highly commend, has expanded steadily over the past few years. It has covered a wide range of topics including fintech, small business financing, statistical data management and cyber risk. It has recently been extended to a particular theme of great relevance in the current context, which is the relationship between the Central Bank and the Parliament. Today, the cooperation between our two institutions takes a new step with this event organized for the first time at the regional level on a topic of great importance for Central Banks. Indeed, cyber attacks against financial institutions and financial market infrastructures are becoming more frequent and more sophisticated. They can generate significant macroeconomic costs and compromise the ability of central banks to carry out their missions. The cyber threat is intensified by new ways of working and new methods of hosting data, in particular the Cloud. As a result, Central Banks are adapting their strategies and are now aiming not only at ensuring cyber security but also cyber resilience to preserve their digital transformation processes, which must take into account these cyber resilience methods and tools in any development and innovation they undertake. Thus, more than ever, they are required to ensure the effectiveness of their cyber resilience systems and their good coordination with those of the other stakeholders in the ecosystem. And this is what we are working on at Bank Al-Maghrib, in order to develop and regularly test our Bank's cyber resilience system, through internal exercises and with the banking community. We are also examining the possibility of extending these cyber crises exercises to a regional or even a more global level, through cooperation, such as what we are striving to build with the Bank of England. 2 Therefore, enhanced and expanded cooperation in this area is not just a good practice, but a necessity for central banks, as effective information sharing is essential to collectively reduce cyber risks, prevent major cyber incidents, and quickly contain them when they occur. This workshop is also intended as a contribution to the momentum of cooperation within the central banking community. It is my hope that it will inspire similar endeavors aimed at pursuing the debate and sharing good practices and experiences within our Institutions. I am convinced that the expertise of the speakers and the spirit of sharing that characterizes our exchanges will make this seminar an opportunity to identify relevant areas of improvement that will enable our institutions to build and strengthen their cyber resilience systems. I am positive that the outcomes of this conference will meet your expectations. Thank you for your attention and I wish you every success in your work. 3

Title: Opening speech by the Director General during The "Global Payments Week 2023"
text: GLOBAL PAYMENTS WEEK2023 Opening speech By Mr Abderrahim Bouazza, Director General of Bank Al-M aghrib Marrakech. May 16th. 2023 Good morning everybody. It is a real pleasure for me to be here with you today, to welcome this great audience, coming from all over the globe to attend this important event. Welcome, everyone, to Morocco and especially to Marrakech. I would like to express my gratitude to the WB for inviting me to deliver these opening remarks. Its an honor for Morocco to host this major event which was expected to happen in 2020 but was post-pond due to the pandemic crisis. This GPW edition is listed among the events organized for the occasion of the WB and IMF annual meeting which will be held in Marrakech this October. For those among you who are planning to attend the October meeting, it will be our pleasure to welcome you back to Marrakech. This city is steeped in thousands of years of history but resolute ly looking to the future, it offers exceptional cultural and gastronomic heritage and exciting tourist attractions, all of which make it one of the most popular destinations in the world. Marrakech is also well known for its archeological sites. As topics on our agenda of this event cover payment issues, allow me to say some words on one of the oldest cities in Morocco called Aghmat, which is located some 30 kilometers from Marrakech. Before 1062, the year when Marrakech was founded, Aghmat was coveted by many empires as it was an important place for minting pieces of money and gold and a crossroads of merchants and scholars. For those of you who will have the opportunity to visit Rabat, the capital of Morocco, it is our pleasure to welcome you to the museum of Bank al Maghrib which has a permanent exhibition of exceptional coins minted in Aghmat. Let me now come back to our agenda. Since the last GPW, the payment landscape has deeply changed due to rapid digital transformation. In this context, central banks are actively working on CBDCs and new and big players are gaining more space in the payment landscape. 2 Indeed, the pandemic accelerated changes in the payments which were ongoing before 2020. At the same time, the demand for physical cash as a storing liquidity rose in most countries as reported by a recent BIS study. In parallel, concerns have grown about major risks for payments that have developed with the digital transformation processes. However, this weeks event has never been more important than at this moment as the world tries to recover from Covid and face a confluence of huge challenges such as the impacts of the war in Ukraine, geopolitical fragmentation, high inflation, the increasing risk of financial instability following the U-S banking crisis, and the acceleration of climate change. These events affect the lives of a lot of people in the world, mainly those who are vulnerable. They come as digital financial services have played a key role in mitigating some of the effects of the pandemic on fragile communities and as efforts are still needed to improve financial inclusion. So, in these dark times, we should reaffirm the critical role of financial and digital inclusion as an engine for inclusive and sustainable economic growth without forgetting that, in many regions, this inclusion requires more investments in numeric infrastructure such as the access to electricity and to mobile and internet networks. Many issues that I spoke about before fall under central bank responsibilities and pose more challenges for them. They have to work hard to maintain public trust in their monetary and financial stability policies and in the payment systems. As I close my speech, let me express my wishes for a successful conference, which will surely deliver insights and reflections that will contribute to making the payments landscape more inclusive, efficient, and secure. Thank you for your attention and enjoy your stay in Marrakech. 3

Title: ISO 37001 Certificate Awarding Ceremony
text: 1959 - 2019 ISO 37001 Certificate Awarding Ceremony Rabat, November 28, 2019 Minister of Employment and Professional Integration, Speech of Abdellatif JOUAHRI Governor of Bank Al- Maghrib President of the National Authority for Probity, Prevention and the Fight Against Corruption, Chairperson and CEO of the Moroccan Capital Market Authority (AMMC), Chairman of the Supervisory Authority of Insurance and Social Welfare (ACAPS), Ladies and Gentlemen members of Bank Al-Maghrib Board, Ladies and gentlemen, First of all, I would like to welcome you all and express my sincere thanks for having responded to our invitation to this ISO 37001 certification ceremony of our Anti-Corruption Management System. Our meeting today coincides with the celebration by Bank Al-Maghrib of its sixtieth anniversary. It also takes place on the eve of the international and national Anti-corruption Days, to be held respectively on December 9th and January 10th. It also reflects the huge importance we accord to the issue, in view of the challenges it raises, and the priority it is given at the highest level of the State. Indeed, the scourge of corruption is no longer considered a taboo. All international institutions agree today to recognize corruption as an impediment to development, as it weakens institutions, saps confidence among social players and threatens the economy and social peace. His Majesty the King, May God Assists him, in his Address to the African Union Heads of State and Government Conference in July 2018, places the fight against corruption at the heart of developmental issues. I quote: "The fight against this scourge must be made a priority, because it is the major obstacle to economic and social development, and to the fulfillment of our youth. The well-being of our peoples depends on the prevention and the accountability of all the actors in our societies ". It is in line with this vision that Bank Al-Maghrib, as a central bank and one of the actors of the national financial sector, has built up its anti-corruption strategy. Ladies and gentlemen, The confidence that our Institution must instill among its partners is essential to the fulfillment of its fundamental missions, particularly at a time when its new statutes, promulgated in July 2019, gave it even broader missions. Enhancing ethics, therefore, represents one of the key success factors to achieve its strategic objectives. To this end, we are constantly mobilizing to stand as a reference player in this area, through a commitment to conduct our missions with independence, rigor and integrity. Since 2005, the Bank has adopted a structured and transparent ethical mechanism, based on: - Ethical codes applicable to Board Members, the Governor of the Bank and all the staff, - specific versions for highly sensitive functions (such as those related to procurement), - strict management of conflict of interest situations, gifts and invitations, - and finally, an ethical whistleblowing system open to the Bank's staff and partners, ensuring the confidentiality and protection of whistleblowers. To enable the effective implementation of all these mechanisms and win the support of all, we opted for a decentralized organization, which is based on a network of "deontology" correspondents within each entity of the Bank, considered as the key vector of the culture of ethics Under such a dynamic approach, the bankd5s ethical mechanism was gradually strengthened in keeping with the changes in the practices of the most advanced central banks in this area. Following the adoption in 2017 by our country of ISO 37001, Bank Al-Maghrib decided, as of 2018, to set up its own anti-corruption system, consolidating thereby the progress made in its ethical mechanism. This system, steered by the top management (according to the Tone-at-the-top principle), also capitalizes on the management systems certification procedures previously adopted by the Bank in terms of quality, environment, health/safety at work and information security. It revolves around key components, namely: - an anti-corruption policy advocating "zero tolerance" for all forms of corruption, made public in accordance with the Bank's transparency principles, - a specific mapping of corruption risk as well as the related measures to control it; - training and awareness raising plan, not only for the Bankd5s staff, but also for our major associates and other interested stakeholders. At the end of this process, the System was subject to a certification audit which was conducted by a specialized firm, selected as part of an open call for tender. The results of this audit, which we received with satisfaction, concluded that our system meets the compliance requirements. On this occasion, I would like to thank the Bank's staff for being mobilized and committed to this certification process. I would also like to express my deepest gratitude to Bank Al-Maghribd5s board members for their support and involvement. We firmly believe that a certification should never be an end in itself, but a genuine tool that allows us, above all, to identify new challenges ahead of us, while confirming the relevance of our approaches. The primary challenge is indeed to maintain our systemd5s compliance over time, while integrating it into a momentum that anticipates and grasps changes in the Bankd5s internal and external context. Ladies and gentlemen; Although it is important for our Institution to achieve the state-of-the-art in terms of fighting against corruption; it remains a high priority for us to contribute to the national momentum in this area, steered at the highest institutional level by the National Anti-Corruption Commission (CNAC). In the aftermath of the National Anti-Corruption Strategy adopted for this purpose, Bank Al-Maghrib also endeavors to actively participate in the efforts to fight against corruption in the financial sector. This ambition, which we share with our colleagues from other authorities, i.e. the Moroccan capital market authority (AMMC) and the Supervisory Authority of Insurance and Social Welfare (ACAPS), was further demonstrated by an ambitious initiative to set up a "Cooperation Agreementd3, in partnership with the National Authority for Probity, Prevention and Fight against corruption (INPPLC). This initiative is in fact in line with our policy of openness towards our ecosystem, as part of priority cross-cutting projects of common interest, such as cyber security and the financial sector resilience. The main objective of our four-party agreement, which will be signed during this ceremony, is sharing experiences and best practices as regards to fighting against corruption. It is delineated in an annual roadmap providing for a number of actions, namely awareness raising, training and monitoring, and will be followed up at the highest level. We are delighted with the first assessment of this fruitful collaboration that has already made it possible to undertake several cooperation initiatives in 2019, for officers responsible of compliance and ethics in Banks, and to launch a project to develop corruption risks mapping in the banking sector, jointly with the National Authority for Probity, Prevention and Fight against corruption (INPPLC), and with the support of the Council of Europe. Before I conclude, please allow me to extend my particular thanks to the teams of the INPPLC for their support and professionalism, as well as those of the AMMC, ACAPS and Bank Al-Maghrib for their sharing and collaboration spirit during the early stages of this project. I believe this will be a solid basis for success in the next steps. Ladies and gentlemen We believe that we have made significant progress in relation to the fight against corruption, namely at the institutional level. Yet, much remained to be done to ensure the efficiency of the reforms undertaken. We all need to double our efforts and strengthen cooperation in this regard to overcome this challenge for our countryd5s development. By all I mean institutional, economic, and civil society stakeholders. Thank you.

Title: At the presentation of the financial sector's roadmap for contributing to sustainable development and the fight against climate change
text: Press conference for the presentation of the financial sectord5s roadmap for contributing to sustainable development and the fight against climate change Opening remarks of Mr. Abdellatif Jouahri Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib Marrakech, November 14, 2016 Honorable Minister of Economy and Finance, Honorable President of the Economic, Social and Environmental Council, Honorable heads of financial sector regulatory authorities, Honorable presidents of professional associations, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a real pleasure for me today to present to you the financial sectord5s roadmap for contributing to sustainable development and to the fight against climate change. This roadmap is the outcome of the collaboration of all industry regulators and professionals, on behalf of whom I am speaking to you today, namely: . The Ministry of Economy and Finance; . The Moroccan Capital Market Authority; . The Supervisory Authority of Insurance and Social Welfare; . Casablanca Finance City Authority; . Casablanca Stock Exchange; . The Moroccan Bankersd5 Association; and . The Moroccan Federation of Insurance and Reinsurance Companies. This roadmap, developed in coordination with the COP 22 Scientific Commission, is in line with the commitments made by Morocco under the historic Paris Agreement, whose implementation process, including its funding component, will be initiated at this 22nd meeting of the Conference of the Parties. Morocco was among the first countries to have presented its Intended Nationally Determined Contribution which targets a 42 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. This requires an overall budget estimated at US50 billion, of which 35 billion remain conditional on access to new external sources of funding. The fulfillment of this commitment requires the strong involvement of all Moroccan stakeholders, first of all the financial sector as a whole, which has to contribute to and support the transition towards a more responsible and sustainable economy. Moroccan banking and financial institutions have been sensitive to this issue for some time now. Actually, the Moroccan banking sector has always supported the Kingdomd5s various sectoral programs aimed at strengthening its energy independence while reducing its environmental impact. Banks are thus significantly contributing to the financing of renewable energy programs, which are expected to meet 52 percent of the countryd5s needs by 2030. Some banks have also developed specific products to support corporations engaged in sustainable development. Others have set up investment funds dedicated to socially responsible corporations and those engaged in energy efficiency. Since 2011, the insurance sector has also offered d2multi-risk climated3 insurance, which currently covers one million hectares. Financial sector regulators are not left behind. Bank Al-Maghrib has started for more than a decade a program aimed at aligning its processes and management practices with the highest standards of quality and social and environmental responsibility. It is in recognition of these efforts that IFC has invited it to join the d2Sustainable Banking Networkd3, established in 2012 to help regulators in emerging countries develop d2responsible lendingd3 policies and environmental and social risk management guidelines. Capitalizing on all these initiatives, the Moroccan financial sector works towards the emergence of an inclusive financial model aligned with the challenges of sustainable development so as to enable Morocco to meet the challenge of its transition to a responsible and low-carbon economy. This ambition is both national and African. In its Moroccan component, the roadmap features five major axes that constitute our commitments to show the sectord5s firm determination to support our countryd5s contribution to the global action in the fight against climate change. Axis 1: Developing sustainable financial instruments and products Banks, insurance companies and other actors in the capital market are committed to mobilizing diversified and stable green resources in order to support sustainable development projects, which have, by definition, a medium and long-term horizon. In addition to drawing on the available international financing lines, it is a matter of contributing to the creation and development of a green capital market, notably through the creation of ad-hoc investment vehicles and the issuance of Green Bonds, the first guide of which was prepared by the Moroccan Capital Market Authority which will make a presentation on the issue next Wednesday. The first two green bond issuances were announced in recent days, the first one by the Moroccan Agency for Solar Energy (MASEN) and the second one by BMCE Bank of Africa, for a total amount of around US170 million1. 1Masen for 1.150 million dirhams and BMCE for 500 million dirhams. It is also imperative to urge the population to join the movement by making available to them green saving products both at the level of banks, in particular a green passbook savings account which would mobilize small saving, as well as at the level of insurance companies, with pension savings products whose premiums would be invested in green assets. Banks also work to enhance and expand their range of financing facilities allocated to sustainable development projects. With the enactment of the new law on disaster risks, insurance companies have undertaken to develop insurance solutions better tailored to environmental and climate risks. Bank Al-Maghrib will set up, if need be, refinancing instruments for bank loans directed to sustainable development projects, particularly for VSMEs. Axis 2: Extending risk-based governance to socio-environmental risks At this level, financial sector regulators must ensure that the green/sustainable resources mobilized are effectively allocated to eligible projects/assets. This requires our financial institutions to put in place, through a risk map, an environmental, social and governance risk management system able to identify risks and measure the environmental impact of the funded projects and to follow up the remedial actions to be implemented by their holders. This risk mapping will help project holders adopt a socially and environmentally responsible approach and give investors better visibility on the risks incurred. In addition, it is also capital for banks, insurance companies, listed issuers and asset management companies to quantify their own carbon footprint as well as that resulting from their assets portfolios and start reducing them through a risk management policy and more responsible practices and investments. In this context, it would be desirable at the international level that the Basel Committee and other standardizing bodies consider accommodations in their respective prudential rules in order to support this momentum in favor of financing energy efficient corporations and green assets investment. Axis 3: Promoting financial inclusion as a vehicle for sustainable development Considering the importance of inclusive finance for achieving a sustainable economic growth, we reiterate our commitment to offering all categories of population, men and women, young people and businesses, better conditions of access to sustainable, innovative, quality and affordable financial products and services, to suit their needs and their income-generating activities. In this regard, we will capitalize on the support of the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI) which our country joined in 2010. Axes 4 and 5: Capacity-building in sustainable finance, and transparency and market discipline As advisors, financial institutions shall raise the awareness of economic operators concerning environmental, social and sustainability concerns. To this end, these institutions pledged, under axes 4 and 5 of the roadmap, to show exemplarity by promoting the emergence of a genuine internal culture of environmental and social risks and by ensuring regular communication on the measures taken in this regard. The Casablanca Stock Exchange intends to set up, in the very short term, an ESG d2Environmental, Social and Governanced3 responsibility index that will integrate listed companies ranked highest in the rating of Vigeo Eiris agency. These requirements require efforts to increase the awareness of the financial sectord5s management and operational staff about sustainable development issues in the accomplishment of their mission. African dimension In line with Moroccod5s reaffirmed commitment to promote South-South regional cooperation, the Moroccan financial community will contribute, alongside the African financial players, to the emergence of a green finance in the continent. As financial market regulators, we are also committed to developing exchanges and sharing experiences with our African counterparts in the field of sustainable development. A first initiative will be launched at the COP 22 in the coming days by the Moroccan Capital Market Authority, in collaboration with the Casablanca Stock Exchange, with a view to gathering African regulators and stock markets to commit to developing green capital markets in Africa. Bank Al-Maghrib intended to gather, in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme, North and South central banks to discuss the issue of sustainable development. This meeting could not be held for scheduling constraints. However, and within the framework of the Moroccan presidency of COP22, we intend to organize a forum that will host several central banks from the North and the South, for the purpose of laying the foundations for a genuine initiative for the emergence of sustainable finance. On the other hand, the Casablanca Finance City (CFC) aims to become a pan-African d2climate financed3 hub in order to contribute to the mobilization of the resources necessary to support the fight against climate change in Africa. This will, indeed, require the establishment of a framework dedicated for d2greend3 investment funds based on incentive conditions, like d2Africa50 Fundd3. CFC is also committed to encouraging the emergence of a research, expertise and know-how center in terms of climate finance for Africa. It will focus on the d2African Forum for Responsible Investmentd3 initiative, which will aim to promote socially responsible investment in Africa. Still at the level of Africa, I would like to announce that Bank Al-Maghrib, on the occasion of COP 22, has invested in the World Bank green bonds for an amount of 100 million. This issuance will be dedicated to financing sustainable development projects, especially in African countries. Ladies and gentlemen, I have tried to make use of the time afforded to me to identify the essential components of the Moroccan financial sectord5s roadmap in favor of sustainable development and the fight against climate change. The details of this roadmap are available in the kit that was distributed to you. In all commitments, the key element is their implementation and follow-up. Here we make a commitment through the Financial Sector Coordination and Systemic Risk Oversight Committee, of which Bank Al-Maghrib ensures the coordination, to scrupulously ensure an annual progress report to make sure that every regulator has made its contribution in accordance with its commitments.

Title: Africa Blockchain Summit 2019
text: AFRICA BLOCKCHAIN SUMMIT 2019 logo Opening speech of Mr Abdellatif JOUAHRI Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib November 21, 2019 Dear Governors, Ladies and gentlemen, Heads of regulatory authorities, Ladies and gentlemen, Presidents and Directors General, Dear colleagues, Honourable assistance, It gives me great pleasure to welcome you in Rabat in this conference that we hold jointly with Paris Europlace, with the support of HPS and Talan. First, I would like to thank you all for having accepted our invitation. I wish you a warm welcome and a pleasant stay in Morocco for those of you who have travelled from abroad. Our meeting today is part of the agenda of events organized by Bank Al-Maghrib to celebrate its sixtieth anniversary, which began last March with a Regional Conference for Africa and the Middle East, held by Bank Al-Maghrib and the International Monetary Fund, on the digital transformation and the implementation of the Bali Fintech Agenda. This shows the importance we attach to this digital revolution, that is gradually transforming the economic, financial and social landscape, and to its national and regional implications. Ladies and Gentlemen, Fintech is now revamping the financial landscape, expanding the range of products and services while improving their quality, accessibility and cost. It transforms customer relations, payment means, as well as the financing and transfer methods. The Blockchain, and more broadly the distributed general ledger (DLT) technology, is by far the most disruptive technology of this decade. It is often presented as an innovation of equal importance as the rise of Internet, considering its contributions which would revolutionize digital value exchange between individuals and substantially transform the business models. This technology is also recognized for its capacity to generate productivity gains for multiple industries, ranging from the financial sector to energy markets, supply chains, intellectual property management, public sector and beyond. Its ability to reduce intermediation, improve transparency and increase verifiability will also help reduce transaction costs, build up efficiency within existing value chains, and open new markets. We obviously cannot approach the Blockchain without mentioning the Bitcoin which brought this technology to light at its release in 2009. Bitcoin is now the most popular crypto-asset and has paved the way for a myriad of crypto-assets launched by private actors, claiming them to be means of payment or even alternative currencies to those issued by central banks. As you know, crypto-assets differ from money, including electronic money, in that they do not have their own legal status or framework and they are not regulated. These are highly speculative assets, which therefore expose their holders to the risk of substantial losses, particularly because they do not correspond to an underlying claim on the issuer. Besides, crypto-assetsd5 high volatility, added to their limited acceptance, discourage their use as a store of value or as a means of payment, and undermines their use as a unit of account. Today, StableCoins pose new challenges to central banks and public authorities as they are said to carry the "advantages" of crypto-assets while linking their value to "real" assets in order to bring a response to the volatility issue. The reactions of several central banks and public authorities to Facebook's announcement of the LIBRA project are themselves an indicator of the importance of this matter. In fact, the G7 hastened to set up a working group to examine StableCoinsd5 challenges, potential gains and risks. In its report published a month ago, the working group stated that StableCoins could improve cross-border payments, which remain slow, expensive and opaque even in the most advanced countries with near instant and inexpensive domestic payment systems. However, issuing StableCoins also entails several risks related to money laundering and terrorist financing, cyber-resilience, consumer and investor protection. These challenges and risks are amplified if StableCoins are made widely available, affecting, in particular, financial stability and monetary policy conduct. On the other hand, as far as central banks are concerned, many studies and experiments are in quick progress to explore the possibility of suggesting a new version of traditional currency that would have the "digital" form of crypto assets while being a full-fledged "currency". This is called Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC). The survey conducted by the BIS as early as 2018 revealed that around 70 percent of the central banks covered have relatively advanced in their works pertaining to CBDCs. This clearly reveals the degree of importance granted to this issue by central banks, and similarly by the major international financial institutions. The IMF's former Managing Director, Christine Lagarde, spoke on this subject at the d2Fintech Festivald3 held in November 2018 in Singapore, and invited Member States to consider the possibility of issuing a digital currency. Ms Lagarde considers that such currency could meet public policy objectives, particularly with regard to financial inclusion, consumer security and protection and privacy in payments. As for Bank Al-Maghrib, we closely monitor all these developments and, in consultation with other national regulators and relevant authorities, examine their implications for the country, both in terms of opportunities and risks. Ladies and gentlemen, We no longer question the role that new technologies may have in developing financial services, particularly in emerging economies. In fact, they help speed up financial inclusion and expand it to the most vulnerable segments of the productive fabric and to the most disadvantaged segments of the population, owing to the broad coverage of mobile networks and Internet penetration. According to a statement made in November 2018 by the UN Secretary-General, 1.2 billion people have had access, over a period of six years, to financial services owing to technology. The Mckinsey Global Institute reveals, in a 2016 report, that Fintech could increase GDP of emerging economies by 6 percent, or 3.7 trillion, and create 95 million new jobs, by the year 2025. According to the same report, two billion individuals and 200 million micro, small, and medium-sized businesses in emerging economies lack access to credit and those who do, face still high costs. In fact, Morocco intends to use the Fintech contribution in implementing its financial inclusion strategy, which aims, according to the definition adopted by Bank Al-Maghrib, at guaranteeing " for all individuals and businesses a fair access to formal financial products and services to be used according to their needs and means, in order to promote economic and social inclusion while preserving their rights and dignity". This national strategy, drafted jointly by the Ministry of Economy and Finance and Bank Al-Maghrib based on a participatory approach, rests on two Fintech-related pillars, namely: (1) developing alternative and lower-costs models to reach the most excluded populations in accordance with their specificities, and (2) creating conditions for greater use of financial products by accelerating dematerialization of payments, particularly between the State and the users, to entrench financial inclusion in householdsd5 behaviour, and by improving financial education. As part of this framework, we have also developed, together with the National Telecommunications Regulatory Agency (ANRT) and other stakeholders, an interoperable and real-time national mobile payment solution, which aims not only to diversify the payment means offered, but most importantly to extend access to financial services to the majority of the population. We also acknowledge the new risks engendered by technological evolution, particularly with regard to money laundering, terrorism financing, cyber security, consumer protection and personal data protection. As a regulatory authority, we are called upon to give enough room to creativity and to the development of innovative financial services, but, at the same time, we are bound to preserve and strengthen the resilience of our financial systems and protect consumers and businesses. This is actually a difficult balance that involves identifying and classifying risks as well as anticipating any potential effects that innovations and new financial activities may have. This is, by the way, one of the priority projects of our 2019-2023 strategic plan. Ladies and gentlemen, Harnessing the potential of new disruptive technologies for the financial sector in our region is still in its early stages. The dynamics of promotion and development of Fintech ecosystems initiated at the international level, particularly through the Bali Fintech Agenda, with which Bank Al-Maghrib is perfectly in line, will better channel the ideas and energies of innovative actors towards reaching digital financial services of higher quality, low cost and with controlled risks. Our open innovation program "Africa Blockchain Challenge", organized on the side lines of this conference, and whose final phases were held here in the last three days, is in fact a strong message we are conveying to our national and regional ecosystem: We are attentive to the needs of the stakeholders which carry value-added projects for our financial system, and are willing to provide appropriate responses to their questions. I am very delighted to see the significant interest this program has aroused among our Moroccan and African start-ups and the friendly atmosphere in which it has taken place. I would like to congratulate all the participating start-ups for their mobilization, creativity and innovative spirit, not to forget the staff, who monitored the organization of this event and provided accompaniment and coaching to the participants. Ladies and gentlemen, The program of this conference, giving the floor to quality panellists, will not fail to shed light on the issues facing us and to enrich the debates on this topical subject. Best wishes of success for all of us. Thank you.

Title: At the signing ceremony of the partnership agreement...
text: SPEECH BY MR. ABDELLATIF JOUAHRI GOVERNOR OF BANK AL-MAGHRIB Signing ceremony of the partnership agreement between the Ministry of Trade, Industry and New Technologies, ANPME and GPBM Rabat Thursday , 12 June 2008 Mr. Minister; Mr. President of the GPBM; Mr President of the CGEM; Presidents and Directors General; Ladies and gentlemen; It is a real pleasure for me to welcome you back to this Bank Al-Maghrib training center. From this same rostrum and in your A year and a half ago, we launched the national campaign on financing of small and medium-sized enterprises, under the theme "For a best partnership Banks/Small and Medium Enterprises at the service of the Human Development". We had then expressed together the hope to see the efforts made by all the partners in this initiative will take the form of measures that would help to remove the constraints that hinder the development of SMEs. This campaign has led to two major lessons:  the first is that access to credit is no longer an obstacle for SMEs, which have nevertheless shown the need for specific credit and support mechanisms for business creation. This conclusion goes against the claims, sometimes irritating, of some international organizations that persisted in designating the difficulties of access to credit as the main obstacle to the development of SMEs in Morocco;  the second is that the main complaints expressed by SMEs have mainly concerned support and supervision for the implementation of projects. For our part, we insisted during the campaign on the development of financial transparency and good governance practices within SMEs. These conclusions are also in line with the analyses carried out internally by Bank Al-Maghrib and reinforce the actions taken to meet the expectations of operators. In terms of financing, recent developments confirm the development of credit for SMEs. Thus, bank loans to companies increased by 14% and 27% respectively in 2006 and 2007, whereas for the previous five years this rate did not exceed 5% on average. In addition, Bank Al-Maghrib's periodic surveys on the conditions for granting credit show that the number of companies that received a first loan in 2007 increased by 20% compared to 2006 and that the outstanding amount of facilities, of a unit amount between 1 and 15 million DHS, amounted to about 80 billion dirhams, i.e. 30% of the total assistance allocated to non-financial enterprises. This range is used by Bank Al-Maghrib as a criterion for the definition of bank loans granted to SMEs. The same surveys also show that the fall in interest rates in recent years has benefited SMEs; a decrease of 170 basis points was recorded between December 2006 and March 2008. Such observations lead me to mention some of the concerns expressed on the occasion of the entry into force in 2007 of what is commonly known as Basel II and its impact on SME financing. It isuseful for me to reframe the debate on this issue. Although it is premature to draw definitive conclusions on the impact of this new regulation, it is already possible, given the trends observed. and which I have just explained, con stater that there is no crowding-out effect against undertakings and in particular SMEs. For their part, loans to very small enterprises (VSEs) enjoy a weighting of 75% under the Basel II Standard approach and therefore require less coverage in funds. own by banks. Similarly, Basel II, which encourages the dissemination of best financial practices, should lead to a greater availability of credit in line with the risk profile of the company. This means that the quality of financial reporting and governance remain paramount to making the most of these new provisions, both in terms of credit allocation and in terms of interest rates applied. In addition, Bank Al-Maghrib was actively involved in the conclusion of the agreement signed in November 2005 between the GPBM and the SME Commission of the CGEM, to facilitate and rebalance reciprocal commitments relating in particular to the favourable and diligent treatment of credit files and the quality of financial information to be borne by company managers. Title: At the 3rd Maghreb Entrepreneurs Forum in Marrakech on February 17-18, 2014
text: 3rd Forum of Maghreb Entrepreneurs Speech by Mr. Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Marrakech, 17-18 February 2014 Dear Head of Government, Dear WBU Secretary General, Madam President of the CGEM, Dear Governor of the Central Bank of Tunisia, Dear Resident Representative in Morocco of the AfDB, Dear Director of the WB Office in Morocco, Presidents and Directors General, Ladies and gentlemen It is a real pleasure for me to take part in this meeting, especially since it coincides, to the day, with the 25th anniversary of the creation of the Arab Maghreb Union, on February 17, 1989, right here in Marrakech. My first thought is quite naturally for the Founding Fathers who worked with conviction to give birth to this Union as a promise of a better tomorrow for the peoples of the region but also as a commitment to the consolidation of historical relations and the creation of an area of common life and free movement of people, services, goods and capital. * * * 25 years later, where are we? Let me first dwell on some of the figures. The region has more than 90 million inhabitants  30% of whom are under the age of 15  and achieves, at the end of 2012, a total Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of about 430 billion and an average GDP per capita of nearly 4,700; however, with significant differences between the five countries. The disparities are still much wider with emerging countries as shown by the example of Turkey, which alone posted a GDP of 791 billion (1.8 times the GDP of the Maghreb) in 2012, for a population of 74 million people, or with European countries such as Spain, which reached a GDP of 1,351 billion (3 times the GDP of the Maghreb) for a population of 47 million inhabitants. During the decade 2000 to 2010, the Maghreb recorded an average growth rate of 4.8%1; a performance  certainly honourable  but which remains insufficient to curb the high unemployment, especially that of young people, from which the region suffers. In 2012, the available data indicate an average unemployment rate in Algeria, Tunisia and Morocco above 12%. This reflects in particular some of our structural failures, in particular those of our education systems, which are still struggling to produce profiles adapted to the needs of the labour market, thus impacting the competitiveness of our countries. It is true that progress has been made in terms of school enrolment and the fight against early school leaving, but the problems linked to the quality of education and the qualification of young people remain acute. 1 Algeria : 3.8% / Libya : 5.2% / Mauritania : 5.5% / Tunisia : 4.7% / Morocco: 4.9% In terms of the international investment position, the consolidated current accounts of the 5 countries in 2012 were close to 27 billion, with total reserves of 352 billion. The differences are obviously considerable between, on the one hand, the oil-producing countries - together with a current account surplus of nearly 42 billion and accumulating more than90%. of the region's reserves  and, on the other, importing countries with a cumulative current account deficit of 14 billion. This position would have been better if inter-Maghreb trade had been more developed. They do not exceed 3% of the region's total GDP between 2007 and 2011, one of the lowest regional integration rates in the world. To illustrate, this rate is 25% for ASEAN2, 16% for MERCOSUR3 and 9% for ECOWAS4. This is not much better in terms of inter-Maghreb investments, which remain very limited, representing less than 1% of foreign investment in the region; which is again extremely low compared to other regional economic blocs: ASEAN (15%) and MERCOSUR (8%). * * * So little has been achieved, although the beginnings have been promising... 2 Association of Southeast Asian Nations 3 Common Market of South America 4 Economic Community of West African States The banking sector has been a pioneer in regional development, notably with the creation in 1990 of the Union of Maghreb Banks (UBM). The UBM  which I had the honour of chairing at its birth  has been at the origin of some great initiatives such as the project to create the Maghreb Bank for Investment and Foreign Trade (BMICE) and continues, despite the difficulties, to work for the strengthening of cooperation between Maghreb financial and banking companies and institutions. For their part, the Central Banks have, from the outset, accompanied the movement with the creation of a Council of Maghreb Central Banks with a view to better coordination in the monetary and financial fields with a view to a gradual convergence towards the achievement of a global economic union. This Council has met 7 times since 1990, the last meeting was held in 2008 in Tripoli. Several resolutions were adopted during these meetings, including the creation of committees (i) banking supervision, (ii) monetary policy and exchange rate regimes, (iii) payment systems, and (iv) financial stability. Aware of this situation, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), in consultation with the Ministers of Finance and the Governors of the Central Banks, took the initiative to organize high-level regional conferences, which were attended by successive Managing Directors of this Institution. The objective was to lay the foundations for Maghreb integration on the financial, economic and commercial levels, while circumventing the difficulties related to the political environment. For example, the first meeting was held in Algiers in November 2005 on the theme of "Trade Facilitation". Then, the Rabat meeting in December 2006 focused on "financial sector reforms with a view to financial integration". In November 2007, Tunis hosted the third meeting on "The private sector as a lever for economic development and regional integration", with a notable participation of the Maghreb Union of Employers. The theme of the fourth meeting, held in Tripoli in November 2008, was "encouraging joint projects". As for the last meeting that took place, five years after, in Nouakchott in January 2013, it focused on "the intra-Maghreb investment and direct investment foreigners and their impact on employment". Nevertheless, these initiatives have not had the expected success with only a few limited achievements, namely: -the establishment of subsidiaries of Tunisian financial institutions in Algeria, Moroccan subsidiaries in Tunisia, and an Algerian investment bank in Tunisia; -the Moroccan approval granted to a Tunisian stock exchange company; -the double listing of a Tunisian stock market value on the Tunis and Casablanca stock exchanges. * * * Today, 25 years after the creation of the AMU, the balance sheet is clearly disappointing. While the global configuration is tending towards the constitution of ever larger integrated economic ensembles and that we are even talking today of a "free trade area" between the United States and the euro zone, and that we are witnessing in Asia the creation of even wider common spaces, and at a time when the sub-Saharan African region, for example, arouses the interest of several economically advanced countries, we remain absent from the scene and far from these polarizations. For several years now, numerous studies  including those carried out by international institutions  have placed the annual cost of non-Maghreb at around 2% of total regional GDP and tens of thousands of jobs lost annually. In this context, the Maghreb Trade and Investment Initiative, which will be officially launched at your conference, will be an important step and will inject new momentum into making up for lost opportunities. * * * Hopes are therefore placed in you, investors, industrialists and private operators and in your Maghreb Union of Employers, to take the lead and relaunch this project that those who preceded us dreamed of and to which our current and future generations aspire. For our part, we, the Central Bankers, will continue to work in the same direction. We pledge to you to once again intensify our efforts to support your initiatives, both national and regional. As an example, look at the successive measures taken by the Central Bank of Morocco in favour, in particular, of SMEs and MSMEs. Mrs. Meriem Bensalah, President of the CGEM but also a member of the Board of Bank Al-Maghrib, can perfectly testify to this. By bringing together the efforts of all and with the hope that wisdom will prevail at the level of our political decision-makers, we will realize  on the ground  the dream made by our Founding Fathers a quarter of a century ago, right here in Marrakech. We remain convinced that the Maghreb Union is not a choice but an imperative dictated by a common past and future. ###

Title: International Conference on Competition Policy and Law
text: Rabat International Conference Competition Policy and Law National experiences and international partnership Speech by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 13 November 2019 Dear Head of Government, Honourable Ministers, Heads of regulatory authorities, Mr President of the Court of Cassation, Representatives of international institutions, Honorable assistance, It is a real pleasure to take part with you in this international meeting dedicated to competition policy and law. I would like to take this opportunity to thank Mr. Driss Guerraoui, President of the Competition Council for his invitation and to compliment him on the organization of this high-level conference. In view of the quality of the panelists, he can only be congratulated for having been able to bring together so many senior officials from such a large number of countries, but I also think that the importance and interest aroused by the topics discussed also contributed to this. With the speed and scale of the economic, social, technological and environmental changes we are witnessing, the relevance and validity of our laws and regulations are constantly being strained. Public authorities in general and regulators in particular face a complex challenge. They are called upon to develop and implement appropriate policies and frameworks in environments that are constantly reshaped by developments with implications that are difficult to predict. This situation is not unique to one category of country, but concerns all economies, developing, emerging and advanced. In these circumstances, the strengthening of cooperation at national level, between the different authorities, as well as at regional and international level is necessary for the exchange of experiences, but also for the development of standard approaches to common challenges. The growing role of some international bodies and the certain emergence of others are only an expression of the need to unite efforts to face new challenges. Paradoxically, these developments are concomitant with a questioning by some countries of the global conventions and agendas developed and adopted sometimes after several years of dialogue and negotiations. Today, with the rise of populism, multilateralism and the rules that govern global trade are being called into question and the common front against challenges such as climate change, terrorism and poverty is cracking, threatening economies and people. Ladies and gentlemen I will not venture to discuss these challenges and their implications in detail in the few minutes of time available to me. Rather, I would like to share with you a few ideas, which challenge me as the person responsible for regulating the banking system. As reflected in the space dedicated to it in the program of this conference, but also the multiplication of meetings and studies dedicated to it, one of the greatest mutations of our time is certainly the digital revolution. It is gradually but profoundly transforming production processes and the organization of markets and trade. The digitalization of services, the uberization of the economy, and the multiple risks of cybercrime among others, pose challenges of unprecedented complexity in terms of regulation. Regulating emerging industries and services requires an approach that combines the necessary flexibility to enable their emergence and development with the rigour necessary to avoid slippage and minimize adverse effects on consumers, activity and economic stability. For example, the boom in the production of data and its use to create added value poses many challenges in terms of competition, the protection of personal information, and sometimes even politics, as illustrated by the case of Facebook-Cambridge Analytica. The development of social media, the scourge of fake news and its political, social and economic impacts are also another illustration of the implications of the digital revolution and the challenges it creates in terms of regulation. In addition, the perplexity and hesitation in the approach to be adopted in the face of the development of crypto-assets and digital currency are another example of the difficulty that national authorities and even international institutions have in defining an appropriate approach to understand all the consequences of technological innovations. Ladies and gentlemen In the financial field, in addition to the implications of digitalization, the multiplication of difficulties in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis has led to an unprecedented tightening of banking regulation. While calls have mounted for further tightening, the resurgence of economic difficulties and sluggish bank credit are instead pushing for easing in the hope of reinvigorating demand and growth. Regulators are thus called upon to find and above all to preserve a difficult and often fragile balance between the tightening of prudential rules for the stability, which is essential moreover, of the banking and financial system and their relaxation to further facilitate financing and contribute to the recovery of the economy. In addition, the development of Fintech and the requirements in the fight against climate change, as well as those increasingly strengthened to combat the financing of terrorism and money laundering further complicate the mission of regulators. Ensuring compliance with international standards such as those of the FATF or those imposed by certain major economies, such as the US FATCA law, is a real challenge for the financial systems of emerging and developing countries. In the end, meeting all these requirements today, including that of preserving financial stability, translates, it must be recognized, into a real regulatory deluge facing the financial sector. Ladies and gentlemen For a country aspiring to emergence through greater openness and wider integration into global value chains such as Morocco, this compliance is a necessity that requires efforts and arbitrations that are often difficult for regulatory authorities. The Competition Council, through its transversal mission, plays a central role in this direction and contributes to the consolidation of the rule of law. It works together with sectoral regulators such as the Central Bank, to which it has been bound by a cooperation agreement for some years now and which we are in the process of updating precisely in the light of the developments we are witnessing. In the same vein, to preserve financial stability, financial sector regulators work together in a coordination committee set up by law and dedicated to the supervision of systemic risks. In the particular case of the banking sector, Bank Al-Maghrib advocates an approach based on regular dialogue and listening with taxable persons, impact studies and progressivity in implementation. The aim is to ensure the compliance and resilience of the banking system while limiting possible negative effects on its ability to finance the economy. Particular attention is paid to the impact on financing of the most fragile segments of the economy, in particular MSMEs. The latter, the dominant component of our productive fabric and a real source of employment, are often the most affected by regulatory tightening, which sometimes threatens their viability. Designing discriminatory regulations to foster their development while ensuring overall stability and ensuring compliance with international rules is often a difficult exercise that calls for continuous assessment of the situation and innovation in regulatory implementation. Ladies and gentlemen The issues that will be addressed in this conference are of great topicality and involve governments, regulators, economic operators and civil society in its various components. Such initiatives should be multiplied, particularly by developing countries, so that their voices would be more audible and so that they could claim to have any influence on the design and implementation of the norms and standards that the international community was called upon to adapt or adopt in order to meet the challenges it would have to face. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Financial Education in the Digital Age; A Lever for Promoting Savings
text: World Savings Day Financial Education in the Age of Digitalization A lever for the promotion of savings Speech by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 7 November 2019 Dear Minister, Dear Presidents and Chief Executive Officers, Dear friends, dear colleagues, Ladies and gentlemen First of all, I would like to thank you for accepting our invitation and tell you that it is a real pleasure to welcome you today to celebrate together World Savings Day under the theme "Financial education in the age of digitalization: a lever for the promotion of savings". Savings are central to a country like ours, which is striving to accelerate its development and growth and consequently has significant financing needs. It is also decisive at the microeconomic level, allowing households, as a priority, to be able to access housing, to better ensure the future of their children, but also to protect themselves against the vagaries of the economic situation and to avoid, for the most vulnerable among them, falling into poverty. I would like to take this opportunity to thank and congratulate the Chief Executive Officer of the Caisse de Depot et de Gestion, Mr. Abdellatif Zaghnoun, for his initiative to organize this meeting within the framework of a tripartite partnership, linking the CDG, Bank Al-Maghrib and the Barid Al-Maghrib Group. We can only support it to maintain this tradition and thus preserve this space for debate on this theme. An annual meeting on savings would make it possible to address the various facets, assess the state of play and identify appropriate measures to promote and channel it towards productive investment. As I mentioned last year on this occasion, I think we often talk about the problem of financing, but we often forget that it is linked and cannot be dissociated from that of savings. This time, we recommended focusing on two particular factors that play a decisive role in its development. These are financial education and digitalization. In the space of time allotted to me, I would like to come back to two important factors, but first I would like to share with you some thoughts on the current context of low interest rates, which is not without implications for savings. Ladies and gentlemen As we all know, the world economy has been experiencing unprecedented developments since the 2008 crisis. While historically its evolution is punctuated by cycles of expansion and slowdown that follow one another without overlapping, we are currently living, on the other hand, a situation where the risks of a new crisis are increasing in a worrying way even though the aftermath of that of 2008 has not yet dissipated. As a result, it is only when the normalization of public policies, particularly monetary policies, takes place that the darkening of the growth outlook again imposes an expansionary stance of fiscal policy and monetary easing in several economies, particularly advanced ones. Under these conditions, interest rates, which have fallen dramatically since 2008 to near-zero levels or even negative in some countries, are set to remain low, and the most pessimistic predict that they will not return to pre-crisis levels even in the long term. The situation of "too low for too long", as it is described, has thus become a stylized fact of the world economy. This situation is not unrelated to the issue we are considering today. Such low interest rates are not without negative effects on the savings of households, whose efforts are virtually wiped out. Similarly, pension funds are experiencing persistent declines and weaknesses in their returns, which are weighing on the viability of some of them. In addition, very low interest rates generally reduce margins and weaken the profitability of the banking system and consequently its soundness and resilience. Moreover, in several countries, abundant and low-cost liquidity has led to a worsening of both public and private debt ratios without necessarily benefiting the real economy. It is more channelled, for speculative purposes, towards investment in assets, particularly stock market assets, thus leading to their overvaluation and amplifying the risks to financial stability and therefore to the savings ecosystem. To summarize, while theoretically low rates can help revive investment and growth after a downward cycle, in a context of persistent slowdown and high uncertainties, they can have adverse effects on the financial system and the economy as a whole. Ladies and gentlemen In our country, the available data on savings show that we have a great challenge in this area. Household savings, which stand at around 14% of their gross disposable income, would be much lower in international comparison without transfers from Moroccans residing abroad and low contributions. Data from the World Bank's 2017 FINDEX survey show that the proportion of the working-age population that saves is half the average for countries in the lower-middle-income category. These levels would be even lower if we were limited to saving with financial institutions. This situation does not seem to be improving, as the evolution of bank deposits suggests. As I pointed out at the press briefings following the quarterly meetings of the Bank Al-Maghrib Board, household deposits have slowed down quite worryingly in recent years. According to our statistics, the growth of demand deposits is clearly decelerating and forward deposits have lost nearly 10% of their volume since the end of 2015. The reasons for these findings deserve a more refined analysis, but it would be in particular the still important, or even growing according to the 2014 data of the HCP, of informal activities that result in a relative preponderance of cash both in terms of payment of transactions and hoarding. This ultimately leads to a weakening of the savings mobilized through the channel of formal financial circuits. To remedy this situation, which could affect our economy's ability to finance its investment needs, two categories of actions need to be considered. The first is to increase the medium- and long-term potential of this saving by accelerating growth, improving employment and, above all, its productivity. In fact, it is a question of setting in motion a virtuous circle of growth that generates income and therefore savings itself necessary to sustain this growth. Of course, we all agree that this is one of the greatest challenges facing our economy today. The second category is to better exploit the mobilizable potential in the shorter term. This challenge first and foremost concerns the financial community as a whole, all of us present here, public authorities, regulators, the banking system, financial institutions... The aim is to further develop our financial system, in particular by broadening and diversifying savings opportunities and products in parallel with expanding access to financial services to a greater number of households. While we have a relatively deep financial system compared to countries of similar levels of development, including a strong and resilient banking system as highlighted in the 2015 WB-IMF assessment, several challenges remain. First, this performance is not generalized to all components, some of them, and I am thinking in particular of the Casablanca stock exchange, are struggling to be part of a sustainable dynamic. Moreover, even in areas where we have made significant efforts, long delays are sometimes necessary to see tangible progress. On the part of the government authorities, despite the efforts made to encourage several products such as savings for housing, education or retirement, there is still work to be done to further improve the legal framework for savings and make it more adapted and incentive-based. Ladies and gentlemen In a country like ours where nearly four out of ten inhabitants live in rural areas and where, according to 2014 data, nearly 32% of the population aged 10 or over cannot read or write, the development of savings also requires literacy and financial education. This is necessary to, as specified in the OECD definition, help agents, particularly households and small economic units, to improve their knowledge of financial products, to acquire the skills and confidence necessary to better understand the risks and opportunities of finance and to make informed and reasoned choices. That said, and contrary to popular belief, financial education is not only for developing or emerging countries, but it is a global issue that also affects advanced economies. An international survey on adult financial education, conducted by the OECD and the International Network on Financial Education (INFE) in 2016, found that even in developed countries, levels of financial education can be relatively low. In the UK, for example, just 47% of adults achieved the minimum score required for financial literacy. Worse still, a broader survey (covering 140 countries) conducted by S&P in 2014 showed that globally, only one in three adults has financial skills. In our country, there has been an awareness for several years now of the importance of financial education. It is in this sense that we have set up in 2013, in collaboration with the entire financial and educational ecosystem, a dedicated institution, the Moroccan Foundation for Financial Education. Thanks to the cooperation of all stakeholders, it already has encouraging achievements for the benefit of young people, the self-employed, and several segments of the population, especially women and rural people. It is now one of the cross-cutting pillars on which the national financial inclusion strategy that Bank Al-Maghrib and the Ministry of Finance have finalized and whose implementation has started since the beginning of this year is based. It aims to reduce the deficit and reduce inequalities for the benefit of young people, women and the rural population. The panel scheduled for the second session of this meeting will provide further information on this subject. Ladies and gentlemen As we all know, technological innovations in the financial sector have been booming in recent years. They are revolutionizing the landscape, expanding products and services, improving their quality and accessibility, and reducing costs. They are transforming customer relations, payment methods as well as financing and transfer methods. Today, they make it possible to accelerate financial inclusion and extend it to the most fragile segments of the productive fabric and to the most disadvantaged sections of the population thanks to the wide coverage of mobile networks and internet penetration. As part of this new dynamic, we have, together with the National Telecommunications Regulatory Agency and other stakeholders, developed for more than 2 years an interoperable and real-time national mobile payment solution. The aim is not only to diversify the offer of means of payment, but above all to extend access to financial services to the majority of the population. Today, while the potential of this new solution is very tangible, with nearly 380 thousand electronic wallets declared, its effective use stumbles in particular on the adhesion of the network of traders. New technologies also offer multiple opportunities for the development of financial education on a large scale. Digital platforms, mobile applications, online educational videos or simulators are all effective tools to help an increasingly connected population understand the basics of financial education. It is in this sense that, since its first strategic plan, the Moroccan Foundation for Financial Education has placed digital as a leading channel for the dissemination of its educational content and the monitoring of the progress of the deployment of its actions. That said, we should not forget that the digital revolution also involves multiple risks that are often difficult to prevent and control. Despite the multiplicity of studies, its implications are still largely unknown. This observation led the World Bank and the IMF to develop last year the Bali Fintech Agenda, a set of general principles to guide everyone's action to face this revolution. In this context, we have, as a company and as a regulator of the banking sector, initiated our own digital transformation and we have erected it as one of the main axes of our 2019-2023 strategic plan. In this context, last March, in collaboration with the IMF, we organized a regional conference at which several countries came to share their experiences. We have made an appointment with the Fund to reorganize next year a new edition of this conference in the wake of the preparations for the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank to be held in 2021 in Marrakech. It will be dedicated to monitoring the implementation of the Bali Agenda in our region. Ladies and gentlemen In a difficult situation such as the one we are currently experiencing, the development of savings should not be relegated to the background in the agendas of public policies and financial institutions. This is a sine qua non for mobilizing the resources needed to finance the economy as a whole and its often excluded components, including young entrepreneurs and small businesses. Our wish, as co-organizer, is that our debates today will make a valuable advance to this project, which is one of the essential dimensions of the more global one in favor of a new model of development that is more efficient and more inclusive, as his Majesty the King wishes. Thank you for your attention.

Les nouvelles technologies offrent, par ailleurs, de multiples possibilit<8e>s pour le d<8e>veloppement de lducation financi<8f>re <88> grande <8e>chelle. Les plateformes digitales, les applications mobiles, les vid<8e>os p<8e>dagogiques en ligne ou encore les simulateurs sont autant d<d5>outils efficaces pour faire comprendre les notions de base de lducation financi<8f>re <88> une population de plus en plus connect<8e>e.
