Title: At the 14th meeting of the National Currency and Savings Council
text: Speech by the Governor of Bank Al- Maghrib 14th meeting of the National Council of money and savings 7 April 2005 Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, I would like to tell you how pleased I am to welcome you today to Bank Al-Maghrib for the fourteenth meeting of the National Currency and Savings Council. Our meeting today will probably be the last of this body under the current Banking Act. The speech of the Minister of Finance and the documents distributed to you specify the developments in the international environment and the performance of our economy in 2004. Therefore, my intervention will focus mainly on the conduct of monetary policy, its impact on the national economy and on reforms aimed at improving the functioning of the system. financial and the financing of the economy. The major developments in the world economy in 2004 were characterized by high volatility in the main currencies, a rapid increase in the prices of raw materials, especially oil, and sluggish growth in the Eurozone, Morocco's main economic partner. Despite these generally unfavourable factors for Morocco, macroeconomic stability has been preserved. The contribution of monetary policy to this good outcome has been essential. For the year 2004, and as announced at the last meeting of the CNME, Bank Al-Maghrib had set a monetary standard by reference to the M1 aggregate between 6.5% and 7.5%. As for the sources of money creation, the increase in net foreign assets was expected to reach 10 billion dirhams, an increase of 7.8%. The increase in loans to the economy, necessary to support economic growth, had been set at 20.5 billion, an increase of 8.3%. Under these conditions, a reduction in claims on the Treasury of 6 billionor 7.6 percenthad been scheduled. At the end of the past year, currency aggregates recorded growth of 7.8% for M3 and 9.8% for M1. The overshoot of the monetary norm adopted at the beginning of the year is mainly the result of a greater than expected strengthening of external assets, and an arbitrage in favour of the constitution of sight assets in a context marked by a fall in interest rates. Indeed, while the increase in domestic credit has generally been in line with what has been programmed, both for loans to the economy and for claims on the State, the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves has proved to be much higher than expected. This is the result of substantial tourism receipts and transfers from Moroccans living abroad, as well as significant foreign investment flows, particularly under the privatization of Maroc Telecom. These factors explain the persistence of a level of excess liquidity, a phenomenon that has characterized the national economy since 1999. In order to prevent the effect of this excess liquidity on inflation, Bank Al-Maghrib has adapted the monetary policy framework. This system, which entered into force in January 2004, is structured around the weekly 7-day liquidity recovery instruments at variable rates and the 24-hour deposit facility at the rate of 2.25%, which thus constitutes a floor for interbank interest rates. It should be noted that these sterilization interventions, as well as the remuneration of the assets of the Hassan II Fund for Economic and Social Development, had a high cost for Bank Al-Maghrib, of about 700 million Dirhams in 2004. These interventions have contributed, crucially, to the continued decline in overall interest rates. Indeed, the weighted average rate observed on the money market fell by about 80 basis points to 2.40% in 2004. In this context, bond yields have also fallen. However, this movement has generally not been reflected in the lending interest rates applied by banks to companies, especially SMEs/ SMIs. In addition, monetary policy has helped to keep the inflation rate below the 2% limit taken into account at the beginning of the year for setting the monetary norm. The efforts required for the proper conduct of monetary policy will continue in 2005. That is why, at the end of 2004, we made a technical adjustment to the monetary policy framework aimed mainly at simplifying and harmonising the procedures for central bank intervention in the money market. It is a question of creating a corridor around the key rate, giving primacy to 7-day tenders, the main channel for injecting or withdrawing liquidity. Regarding the outlook for 2005, Bank Al-Maghrib forecasts a real GDP growth rate of 2.8%; this is based on an agricultural value added down by 1.4% and a non-agricultural GDP growth rate of 3.6%. In order to ensure adequate financing of the economy while limiting the rise in prices to a rate of less than 2%, the reference value for the increase in M1 should again be set in a range of 6.5% to 7.5%. In this context, a reduction in liquidity, at the end of 2005, is planned for an amount of 4.5 billion Dirhams. This objective is based on the assumption of a strengthening of net foreign assets of 10 billion dirhams and an increase in loans to the economy of the order of 23 billion dirhams. The achievement of the reference standard requires a reduction in claims on the Treasury of about 7 billion Dirhams. In addition to allocating part of the privatization revenues to the account of the Hassan II Fund for Economic and Social Development, achieving this objective requires an improvement in the Treasury's net position vis-a-vis the banking system. Indeed, the conduct of monetary policy will be all the easier if fiscal policy contributes to it in a coordinated manner. I would also like to stress that we support the Government's efforts to reduce the budget deficit to a level consistent with the international standard in this area in the medium term. A review of international experience reveals that macroeconomic stability is an essential foundation for rapid economic and social development. This was recalled by the Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Mr. de Rato, during his visit to Morocco on February 28. While welcoming Morocco's efforts, particularly in the areas of monetary policy and macroeconomic stability, the Managing Director of the IMF stressed that certain fragilities needed to be given special attention in order to accelerate growth and job creation, whether at the fiscal level or in structural reforms. It welcomed the provisions introduced by the Government regarding the independence of the Central Bank and recalled the need to strengthen the soundness of the financial system. Finally, he focused on the level of outstanding debts. It is on the basis of further macroeconomic stability and a sound financial system that the continuation of the process of opening up the economy to the outside world, in particular through greater flexibility in the exchange rate regime, can be carried out smoothly. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, As the Minister of Finance pointed out, the Central Bank will enjoy a very wide autonomy in monetary policy and in the field of banking supervision, under the provisions of its new statutes and those of the banking law. In return, this autonomy requires it to meet reinforced governance and communication requirements. Thus, the Central Bank's monetary policy decisions will now be sanctioned by communiques. This good practice has already been adopted with the publication of a communique at the end of the last two meetings of the Bank's Board. Bank Al-Maghrib will also have to refrain from granting credit to the public sector, submit its accounts to an external audit, no longer participate in the capital and the administrative and management bodies of the institutions under its control, and publish an annual report on banking supervision. In order to be able to carry out its tasks properly and meet the requirements of the new legislation, Bank Al-Maghrib has upgraded its structures and management methods. It has thus adopted a strategic plan covering the period 2004-2006, with a view to modernizing its organization and operation, and has adopted appropriate mechanisms for the prevention and control of risks, and for the search for optimization and quality in its management. In the same way, it must improve its capacity for analysis and forecasting at the level of international standards. In consultation with the international financial institutions and our other partners, we have already taken action to develop our technical capacity to forecast the evolution of monetary aggregates and prices and to set the intermediate objectives of monetary policy. To support its modernization plan, the Bank has strengthened its human potential through the recruitment of appropriate skills and the adoption of structuring actions. These include the establishment of an IT master plan and a human resources master plan, the development of procedures manuals and the adoption of a code of ethics. This upgrade became all the more urgent as the Central Bank, like other banking supervisors abroad, is called upon to take on major new challenges, including the application of the new Basel Capital Adequacy Agreement and the transposition of international accounting standards to the banking sector. The implementation of Basel II implies an in-depth reform of risk management and coverage. It requires both the supervisory authority and the banks to rethink their organization and their information systems while mobilizing significant resources and adequate skills. Nevertheless, these requirements and the costs involved should be offset by the expected positive impacts in terms of risk selection and management, governance and transparency in financial reporting. The transposition of the new Agreement to Morocco will be based on a timetable whose priorities have been drawn up, in consultation with the profession, whose resolute commitment to complete this project I would like to welcome. The approach adopted is intended to be progressive and incentive and takes into account both the reality and the structure of the Moroccan banking system. With this in mind, priority must be given to accelerating the consolidation of the public financial centre and repositioning it in a rapidly changing financial landscape, to enable it to assume its role, particularly in the development of banking, which remains, as the Minister of Finance has just pointed out, below our expectations. In the same way, the consumer credit sector needs special attention. Indeed, the financial situation of several companies operating in this sector is weakening from year to year, under the combined effect of the fall in the maximum rate of conventional interest, the increase in the cost of credit risk and the importance of structural costs. Therefore, urgent measures must be taken to review the methods of calculating this rate, which no longer seem to be adapted to the current context. Having said that, it seems to me that we will not be able to avoid restructuring this sector. With regard to the financial institutions that will be subject to the new banking law, Bank Al-Maghrib has already initiated, with each of them, a consultation process; the objective being to examine the regulatory provisions applicable to them, to deepen the knowledge of their activities and their risks and to get them to take the necessary accounting, governance and internal control measures quickly. In addition, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), mandated by Bank Al-Maghrib to study the feasibility of a central balance sheet, recommended relying on the database managed by the Moroccan Office for Intellectual and Commercial Property (OMPIC), which requires a partnership between OMPIC, Bank Al-Maghrib and the banking profession. In the same spirit, in order to enable Bank Al-Maghrib's Central Risk Department to efficiently ensure its role as a credit risk management tool, I urge all credit institutions to be more diligent in the timely transmission of information and more vigilant with regard to the quality of the information communicated. Given the various customer databases that are already in place (Central Payment Incident Service, Central Risk Service, APSF Risk Assessment Assistance Service), or that are in the process of being developed (GPBM Customer Information Centre, Risk Centre for Microcredit Associations), it is important to ensure synergy between these different tools by adopting a common identifier for companies. To complete the various measures I have just mentioned, it seems essential to me that the implementation of the recommendations of the national steering committee on the "Report on compliance with standards and codes", known as ROSC, on auditing and accounting standards, be initiated as soon as possible. A significant backlog has accumulated and it is necessary for all parties concerned to make up for it. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, This improvement in the quality of financial and accounting information is likely to promote a more efficient dissemination of monetary policy impulses, particularly in favour of SMEs. However, the efficiency of monetary policy also remains dependent on the convergence of actions at the level of other components of economic policy, the business environment, as well as the efforts of SMEs to improve the quality of financial reporting. To this end, the Central Bank acts together with other public and private partners to contribute to the development of an investment-friendly environment. I would like to recall here the actions carried out by Bank Al-Maghrib jointly with the Ministries of Finance and Justice as well as the banking profession. The objective of this consultation is to provide solutions to the problems related to the recovery of outstanding debts, the realization of guarantees, garnishments and judicial reorganization of companies in difficulty. Bank debts on companies in receivership relate to 436 companies on an estimated amount of three and a half billion Dirhams, according to the statements provided by the GPBM. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Minister of Justice and his departments for the spirit of consultation and cooperation that drives them and for their willingness to implement the conclusions reached by mutual agreement. It also remains highly desirable and urgent to achieve convergence between the tax rules and the accounting rules applicable to the banking sector, in particular with regard to provisions for overdue debts. Discussions between the Ministry of Finance, Bank Al-Maghrib and the banks are already under way and augur well for conclusions. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, Weak export performance, in a global context marked by increasing competitive pressures and a erosion of Morocco's market shares , is another serious concern. We invited the GPBM to examine this issue through a global approach. Therefore, I can only support the dialogue that has been established between the GPBM and the Moroccan Association of Exporters (ASMEX), and indicate that we remain involved in everything that can allow our exports to find very quickly their performances of the 80s. The new direction taken by the GPBM for its rapprochement with the professional organizations; such as ASMEX, the National Federation of SMEs/SMIs and the Federation of Marine Industries and the Offshore Fishing Association, can only collect our appui. Bank Al-Maghrib therefore remains determined to make its contribution to bringing to a conclusion the conclusions of the dialogues undertaken. We also asked the GPBM to conduct an in-depth study on the development of long-term savings; Essentialcomponent of balanced financing of the needs of the economy on a sound basis. It is also important that savings products are remunerated at positive interest rates in real terms. While the recent decision of the Minister of Finance to revise the method of calculating the rates applicable to accounts on carnets has made it possible to improve their remuneration, it is important to also look at the remuneration of the booklets of the National Savings Bank. Dear Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, The Central Bank has defined a strategy of presence of place and is refocusing its network with a view to developing a policy of proximity with economic operators, to which I invite them, through their associations present here, to associate. We believe that this is a useful approach, both for Bank Al-Maghrib to enable it to better monitor the business climate and develop a culture of communication, and for economic operators who will thus have better access to our services. On payment systems, the shared objective of the banking profession and Bank Al-Maghrib is to improve their credibility, efficiency and security to bring them into line with international standards. For example, Bank Al-Maghrib, in collaboration with the Ministry of Justice and the GPBM, has recently embarked on a campaign to strengthen the credibility of the cheque as a means of payment. In parallel, Bank Al-Maghrib has established an action plan for the modernization of payment systems, in particular by extending telecompensation, both geographically and in terms of the different values exchanged, and through the development of a large-amount settlement system. One year after the entry into force of the Bank Al-Maghrib Circular on the Duty of Vigilance, the efforts made by banking institutions to preserve their integrity and prevent their networks from being used for illicit purposes should be highlighted. The establishment of such a system, which is inspired by the recommendations of the Basel Committee, is an extension of efforts to bring our regulatory framework into line with international standards. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, Important progress has been made through active and responsible consultation. The legal and regulatory framework applicable to the financial sector today meets the highest international standards in terms of prudential standards and methodologies for the management of risks. Of course, together we must constantly adapt it. Efforts in this direction will continue in 2005, in particular with regard to the Money Laundering Act and the harmonization of legal provisions on means of payment. We are challenged by the evolution of globalization and the increasing trade opening of our economy. To meet this challenge and maintain a virtuous dynamic, we must rely on an independent monetary policy that displays its objectives in full transparency, a prudent budgetary policy that preserves macroeconomic balances, and economic operators contributing as a force of proposal to the success of our structural policies. At the same time, our consultation processes must be deepened, in the same way as the active dialogue already under way between the Government and Bank Al-Maghrib, the GPBM and Bank Al-Maghrib, and the GPBM and professional associations. It is only under these conditions that Morocco will be able to make a qualitative leap and succeed as soon as possible in its integration into a rapidly changing world economy.

Title: At the conference of the African Confederation of Internal Auditors
text: CONFERENCE OF THE AFRICAN CONFEDERATION OF INTERNAL AUDITORS Casablanca, 27 and 28 June 2018 ----------------------------------- SPEECH BY MR. WALI --------------------------- Mr. President of IIA Global Mr. President of the African Federation of Internal Auditors Mr. President of the Francophone Union of Internal Audit Mr. President of the Institute of Internal Auditors of Morocco Ladies and gentlemen I am particularly pleased to address the participants of the 5th conference of the African Confederation of Internal Auditors organized under the theme: "Internal Audit and Integrated Approaches to Governance and Performance". I welcome all those who have kindly taken part in this event, in particular, those from abroad and among them our African friends. The organization of this conference in Morocco gives me the opportunity to underline the importance I attach to the internal audit function, which is a key element of good governance, essential for the sound conduct of activities, particularly in the banking and financial sector. The last international financial crisis demonstrated that good governance is a real challenge for financial and economic stability. It requires credit institutions to have a system of powers and checks and balances, responsibilities and accountabilities, not only at the level of the board of directors but also at the level of management and the risk management, compliance and internal audit functions. In this context, Bank Al-Maghrib, which had issued a circular in 2001 requiring credit institutions to adopt a sound internal control framework, revised these regulatory texts in 2007 and then in 2014, to take into account the evolution of the Basel Committee's standards after the crisis and further consolidate the risk governance framework. At a global level, the regulatory framework for banking governance in Morocco defines the roles, composition and operating procedures of administrative and management bodies. It also sets out expectations of the key bodies that assist these bodies, in particular the audit committee, the compliance function, the risk management function, the ongoing control function and the internal audit function. It is in this context that the Internal Audit function is a cornerstone of the governance system, ensuring periodic and independent control of the management body. It constitutes the 3rd line of defense of the internal control system and has the role of providing the administrative body, through the Audit Committee that emanates from it, with an assurance as to the effectiveness of the governance processes, risk management and the different levels of control. It also periodically evaluates the financial communication process, internal and regulatory reporting as well as the information system. To strengthen its independence, the appointment of the head of this function is approved by the Board of Directors or the Audit Committee. Also, the internal audit function interacts closely with the latter. It shall submit the audit plan to the Commission, report regularly on the performance of its tasks and inform it of any major anomaly likely to have an impact onthe institution. At the operational level, the internal audit function must have at all times and as a priority, the resources, expertise and technical means necessary for its proper functioning. In the context of banking groups, the scope of intervention of the internal audit function is to be expanded to cover financial and non-financial subsidiaries, both in Morocco and abroad, in coordination with the competent bodies of these subsidiaries. Thus, as you can see, Bank Al-Maghrib, as a supervisory authority, attaches great importance to the effectiveness of the internal audit function within credit institutions, not only because it is essential for their safety and soundness but also because it contributes to the maintenance of an efficient banking supervision process. Indeed, a sound governance framework allows the supervisory authority to rely more on the Bank's internal governance processes and to reduce its need for intervention as a prudential authority. Ladies and gentlemen Aware that it is important for a central bank, as a regulator, to be at the state of the art in terms of governance, by first imposing on itself what is required of the bodies it controls, I would like to dwell here on the internal audit function within Bank Al-Maghrib. Title: At the International Days of Macroeconomics and Finance
text: Speech by the Director General TheLogo International Days of Macroeconomics and Finance Rabat 23-24 April 2018 Honourable guests and speakers Dear members of the Organizing Committee Dear professors and researchers Colleagues Let me first of all welcome you to the Bank Al-Maghrib Vocational Training Center, on the occasion of this new edition of the International Days of Macroeconomics and Finance that Bank Al-Maghrib is organizing for the third consecutive year in collaboration with its partners from the University of Cadi-Ayyad and the University of Basel. I would also like to express my deep thanks to our partners and distinguished speakers for agreeing to participate in this conference. Year after year, this annual meeting brings together more and more participants and is a privileged place for exchange between decision-makers and researchers. Such a diverse and distinguished audience here testifies to the interest of the research and academic community, both nationally and internationally, in this event and the topics it covers. Today, a dozen countries are represented in this international seminar: Australia, England, United States of America, France, Greece, Italy, Mexico, Morocco, Switzerland, Tunisia. The quality of the contributions submitted by the researchers present here and which will be the subject of presentation and debate from this afternoon, leaves no doubt as to the growing interest aroused by this conference. The ambition shared by all the organizers is that this event continues to be a most important event for the promotion of scientific research in Morocco. Through this meeting, we wish to stimulate debate, enrich reflections and above all bring practical recommendations around economic and financial topics of interest to our country. Today's conference is part of that perspective. It focuses on the theme "Finance for growth". The choice of this subject is motivated by the evolution of the international and national context: Thus, the global economic and financial spheres are just beginning to recover from the financial crisis of 2007-2008 and the ensuing economic crisis. The lessons learned from these crises continue to challenge us in particular on the nature of the links between finance and economic growth and on the issue of reforms aimed at controlling systemic financial risks. In terms of the national context, while the financial system has not been directly affected by the international financial crisis, it has been affected through real channels. Let me remind you that economic growth Non-agricultural has slowed down following the crisis and is on average around 3% over the last five years compared to almost 5% between 2001-2008. This level of growth does not make it possible to absorb unemployment, particularly among young people, which remains very high. Also, the question of an inclusive and sustainable economic development model in Morocco is the subject of several debates, which also leads to reflection on the role of the financial system in the dynamics of economic growth, and in particular on the allocation of financial resources and policies to facilitate the financing of companies and in particular MSMEs. Ladies and gentlemen An overview of the academic literature suggests significant divergences in the importance of financial systems for growth. On the one hand, some illustrious academics, such as the 1995 Nobel Prize in Economics, Robert Lucas, believe that the role of finance has been excessively amplified when it comes to promoting economic growth. From this point of view, the financial offer is only an automatic response to the needs expressed by companies in terms of financing and "where companies advance, finance is content to follow". Another economic current remains firmly convinced that the financial system is vital for economic development. When sufficiently sophisticated, it increases the efficiency of economic financing decisions and thus contributes to a better allocation of resources and support for growth. In addition, according to this trend, in sectors marked by a strong asymmetry of information, financial intermediation seems quite designated to address adverse selection and moral hazard issues and reduce transaction costs between lenders and borrowers. Thanks to their expertise, financial actors are better positioned to distinguish between good and bad investment projects and to properly manage individuals' savings. Finally, economists in this current point to the ability of the financial system to innovate in terms of hedging against different categories of risks, which is likely to strengthen the resilience of economies. Ladies and gentlemen Today, the debate on the nature of the links between finance and growth remains topical and research work continues to reconcile these two antagonistic currents. In practice, international experience, particularly that of developing countries, has shown that economies with developed financial systems have a proven comparative advantage. The latter is essential for the emergence and development of innovative enterprises that are at the origin of the structural transformation of the economy and the dynamism of long-term growth. In an international context marked by globalization and the race for innovation, the deepening of the financial system is therefore essential for the preservation of competitiveness. Nevertheless, the lessons of financial crises have shown that globalization and the increasing integration of financial markets can have profoundly adverse effects on growth and employment. Honourable guests, As for Morocco, the policies and measures undertaken by the public authorities in recent decades have enabled the Moroccan financial system to play a leading role in financing the economy and to position itself at the forefront of the countries of the MENA region. However, the experience of the last decade challenges us. After a phase of rapid credit growth of 16% on average between 2005-2011, the financing of the economy by the banking system slowed down to around 3% on average between 2012-2017, this slowdown would be explained by factors related to both the demand and supply of credit. As a result, Bank Al-Maghrib has conducted an accommodative monetary policy and has put in place specific arrangements to support SME financing. For its part, the government has strengthened the guarantee systems for bank loans benefiting SMEs and the accompanying measures for this category of companies. In parallel and with the aim of strengthening the resilience of the Moroccan banking and financial system in the face of shocks, prudential regulation applicable to banks has been strengthened to converge towards Bale 3 standards and a macroprudential supervisory framework has been put in place to control systemic risks. Ladies and gentlemen During this morning, we will listen with great interest to the interventions of our academic partners, financial experts and university professors who will undoubtedly enrich the ongoing reflections on the issues of financing the economy.

Title: At the International Days of Macroeconomics and Finance in Marrakech
text: Speech by the Director General International Days of Macroeconomics and Finance Marrakech 15-16 May 2017 Honourable guests and speakers Dear members of the Organizing Committee Dear Professors, Researchers and Students Colleagues It is a real pleasure for me to participate in the opening of this 2nd edition of the International Days of Macroeconomics and Finance, organized by BANK AI-Maghrib jointly with Cadi Ayyad University and the University of Basel on the theme "flexibilization of the exchange rate regime, inflation targeting and capital account liberalization. The 1st edition was organized in May 2016 with the theme "The new monetary consensus in the face of the financial crisis", and was attended by about fifty researchers and academics. Today, we are about 200 participants in this conference representing the academic and research community, ministerial departments, central banks and international _institutions, professionals from the economic fabric. and the financial sector, as well as the media. As for the 2nd day of this event to be held tomorrow at Cadi Ayyad University, it will see the presentation of the work of 16 researchers from Germany, France, Morocco, Switzerland, Tunisia and Turkey. Such a large and distinguished audience testifies to the interest shown by the research and academic community in this event and the topics it covers. Our wish, shared by all the organizers, is that this event be a most important annual meeting for the promotion of scientific research around economic and financial topics of interest to our country. Bank AI-Maghrib places particular emphasis on research in relation to its fundamental missions on monetary policy and financial stability and more generally, in relation to public policies. In this context, it has established relations with the research departments of several central banks and financial institutions and seeks to consolidate its openness to the academic and research world by organizing seminars and conferences and developing cooperation with partners Academic. This conference fits perfectly into this orientation. The choice of the theme that will be debated during this day is not fortuitous. As you know, the Moroccan authorities recently announced the decision to make the exchange rate regime more flexible. Following this announcement, the Ministry of Finance and Bank AI-Maghrib have launched a large-scale communication targeting several segments including banks, financial market players, economic operators, public institutions, universities and the general public, with a view to informing about the motivations for this reform, the modalities of its implementation, its implications and the necessary prerequisites for a successful transition. This reform is thus the subject of broad public debates sometimes expressing divergent points of view and analysis. I believe that this conference, which brings together eminent experts from the academic and professional world, is likely to contribute to enriching these debates and examining on a scientific basis the reform that Morocco wishes to carry out. During this morning, these experts will talk to us about international experiences and theoretical lessons on the flexibilization of the exchange rate regime and the adoption of inflation targeting. The 2nd session of the day will see the presentation of the reform project by officials of the MEF, BAM and THE CB. For my part, I would like to highlight in my speech three points which seem to me to be important in the debates around the flexibilization of our exchange rate regime: : The 1st concerns the Central Bank: the reforms and projects carried out over the last decade have enabled this institution to rise to the best practices of the BCs. Thus, in 2006, it was granted institutional and operational independence, enabling it to free itself from any political influence in the conduct of its fundamental tasks, in particular monetary policy. At the same time, the Bank has strengthened its analytical and forecasting capabilities, strengthening its human skills and implementing high-performance models of macroeconomic projections and simulations. These tools and arrangements, which are tailored to the specificities of our economy, help the BC make informed decisions on monetary policy and financial stability. In order to communicate its decisions, the Bank has increased its transparency through the deployment of a wide range of information media such as the Policy Report. monetary, and the Financial Stability Report, and the organisation of meetings with economic operators and the media In sum, and thanks to these efforts, Morocco has been ranked by the IMF among the countries adopting a monetary policy of anchoring the exchange rate with an analytical framework close to that of inflation targeting. !The 2nd point concerns the macroeconomic and financial framework: the many structural reforms carried out by Morocco in recent years have made it possible to strengthen the resilience of the economy. As a result, economic fundamentals are sound both fiscally and in terms of external accounts and inflation. On the other hand, Morocco has been part of a process of trade and financial openness in recent decades that is increasingly marked in connection with the desire to strengthen the integration of our economy on a global scale. In this sense, a series of free trade agreements have been concluded with several countries and economic zones and a gradual liberalization of exchange regulations has been carried out. As a result, the rate of openness of the economy integrating goods and services has increased significantly over the last fifteen years, from 60% of GDP to about 80%. In the same vein, Morocco, driven by the ambition to become a regional financial hub, launched a few years ago the structuring project of Casablanca Finance City which was awarded in the latest ranking of the Global Financial Centers Index the first place in Africa. This opening of Morocco to the international market is also supported by the domestic financial sector and particularly banking, whose strength and resilience have been attested by the conclusion of the latest mission of the FSAP (The Financial Sector) Assessment Program) carried out by the WB and the IMF. Moroccan banks are thus present in about thirty countries and recently this dynamic has expanded to the insurance sector and specialized financial institutions. !As for the 3rd and final point I would like to make, it concerns the current exchange rate regime and its reform. Admittedly, the current fixed exchange rate regime has its advantages and has contributed to the moderateinflation experienced by Morocco. However, the latest economic and financial crisis has highlighted some vulnerabilities related to this regime. In an international context marked by the persistence of economic and financial uncertainties, our economy is not immune to a global demand shock or raw material prices that could deteriorate internal and external balances. By way of example, I recall that following the double monetary and commodity shock experienced by Morocco in the early 80s, the economic situation deteriorated sharply with record twin deficit levels and a drying up of foreign exchange reserves, which led the authorities to carry out a significant devaluation of the national currency and to submit to the Structural Adjustment Plan prescribed by the IMF with socio-economic consequences. very heavy. The Moroccan authorities have thus learned from past experiences. They have conducted several studies and studies in recent years, whose conclusions, supported by several partners, such as the IMF and central banks, show: 1-that the changes in the Moroccan economy require the reform of the exchange rate regime has even consolidated the competitiveness and resilience of our economy. 2-The conditions are right and the timing is right to start a gradual transition to a more flexible exchange rate regime. I am convinced that the programme of this conference, which will confront this reform with international experiences, will not fail to give rise to interactive debates between academics and national and international experts present here, whom I would like to thank warmly for accepting our invitation. Thank you for your attention.

Title: International Seminar on Greening Africa's Financial System
text: Global Green Finance Leadership Program International Seminar on Greening Africa's Financial System -------- Casablanca, June 25 to 27, 2019 -------- Good morning everybody, It is a real pleasure for me today to take part in the opening session of this 4th event of the Global Green Finance Leadership Program (GGFLP), which Morocco is honored to host. First of all, I would like to greet the representatives of this program present today and to recognize the initiatives undertaken since its launch. I particularly want to welcome Dr Ma Jun, the well known green finance international expert. Today I want to speak about some climate challenges of our continent, the role of central banks and ongoing climate policies in Morocco. It is now widely recognized that if global warming is not contained below a certain threshold, our planet and its ecosystems will face an irreversible impact. In fact, according to a study of the OECD, global warming would cause a decline of the world GDP by 1.0 to 3.3 percent by 2060, and by 10 percent by the end of this century. Africa, despite its small contribution to greenhouse gas emissions, is largely threatened by climate change impacts due to its geographical characteristics. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), climate change could reduce GDP across Africa by 2 to 4 percent by 2040 and by 10 to 25 percent by the end of the century. To face this issue, huge investments are necessary to support the ecological transition of the continent and to guarantee the countriesd5 respect of their commitments to reduce their carbon footprint. Despite the promises made under the Paris Agreement to provide financial support to match these commitments, capital flows to the African continent remain lower than 4.5 percent of annual global flows, according to the African development bank. Most of the investments benefiting Africa are intended to finance climate risk mitigation policies, particularly renewable energy programs. At the same time, it should be noted that the needs of financing adaptation policies are more important and should be covered by large investments, given their dependence of African countries on the agricultural sector, the concentration of economic activities along the coastal areas, and the increasing frequency of natural disasters. As for Morocco, it has undertaken, for several decades now, a series of initiatives contributing to climate resilience and environmental protection. Among these is the dam policy carried out since the 60s as part of the National water strategy, and the Green Morocco Plan, launched in 2008 with the aim of making the agricultural sector a lever for sustainable development. In the energy sector, Morocco has put in place a vast solar and wind energy development program, aiming to reach a 52 percent energy mix by 2030, and to also reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 42 percent. To support these policies, the Moroccan authorities consider the implementation of an eco-tax and a suitable financing policy as important levers for the greening the national economy. In recent years, central banks in general have started measuring the impact of global warming on the financial sector. The Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for the greening of the financial sector (NGFS), created in December 2017 by eight founding central banks, at the initiative of the Banque de France, is proof that financial authorities are now aware of the urgency for action and of their important role in greening the financial system. The NGFS is a knowledge-sharing platform which aims to provide global recommendations to facilitate the financial sectord5s contribution to the implementation of the Paris agreement and to encourage central banks, supervisors and financial institutions to develop climate and environmental risk management practices. In this context, the first report of the NGFS, published in April, called central banks and regulators to improve their understanding of the structural changes affecting the financial system and the economy, and to carry out their fundamental missions with regard to price and financial stability. It also recognized that climate-related risks are a source of financial risks which could threaten financial stability. As such, the report urged central banks and supervisors to start integrating climate-related risks into their micro and macro prudential supervision, incorporating sustainability factors in their investment policies, fostering capacity building of different stakeholders and developing their understanding of this issue. The NGFS encourages policy makers to act together in order to facilitate green finance development, to provide reliable and comprehensive climate data, and to develop taxonomy of sustainable economic activities. Besides, the NGFS highlights the importance of setting up an internationally consistent climate and environmental disclosure framework and encourages large firms and financial institutions to publish financial information related to climate risk in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures d0 TCFD). By joining the NGFS, in April 2018, Bank Al-Maghrib has translated its will to speed up its actions aiming to integrate climate issues in the banking ecosystem and to promote orderly development of green finance. In this vein, I would like to recall that during the COP 22, which took place in Marrakech in 2016, the Central Bank coordinated with other regulators and financial institutions in drawing up a roadmap to better address sustainable development challenges. Adoption of this roadmap generated an ongoing dialogue between financial sector regulators and financial institutions as well as the organisation of several forums to raise awareness and exchange experiences. As a result, many actions have been achieved: financial institutions developed green financing offers, a public guarantee of green financing for SMEs was established and Green bond issues were carried out by public and private institutions. Such initiatives represent a promising start for a smooth transition to a green financial ecosystem. Therefore, new steps are to be taken by Central Bank by drawing up a regulatory directive laying down principles and provisions aimed to define our expectations for banks and to establish best practices regarding their governance , risk management, disclosure of financial information related climate risk and customers awareness. However, in Morocco, as at the African level, compliance with the commitments made under the Paris Agreement is facing many challenges, mainly the issue of financing. Considering its crucial role, the financial sector needs to be creative to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. Initiatives that have emerged in recent years need to be reinforced, just as continent-wide financial markets need to attract private investments to Africa. In this sense, green finance can only be beneficial given the new opportunities the emergence of new markets and new technological innovations presents. However, sustained regional and international cooperation is also necessary if we want to rise to our respective missions in response to global climate change. Besides, the greening of finance in Africa also requires greater collaboration with scientists and researchers as well as with multilateral development institutions such as the World Bank, African development bank or EBRD. Morocco has taken many cooperation initiatives with several countries of the continent. Among these, I would especially like to highlight the initiative for the Adaptation of African Agriculture (AAA) that the Kingdom launched at COP 22 with the aim of reducing the risks of African agriculture to climate change. This initiative stems from the finding that the stakes of African agriculture are rarely taken into account in international negotiations on climate change and in the allocation of climate funds. As a member of the NGFS, Bank Al-Maghrib is firmly committed to developing exchange and experience-sharing concerning green finance and climate resilience. We are considering that the cooperation mechanisms established with some individual African central banks and within the The Association of African central banks), as important levers that should be built around these issues. In the same vein, we encourage our banks present in Africa, throughout 27 countries to deploy in the future their green finance policies. To conclude, I would like to wish a complete success to this event, which will surely contribute to reflections and debate around the issues of a resilient and sustainable African economy.

Title: At the second meeting of the National Credit and Savings Council on July 15, 2008, RabatJou
text: Address by the Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib at the second meeting of the National Credit and Savings Council 15 July 2008 Rabat Dear Minister, Dear Secretaries General, Dear Chief Executive Officers, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a real pleasure for me to welcome you today to Bank Al- Maghrib for the second meeting of the National Credit and Credit Council Savings. On this occasion and on your behalf, I would like to address a special mention to the Minister of the Economy and Finance, in his capacity as new President and to others new members. Their great experience will, I am sure, contribute to enrich our debates on the issues we will have to deal with in the of this Council. I would also like to pay tribute to Mr. Fathallah Oualalou who participated in the work of this council for ten years years and whose contributions have always been of high quality. My intervention will focus on the progress made since our last meeting in the process of formulating and implementing monetary policy, in the context of the mission of price stability conferred on Bank Al-Maghrib by its statute. I will also discuss with you recent developments in the activity and results of the banking sector but also the main measures taken to strengthen its regulatory framework, which are essential for the preservation of the soundness and stability of the national financial system. I would also like to discuss the progress made in terms of payment systems and means, as well as those relating to the relationships that banks have with their customers. Finally, I would like to focus on the major challenges that need to be addressed, so that our financial system can increase its efficiency in financing the national economy and become a reference centre at regional level. Dear Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, As you know, Bank Al-Maghrib is responsible for ensuring, as a matter of priority, price stability in the medium term, which is the best contribution a central bank can make to the economy. In this context, the Bank is resolutely and continuing its efforts to develop its capacity to analyse monetary policy, monitor and forecast economic activity and inflation, as well as macroeconomic modelling and research on monetary policy transmission channels. Many actions have been carried out, and will continue to be carried out, to strengthen the information and data collection system for better monitoring of the financial and real spheres. Surveys are thus regularly conducted: quarterly survey on lending interest rates, annual survey on credit granting conditions and forecasts, which from this year will be semi-annual, and monthly business survey in industry. In particular, the Bank closely monitors credit developments by analysing these data by economic object, sector of activity, customer segment, as well as by group of clients with capital links. Contacts are also underway with our external partners to expand the Bank's system for collecting data on wages and real estate asset prices, in particular. At the same time, Bank Al-Maghrib continues to work to deepen the transparency of the monetary policy decision-making, implementation and evaluation process. In this sense, the Bank has set out to improve the content and frequency of its communication, with explicit commitments on the deadlines for the dissemination of its publications, justifying its ex ante decisions and explaining the results of ex post monetary policy. For example, the Monetary Policy Report, intended to inform the decisions of the Bank's Board, is circulated to the general public 10 working days after each of its meetings. In its seventh edition, the content of this report is continuously enriched in its analytical and predictive dimension. In addition, the annual calendar of Council meetings is published in advance and its decisions announced by a press release. In addition, quarterly meetings are held with bank directors and trading room managers to ensure that the Bank's messages are understood. An annual meeting between the Governor and the press is also organized, and regular contacts take place between the bank's various directorates and the media. Finally, the launch since last May of a new Internet portal, provides economic agents and users with information and tools with a more analytical content, allowing both a good understanding of its action and its decision-making process in the field of monetary policy, as well as a better readability of its messages. Internally, the Monetary and Financial Committee, a body of the Bank which meets monthly under the chairmanship of the Governor, carries out, in particular, a monitoring of monetary policy between the Councils, the frequency of which is quarterly. Whenever the risk factors on inflation increase, it shares with the Bank's Board its work and analysis. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, As in 2007, which saw inflation of 2% instead of 3.3% a year earlier, the recent evolution of inflation is close to our forecasts and the Council's assessment. At its last meeting (June 2008), the Board of Bank Al-Maghrib decided, while raising its level of vigilance regarding the evolution of inflation and risk factors in the coming months, to keep the key interest rate unchanged at 3.25%. At the operational level, the Bank's interventions will therefore aim to keep the rate on the interbank market at the level of the key rate. At the end of 2008, inflation is expected to reach 2.7%, significantly higher than the forecast presented in the March 2008 Monetary Policy Report (2.2%). For the second quarter of 2008, we expect inflation to increase, mainly driven by higher food prices. From the third quarter of 2008, inflation is expected to return to 2.5% and stabilize around this level over the forecast horizon. Compared to the previous Report, the inflation forecast has been revised upwards. At the date of the last Council meeting (17 June 2008), year-on-year inflation stood at 3.7% in April, after reaching 3.2% in March and 2.4% in February. Core inflation remained at a high level, at 4.8% in April, after 4.7% in March. Recent price developments are driven mainly by the upward trend in international commodity prices, which is also beginning to spread to other goods and services. The increase in import prices is also reflected in industrial producer prices. In May, year-on-year inflation stood at 5.4%. Core inflation remained at a high level of 4.9%. Most of the increase in LCI came from tradable goods, which contributed 3.78 percentage points, an increase of 8.9% year-on-year due to higher food and fresh commodity prices. At the same time, the prices of non-tradable goods rose by 2.7%, contributing 1.6 percentage points to inflation. The Central Bank closely monitors the evolution of the various factors that can affect inflation: the price of hydrocarbons and basic food products, their impact on the compensation system, including petroleum products, wages and the pace of credit growth. Many uncertainties persist about the evolution of these elements. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, Let me address here two important points that are the subject of intense debate in all countries. Most countries, both developed and emerging, are currently facing a significant increase in inflation, often double-digit for the latter, mainly driven by the sharp increase in the price of hydrocarbons and food products. In the case of Morocco, the effects of the international prices of these imported products, quoted in dollars, on inflation are partially cushioned by the evolution of our exchange rate, indexed at 80% to the Euro, and by the compensation system which mitigates to a large extent, through the State budget, their impact on the consumer. As in many countries, there is a gap in Morocco between the general public's perception of inflation and the measurement of inflation as reflected in official indices. All central banks are facing this problem. Bank Al-Maghrib is well aware of this perception gap, which varies according to the income and expenditure structure of each household category, and is working on the implementation of educational tools for the general public to facilitate their understanding of the dynamics of inflation. As with all central banks, it is a long-term pedagogical work. In addition, the forthcoming publication by the Office of the High Commissioner for Planning of a new Consumer Price Index, whose coverage in geographical terms, products and varieties will be extended, and weights based on a more recent household consumption survey, will be an important step forward. Dear Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, Regarding the evolution of the banking sector, 2007 was an exceptional year in more ways than one. As a result, the recovery process for state-owned banks has been completed, fundamental indicators have also improved significantly and the regulatory framework has been fully aligned with international standards. In terms of bank activity in 2007, sustained growth in net banking income on the back of strong credit activity, combined with a decline in the operating ratio and cost of risk, led to a significant increase in banks' profitability. The overall outstanding amount of bank loans increased by 29% to 422.6 billion dirhams at the end of 2007, against 17.7%. It was driven by strong lending to both businesses and individuals, while the ratio of credit to the private sector to GDP rose to 69 per cent from 57 per cent in 2006. At the end of May 2008, credit increased by 26.3% compared to the same period of the previous year. However, the pace of credit growth is expected to slow down in 2008; the banks, as part of the forecasts transmitted to Bank Al-Maghrib, estimating its increase at about 18%. By category, bank lending to businesses increased by 27% at the end of 2007 compared to 14% in 2006. The outstanding amount of real estate loans increased by 32.5% to 107.5 billion dirhams, representing nearly 28% of the total healthy loans distributed by banks. At the end of May 2008, this outstanding amount increased by 27% compared to the same period last year. The quantitative increase in credit is accompanied by a change in the structure of bank credit portfolios, which reveals a process of gradual extension of maturities and a greater share of variable-rate loans. The available data indicate an increase in the distribution of variable-rate loans. Thus, the share of these credits in the total outstanding amount of housing loans has increased, in one year, from 43% to 49%. This dynamism is also reflected in the level of finance companies, whose activity remains well correlated with that of banks. Thus, for consumer credit companies, the gross outstanding amount of loans increased by 17.9% to 33.4 billion dirhams, under the effect of the development of the consumer credit activity and lease operations with option to purchase. Similarly, leasing companies recorded a volume of activity of 26.5 billion dirhams, up 24.8%, a pace comparable to that of 2006. For its part, the microcredit sector has experienced remarkable development both in terms of the number of beneficiaries and the volume of loans whose outstanding amount has been multiplied by 3 in the space of 2 years, to reach 5.5 billion dirhams at the end of 2007. At the same time, the consolidation of credit institutions' balance sheets continued. The delinquency rate stood at 7.9% at the end of 2007 and 7% at the end of May 2008. Excluding public banks, this rate is less than 5% at the end of May 2008. Convergence towards international standards is a realistic objective, thanks in particular to the relaxation of tax rules relating to the write-off of the oldest debts from banks' balance sheets. However, vigilance is still required. This is why two codes of ethics on the financing of real estate and financial assets have been adopted by the banking sector. In addition, the ongoing reflection on the long-term sustainability of the FOGARIM Guarantee Facility should be completed quickly. In the same spirit, Bank Al-Maghrib closely monitors the evolution of risks related to real estate loans and consumption through annual surveys. In terms of liquidity, 2007 was a year of disruption, following a structural surplus recorded by bank treasuries since 2000. In order to fill the liquidity gap of bank treasuries, Bank Al-Maghrib has been working since March 2007 through its main instrument; 7-day advances on call for tenders, which allowed the overnight interbank rate to move within a relatively close range of 3.25%. At the same time, the collection of deposits increased by 18.1%. Banks have also stepped up their collection of long-term resources, notably through the issuance of certificates of deposit, which experienced remarkable development in 2007. In this environment, the aggregate net income of all credit institutions, calculated on a social basis, increased by 32.7% to 10 billion dirhams. This achievement is due to the 17% increase in net banking income as well as the control of the cost of risk, the provisioning expense having constituted 10% of gross operating income compared to 14% in 2006. Similarly, the operating ratio, despite the increase in structural costs at a higher rate than in the previous year, fell by 1.6 points to 45.5% at the end of 2007. At the heart of the momentum of financial reforms, the banking sector has been able, thanks to the progress made, to accelerate its modernization, thus contributing to further the financial deepening of our economy. Substantial regulatory advances have undoubtedly acted as an accelerator in this process in the recent period. This framework is therefore now in line with international standards, especially after the entry into force in 2007 of Bale II in its "standard approach" form. This is a long-term process that will be implemented on a continuous and gradual basis. In this sense, Bank Al-Maghrib's decision to raise the solvency ratio to 10% at the end of December 2008 further reinforces this process of convergence towards the best international standards in this area. The Central Bank intends to target a higher objective based on the profile of the banks and their risk mapping. In addition, Bank Al-Maghrib has raised liquidity risk management standards. Compliance with the provisions of the directive on this subject published by Bank Al-Maghrib will help banks to better control this risk. Finally, in terms of governance, Bank Al-Maghrib has asked banks, through a directive, to apply more rigorous principles of governance and internal control. Importantly, the accounting framework for banks has also been redesigned with the entry into force of the new IFRS accounting standards in 2008, which imply an improvement in the quality and transparency of financial information. Finally, the effective start-up of Credit Bureau, scheduled for the first months of 2009, will make it possible to pool and globalize credit information. The completion of this project will be an effective mechanism for improving the functioning of the credit market. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen With regard to financial stability, it is important to highlight the work carried out by the Coordination Commission of Financial Sector Supervisory Bodies, which in 2007 adopted rules of procedure governing the modalities of its operation. Its meetings during 2007 were devoted to the preparation of the assessment mission of the Moroccan financial sector by the IMF and the World Bank, and to issues relating in particular to bancassurance, the fight against money laundering, as well as the draft law on the futures market and the financing of real estate and financial assets. The Commission has also launched discussions on the drafting of a Monetary and Financial Code (COMOFI). This project, which is to mobilize the Ministry of Economy and Finance and all the actors of the financial sector, aims to codify all the texts applicable to this sector with a view to their grouping in a single document. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen The process of modernization of payment systems and means continues with the generalization to the entire national territory of the dematerialized exchange of checks, adopted more than a year ago, and bills of exchange set up since last Year. The dematerialization of foreign currency transfers that is underway will complete this system, which has a direct impact on the competitiveness of banking services, as transaction costs for all bank customers are decreasing. Efforts to improve banks' relations with their customers continued in 2007. As such, the development of the country's banking continues to be a constant concern of the Bank. In terms of access to financial services, banks have strengthened their networks. At the end of 2007, it had 2,748 counters. 301 units were opened in 2007, compared to 224 a year earlier and an average of 105 counters in the period 2002-2005. This expansion reflects the continuation of the retail banking's development policy. As a result, the rate of banking increased from 25% to 27% between 2006 and 2007 and to nearly 40% if we take into account the number of accounts opened on barid Al-Maghrib's books. At the end of 2007, there was one counter for every 10900 inhabitants against 12300 in 2006 and 13500 in 2005. This orientation is expected to continue as competition intensifies and the products to be offered are diversified. However, the current data place us below the performance of countries such as Turkey, Chile or Brazil. The optimization of actions driven by the banking profession calls for the concomitant mobilization of all the components of the national economic and financial fabric. Banks and professional associations in the financial sector are invited to renew their efforts to support the current dynamic and contribute to raising the rate of banking. Similarly, banks have been encouraged to improve the transparency and quality of banking services and to moderate their pricing to allow access to financial services for a large segment of the population. The practice of alternative products could also gain momentum with the expected tax easing. At the same time, the banking mediation system, whose mechanism is now defined, should be operational by September 2008. This mechanism will facilitate the amicable settlement of disputes that arise between banks and their customers in the context of their business relations, in particular through a mediation committee set up for this purpose. As part of the improvement of Bank-SME relations, the partnership agreement signed on 12 June 2008 between the Ministry of Industry, Trade and New Technologies, the GPBM and the ANPME is an important step forward. The implementation of this mechanism took place in the light of the conclusions of the national awareness campaign on SME financing, organized in 2007 in collaboration with the Ministry of Trade, Industry and New Technologies, the GPBM, the CCG, the CGEM and the AMPME, according to which access to finance was no longer an obstacle for these companies, the main complaints expressed by SMEs, which mainly concerned support and supervision for the implementation of projects. In the same perspective, an action of presence of pilot place is planned in Agadir next October, in coordination with the local authorities, in order to develop a greater proximity with all the operators and deepen our knowledge of the economic fabric. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen For the future, Bank Al-Maghrib will continue to act to consolidate and develop all the achievements in monetary policy and modernization of the banking sector. In terms of monetary policy, efforts to maintain price stability in the medium term and the anti-inflation reputation of the Central Bank will be continued, within a framework of full transparency of the foundations and results of the decisions of the Bank Council. In this sense, inflation forecasting now plays a central role in monetary policy decisions. Bank Al-Maghrib has published its inflation forecasts for a rolling four-quarter horizon since December 2006 as part of the Monetary Policy Report. Our regular assessments of the quality of these forecasts show that inflation achievements are close to it. More specifically, the observed inflation is, in almost 90% of cases, within the intervals defined by the Fan Chart of forecasts published as part of each Monetary Policy Report. On this basis, work is underway to extend this horizon to eight quarters in order to better anchor the medium-term inflation expectations of economic agents. In order to strengthen the information base, a fundamental pillar of monetary policy decisions, new data will also have to be collected from the various partners, in particular the HCP and certain other public administrations, on real estate assets, unemployment, employment and wages, etc. More generally, Bank Al-Maghrib will continue to work to prepare the economy to manage the acceleration of financial openness under the best conditions. Work and action on all components of the monetary policy decision-making process will continue in order to adequately prepare for the transition to an inflation-targeting regime. At the banking sector level, Bank Al-Maghrib will support banks in their efforts to adopt the advanced Basel II approaches for better resource allocation, strengthen governance for better risk management and improve financial transparency. For this sector, two major challenges lie ahead for the coming years. First of all, the deepening of the national market through a proactive policy to expand financial services, a development of long-term savings requiring a global strategy for the promotion of innovative products, a strategy adapted to VSEs and the continuation of the supervision of the microcredit sector for developments on a sound and solid basis. The second challenge relates to the further strengthening of the positioning of banks abroad, in particular to support the integration of our economy into the international environment. Thank you for your attention.

On this point, allow me, ladies and gentlemen, to illustrate my remarks by some reflections on the experience of our country. First of all, I would like to come back to the orientations that the Kingdom has adopted since the beginning of the 2000s. In the first place, Morocco is part of a process of trade and financial openness that is increasingly part of the desire to further integrate the Moroccan economy into the world economy. In this sense, Morocco has concluded a series of free trade agreements with 56 countries including the European Union, the United States, Turkey and a number of Arab countries and has gradually liberalized exchange regulations. As a result, the opening rate of the economy increased sharply from 61% of GDP in 2000 to more than 80% in 2013 and net foreign investment increased from 0.6% of GDP to 3.2% over the same period. Secondly, and driven by the ambition to become a regional financial hub, linking Europe, the Middle East and Africa, the Kingdom has launched the Casa Finance City structuring project, benefiting from several reforms that have related, in particular, to taxation, foreign exchange regulations, human resources training and the legal framework. The efforts made in this direction have not failed to bear fruit and Casa Finance City has been awarded the 42nd place in the ranking of the Global Financial Centers Index and the 2nd in Africa. These guidelines have challenged us in relation to the adequacy of the fixity of our exchange rate regime. For example, BAM and the Ministry of Finance agreed on the desirability of a gradual shift to a more flexible exchange rate regime and the adoption of inflation targeting. First of all, in 2006 the Central Bank was given institutional and operational independence, enabling it to free itself from any political influence in its mission to ensure price stability. As a result of these developments, the internal and external balances have been weakened, which has not failed to challenge the government authorities. In order to redress macroeconomic balances, the Government has undertaken a series of structural reforms aimed at strengthening the country's fiscal and external sustainability, including phasing out subsidies for petroleum products, stabilizing the wage burden relative to GDP, increasing the efficiency and transparency of the current tax system, and accelerating the pace of pension fund reform. To strengthen internal work, we have also requested a technical assistance mission to the IMF. It aims to support us in the improvement of our structural forecasting and analysis system, while integrating the specificities of our economy. You will have the opportunity to appreciate in more detail the progress made in this area during the next presentations. More recently, BAM and the Ministry of Finance have also called on an FSAP (The Financial Sector Assessment Program) mission to assess our financial sector in its various components. At the same time, we called for imf support, particularly on the operational aspects of the transition to greater flexibility in our exchange rate regime and the adoption of inflation targeting. I remain convinced that this seminar will give rise to interactive exchanges and debates, both institutionally and operationally, highlighting the experiences of our respective countries. Given the quality and expertise of the stakeholders, it will not fail to constitute a certain enrichment. I take this opportunity to invite you as much as possible to combine business with pleasure by visiting the city of Rabat, which has just been classified as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO. I thankyou for your attention and wish our work every success.
