Title: At the fourth meeting of the National Credit Council on July 6, 2010
text: Fourth Meeting of the National Credit and Savings Council 06 July 2010 Rabat Dear Minister, Dear Secretaries General, Dear Chief Executive Officers, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great pleasure for me to welcome you today to Bank Al-Maghrib for the fourth meeting of the National Credit and Savings Council. This meeting takes place in an international context marked by the persistence of the effects of the crisis, in particular its impact on the sustainability of public finances in developed countries, thus creating a climate marked by great uncertainty about the prospects for global economic growth. My intervention will first focus on the issues and challenges that our country must face in the short medium term in this uncertain international context. In a second step, I will discuss the progress made by Morocco at the macroeconomic level as well as in terms of the development of the financial system, which are assets to be preserved in the current context. Finally, I would like to mention the measures taken to make this sector a lever for growth, as well as the progress made in strengthening financial stability in a profoundly changing international context. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, Despite the gradual recovery in global activity since the second half of 2009 and the relative normalization of financial market conditions, financial stability has deteriorated sharply in the in recent months. This deterioration is due to a loss of confidence in the sustainability of fiscal policies, particularly in the euro area, and more generally in the relevance of economic policies, understood the limits at the level of coordination, aimed at responding to this challenge and ensuring sustainable growth. Indeed, the public debt of several advanced economies reached very high levels, of the order of 90% of GDP for the G7 countries taken together in 2010, thus increasing the risks to financial stability. Thus, an amount of 4 trillion dollars, the equivalent of about 30% of the GDP of the United States, matures in the third and fourth quarters of this year for the sovereign debts of the United States, England, Japan and those of some countries in the euro zone. This has resulted in a climate of widespread uncertainty which, if left unchecked, could have significant consequences for financial stability and the real economy, making it difficult to trade-off between growth-boosting and austerity measures aimed at reassuring the credibility of countries' commitment to fiscal sustainability. The difficulties on the European sovereign debt markets have thus quickly been transmitted to all markets, particularly interbank markets, with a magnitude that threatens the gradual and fragile recovery underway. These tensions have resulted in a return of strong risk aversion that has been accompanied by an increase in risk premia and volatility and a sharp decline in the parity of the euro against the dollar, which has depreciated significantly and rapidly, by around 14% since the beginning of the year. In addition, credit activity in advanced economies continues to be severely constrained, as shown by the latest data available at the end of April 2010, with a year-on-year decline of 4.7% in the United States and a near stagnation in the euro area. All in all, the international environment for Morocco remains subject to significant uncertainties regarding a sustained and sustainable return to growth in several developed countries, especially in Europe our main economic partner. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, The challenge for Morocco today is to continue its efforts to preserve macroeconomic stability and growth in the face of the repercussions of a difficult external environment, particularly in the euro area, including growth is expected to average around 1% over the next two years. The uncertainties surrounding the resulting outlook for the balance of payments also challenge us. These unfavourable prospects represent real challenges for Morocco at various levels. This is well reflected in the experience of the recent crisis. Thus, non-agricultural growth was limited to 1% in 2009 against 4.3% in 2008, showing the close link between the evolution of economic activity in Morocco and in our main European partners. The update of the quarterly national accounts following the publication of the annual data indicates a significant deterioration in non-agricultural growth, with a decline of 2.2% in the first quarter of 2009 against a first estimate of an increase of 0.6%. This situation reflects the very high dependence of several sectors, in particular industry, on external demand. This high dependence on external demand is also reflected in current transfers, travel receipts and foreign direct investment. The persistence of the trade deficit as well as the contraction of current transfers, travel receipts and foreign direct investment thus represent important sources of vulnerability for the national economy, through their impact on external accounts. For example, the deficit in current transactions with foreign countries stood at 5% of GDP in 2009, after 5.2% the previous year and an average surplus of almost 2.4% between 2001 and 2007. While the risks to growth developments in the euro area have major implications for macroeconomic policies, the fundamental challenges remain improving productivity and increasing the competitiveness of enterprises, as well as maintaining macroeconomic balances. The strategic challenge is to deepen structural and sectoral reforms, with a view to stimulating growth. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, In this context, Bank Al-Maghrib is determined to continue to contribute to the preservation of the necessary conditions for a better integration of the Moroccan economy into its global environment and to respond to the challenges linked to post-crisis changes. The main projects planned by the Bank in this regard revolve around the further adaptation of monetary policy, the development of the macro-prudential supervision framework, drawing lessons from the recent financial crisis, as well as the consolidation of the banking supervision mission. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, The national economy is able to meet these challenges, thanks to the strength of macroeconomic fundamentals. Indeed, in a highly disrupted international context, our country has demonstrated a real capacity for adaptation, particularly in terms of macroeconomic management and a strong resilience to exogenous shocks, the result of a continuous process of macroeconomic and structural reforms, carried out over the past three decades. These reforms have helped to consolidate fundamental balances, as reflected in long-term data on growth, fiscal position, inflation and external accounts. In addition, the resilience of domestic demand and the normal functioning of the credit market, combined with the climate of confidence and policy measures, including through the Strategic Intelligence Committee, have contributed to mitigating the impact of the last global recession on macroeconomic stability. Thus, overall economic growth remained at a rate of 4.9%, following the 30.6% increase in agricultural value added. Inflation stood at 1%, compared to an annual average of 1.9% over the past decade, while core inflation returned to 0.7%. In terms of public finances, the budget deficit stood at 2.2% of GDP in 2009, not calling into question medium-term sustainability, while the debt-to-GDP ratio stabilized at around 47%. Along with these advances, the soundness of the national banking and financial system has contributed significantly to the resilience of the economy. Credit dynamics, while decelerating, remained strong. The decline in the increase in credit, according to the new monetary statistics, to 13.6% at the end of May 2010 against 19.1% and 28.6% during the same period, respectively, in 2009 and 2008 reflects the return to a level consistent with the fundamentals of the economy. This development had no impact on the banks' profitability, as their overall net income increased by 7%. Similarly, the return on assets and that of equity were 1.2% and 15.2% respectively. In this context, outstanding loans continued their downward trend, representing only 5.5% of total loans in 2009 and 5.3% at the end of May 2010, due to both the balance sheet consolidation process and the reduction in the cost of risk. These developments took place under conditions of strengthening the solvency of banks after the Central Bank raised the regulatory minimum from 8% to 10% at the end of 2007. The average solvency ratio, according to the Basel II standard approach, thus amounted to 11.8% and core capital to 9.2% in 2009. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, For the future, the continued development of the financial sector is one of the central bank's priorities in the coming years, with a view to supporting the dynamism of growth. and to promote greater diversification, both sectorally and geographically, while establishing it as an engine of growth in its own right. Thus, as part of the financial inclusion strategy, the banking process has been strengthened and the goal of reaching a rate of 50%, including Barid Al-Maghrib, seems achievable by the end of 2010. Similarly, efforts to improve banks' relations with their customers will continue, with the regulatory definition in 2010 of basic free banking services, the introduction of a banking services price index and the sending annually to customers of a statement of all commissions charged. Banks will be asked to provide all the necessary transparency in terms of the conditions they apply to customers and allow access to financial services to a large segment of the population. At the same time, the banking mediation system, established in 2009, will facilitate the amicable settlement of disputes that arise between banks and their customers in the context of their business relationships, in particular through a mediation committee set up for this purpose. Bank Al-Maghrib will also support banks in their efforts to mobilize long-term savings to meet the challenge of financing sectoral roadmaps, which will however have to go through the triple filter "selection-monitoring-evaluation", and this to set priorities in a context of financing constraint, since the preservation of financial stability requires a balanced and sustainable asset-liability adequacy in the long term. To promote long-term savings, specific plans, with a tax incentive, will have to be proposed in the near future. It will also increase the savings rate, which currently stands at around 30% of gross national disposable income. The efficiency of the financial system is bound to be enhanced by recent legislation. This is the text on the futures market that will allow economic agents to hedge against the risks of fluctuations in the prices of the assets they hold, allowing them a better allocation of their financial resources. The purpose of the second text is to regulate the buyback programmes initiated by companies of their own shares with a view to regularising the market, by laying down the forms and conditions under which these operations may be carried out. Another text sets out the new shareholding structure of the managing company of the Casablanca Stock Exchange, facilitating the opening of its capital and diversifying its shareholding. Finally, the new text on securitisation allows not only banks but also large private and public companies to raise financing and at attractive costs. Bank Al-Maghrib also plans to learn all the lessons of the recent financial crisis by revising its Statute and the Banking Law, in particular with a view to giving Bank Al-Maghrib a financial stability mandate and strengthening mechanisms for the prevention and management of systemic crises. In addition, bank Al-Maghrib published on 30 June 2010 the monetary statistics in accordance with the requirements of the Manual of the International Monetary Fund, thus aligning itself with best practices in this area. The adoption of this methodology will make it possible, in particular, to contribute to improving the analysis of monetary developments and to the assessment of the stability of the financial sector, through the provision, on a monthly basis, of more detailed information to economic decision-makers and market participants. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, As part of the improvement of bank-SME relations and in order to make the financial sector an engine of growth, efforts have been made to strengthen access to these companies to financial services. In addition, a number of measures have been adopted in favour of SMEs, including tax incentives, simplification and facilitation of administrative procedures, the adoption of sectoral strategies that constitute roadmaps for enterprises and the National Charter for SMEs with the creation of the National Agency for the Promotion of SMEs. At the same time, in order to improve SMEs' access to bank financing and reduce the cost of intermediation, regional information campaigns are being conducted to raise companies' awareness of the new support dynamic set up jointly by the banking sector and the State and to facilitate their access to financial services. The project to transform Casablanca's market into a financial hub opens up promising prospects for Morocco to attract capital flows and develop new businesses. Our country has certain assets to succeed in this direction, but for this it must accelerate and adapt in depth the pace of reforms so as not to be overtaken by competing countries. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, More generally, the persistence of certain fragilities imposes on us not only an obligation of vigilance but also and above all an imperative need to accelerate the reforms made unavoidable by the new global context. Thus, at the level of fiscal policy, itis important to continue to consolidate sustainability in the medium term. As such, the reform of the compensation system must be accelerated and actions to rationalize operating expenditure deserve to be implemented, in order to release surpluses to support efforts to reduce social deficits. Similarly, it is imperative to address the current account imbalance in the balance of payments, by reducing the concentration of exports on products with low added value as well as on markets with limited growth potential. Indeed, in the absence of fundamental developments, the importance of import demand, combined with limited export dynamics, could only increase tensions on foreign exchange reserves or increase the dependence of the national economy on current transfers and external financing, subject to fluctuations in international economic and financial conditions. To successfully meet these challenges, the coordination of the strategies adopted is necessary. Similarly, the proliferation of sector-wide approaches must not take precedence over the macroeconomic vision. Social issues must also be taken into account, in particular the reduction of unemployment, which represents a major challenge for our economy, and the gaps in education and health that must be quickly filled. At the same time, the fight against poverty must be pursued and the functioning of justice must finally be reviewed in order to promote the improvement of the business climate and raise the pace of economic growth.

Title: Opening address at the First meeting of the Francophone Supervisors Group
text: First meeting of the Group of Supervisors Francophone Rabat , March 8, 2005 Opening speech by Mr Abdellatif JOUAHRI, Governor of Bank Al Maghrib Dear Secretary General, Ladies and gentlemen, First of all, I would like to tell you how pleased I am to welcome you today to Bank Al-Maghrib for the first conference of the Group of Francophone Supervisors. I have the privilege of assuming the presidency of this group for two years, with the assistance of Mr. Jean-Philippe TROUSSARD, of the French Banking Commission, who will ensure the General Secretariat for a period of time. of three years. Our group, whose creation follows the wish expressed by the governors of the French-speaking central banks at their meeting held in June 2004 in Paris, was officially born in September 2004 at the occasion of the 13th meeting of the International Conference of Supervisors of Banks held in Madrid. The establishment of thisnew group comes at a time when the community of banking supervisors is preparing to take a new step towards greater convergence of banking arrangements and practices. banking supervision. The initiative to bring together such a wide range of countries whose common vector is the use of the French language is, in itself, a major asset to accelerate this process of convergence. for the benefit, of course, of all current and future members. The presence in our group of G10 countries, which have made definite progress in the basel II implementation process and in general in the field of surveillance prudential, will undoubtedly allow other members to capitalise on this experience to improve their own supervisory systems. With this in mind, the draft charter, which will be presented to you for approval by Mr Jean-Philippe TROUSSARD, provides that the group is called, like the other regional groups, to banking supervisors, to promote the exchange of information between its members and to ensure, with the support of the Institute for Financial Stability, joint training actions provided in French, while developing close and regular relations with the Basel Committee. In this context, and in order to ensure the sustainability of contact and the spirit of cooperation outside the annual meetings, the creation of expert committees within our group to examine I think that certain specific aspects specific to our countries are extremely useful. The same applies to communication through the dissemination of our work and recommendations to the widest possible audience. Discussions on the other topics on the day's programme, in particular those relating to the conditions for the successful transition from Basel I to Basel II. as well as the challenges of the second pillar will also provide us with the opportunity to discuss the issues raised in our respective countries and the means to deal with them. Mr. Secretary General, ladies and gentlemen, The new capital adequacy framework, published last June by the Basel Committee, constitutes an innovative and structuring framework within which our actions as supervisors should be inscribed in order to strengthen the safety and soundness of our national banking systems. However, it should be agreed that the implementation of this new arrangement, due to its complexity, requires significant human and technical skills on the part of both supervisory authorities and banks. In addition, a set of prerequisites would be necessary prior to the implementation of the new system to ensure its success, including the existence of an effective supervisory framework that meets the 25 fundamental principles laid down in this area by the Basel Committee. The document published in July 2004 by the Basel Committee entitled "Application of Basel II: practical considerations" is very instructive in this regard and constitutes, in my opinion, an indispensable reference framework for prudential authorities, particularly those in emerging countries. I would like to take this opportunity to thank, on your behalf, Mr Jean-Philippe Svoronos of the Institute of Financial Stability, for the effort he has taken to make available to us the French translation of this document and to congratulate him on the spirit of conciseness and objectivity he has shown. This document has the merit of highlighting the main pitfalls likely to hinder the implementation of the new system, in particular the inadequacy of the legal framework and the insufficient resources for supervision or financial transparency. This is true for many of our respective countries, as shown by the findings of the Financial Systems Assessment Missions (PSFs), conducted jointly by the Bank and the IMF. In this regard, let me point out that the FSAP, carried out in Morocco in 2002, has made it possible to better understand the weaknesses of our banking supervision system and to initiate an action plan articulated around three main axes: - 1st axis: the overhaul of the banking law, the draft of which is currently before parliament. The resulting new requirements should enable the Central Bank to have a supervisory framework that is largely in line with Basel standards, - 2nd axis: the participation of the Central Bank in a national project, supported by the World Bank, aimed at the convergence of accounting and auditing standards with international standards, - 3rd axis: the consolidation of supervisory resources through, in particular, the reinforcement of the workforce and the establishment of proactive, risk-based control procedures. However, it must be recognised that whatever the quality of the regulatory framework and the means dedicated to supervision, the safety of banks is primarily the responsibility of their management. The second pillar of Basel II, which has not been sufficiently explored until now by the supervisory community, fits perfectly into this perspective. Indeed, this pillar requires banks to have mechanisms in place to assess, on an ongoing basis, the overall adequacy of their own funds to their risk profile and places the onus on the supervisory authorities to intervene upstream of the risk management process and to ensure the efficiency of these arrangements. The implementation of the recommendations of this second pillar is all the more a priority since in several countries the cost of credit and operational risks is at alarming levels, which negatively reflects the cost of bank intermediation. In Morocco, for example, despite a situation characterized by the easing of interest rates in a context of overliquidity, SMEs, which constitute the bulk of the productive fabric, continue to bear relatively excessive interest rates due to the high cost of risk and the low quality of financial information. To help remedy this situation, we have asked banks to set up internal rating systems for their customers, based on recommendations issued by the Central Bank and derived from the standards issued by the Basel Committee. This new process has strengthened a dialogue with the banking profession that is more focused on banks' internal risk management practices. The successful implementation of the new Basel framework, due to its complexity and the scope of the issues it entails, remains dependent on the availability of highly qualified skills and training actions adapted to the specific needs of supervisors. The seminar, scheduled for the next three days, which will be given in French with the valuable assistance of the Institute for Financial Stability concretizes the process of cooperation that is expected to develop with this Institute. The training needs that will be expressed by the members of the group during this day should give rise to other actions of this kind. Without further ado, I give the floor to Mr TROUSSARD and hope that the group's work will be crowned with success. Thank you.

Title: Introductory remarks at the round table on sustainable finance in Morocco
text: Sustainable Finance Strategy: Kick-off meeting Tuesday , May 19, 2015 Introductory word from Mr WALI Dear Secretary General of the Ministry of the Environment, Mr. President of the GPBM, Dear Presidents and Chief Executive Officers, Ladies and gentlemen It is a real pleasure for me to welcome you today to Bank Al-Maghrib for the launch of the reflection on the sustainable finance strategy, a subject of great national importance and of interest to the Government of Morocco, the supervisory authorities of the financial sector and financial institutions as well as professional associations. As you know, our country has adopted in its emergence strategy, under the impetus of SA MAJESTE, the concept of sustainable development that promotes the balance between the environmental, economic and social dimensions, with the objectives of improving the living environment of citizens, strengthening the sustainable management of natural resources and promoting economic activities that respect the environment. The National Charter for the Environment and Sustainable Development has also defined the objectives, principles and obligations relating to the activities carried out by the Government, Public Establishments and Private Companies in the field of environmental protection and sustainable development. For these policy initiatives to be efficient, the involvement of the private sector is essential. Financial institutions are well placed to help economic agents adapt and contribute effectively to the national sustainable development agenda. But sustainable finance is above all the primary responsibility of the financial community. It also brings great opportunities for financial institutions that can reduce losses in their own credit portfolios that may result from corporate failures due to sustainability risks. They can also generate new credit opportunities in areas such as clean technology and financing for underserved or excluded customers in the financial sector. To this end, more and more financial institutions around the world have adopted credit granting policies, systems and practices that support this. eQuator Principles, launched in 2003 on the basis of IFC's performance standards and to which 80 institutions in 34 countries have voluntarily joined, are an example of how financial institutions can collectively organize to achieve this goal. In addition, the role of regulators is essential to ensure a successful shift towards sustainable finance practices through the establishment of an enabling regulatory environment that ensures a level playing field and provides appropriate incentives. For example, some emerging countries have put in place regulatory guidelines to encourage banks to adopt sustainable finance practices. This includes more effective management of environmental and social risks in the projects they finance and support for the greenest companies that respect the climate and social inclusion. These guidelines are either (1) issued by financial or banking regulatory authorities such as brazil, Bangladesh, China, Indonesia, Nigeria, Peru, the Philippines and Vietnam; or (2) the result of proactive actions, carried out by professional groups of banks and financial institutions such as in Colombia, Kenya, Mongolia and Mexico. These sector-wide regulatory efforts are based on the belief that important results can be achieved by mobilizing the financial sector for broad national sustainability goals. Emerging markets have taken a particularly important step in this direction, with some like-minded regulators and banking groups coming together to create the Sustainable Banks Network in 2012, a global platform for the exchange of experience and know-how, to which Bank Al-Maghrib joined in June 2014. Ladies and gentlemen At Bank Al-Maghrib, aware of all these issues, we have always been strongly committed to working for the development of a sustainable and inclusive economy, particularly through the action we have taken with our partners in favor of financial inclusion, financial education, the promotion of MSMEs, consumer protection, etc. Like what we have achieved in these various projects, I would like our sustainable finance strategy to be the result of collective work and in consultation with all the stakeholders concerned by this aspect. The round table, which we are organizing today, will allow us to identify together the main lines of our common strategy for a better contribution of the financial sector in the development of a sustainable national economy and to define a work organization and a roadmap for its elaboration and implementation. I would like to warmly thank the representatives of the Finance Initiative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNEP  FI) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) as well as all the banking institutions present here, for their participation and their strong contribution to the organization and animation of the work of this meeting. I would also like to thank the insurance sector represented by the Directorate of Insurance and Social Security and the Insurance Federation. My thanks also go to the panelists for sharing their experience, which will enrich our debates. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech at the certificate award ceremony
text: Certificate Award Ceremony Speech by Mr Abdellatif JOUAHRI Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 17 March 2009 Her Majesty's Counsel, Dear Ministers, Dear members of the Board of the Bank, Vice President of Bureau Veritas Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, I would like to express my sincere thanks for having responded to our invitation to this ceremony to award the ISO 9001 certificate, and more particularly to the Councillors and Ministers who took their time, as well as to our host Mr. Serge ANTONINI, Vice President of Bureau Veritas. This event is the starting point for the events we are organizing to commemorate the fiftieth anniversary of Bank Al-Maghrib. First of all, I would like to take this opportunity to express our deep gratitude to the pioneers who paved the way for us. In the first place, to His Majesty the late King Mohammed V who, at the beginning of July 1959, decided to create the Bank of Morocco and presided over its inauguration by affirming in his historic speech in terms that remain relevant and I quote "the sovereignty of every nation is manifested by attributes, including freedom of action in the conduct of financial and monetary policy and the orientation of its economy, in accordance with its interests, and by the possession of a national currency issued by a national bank'. To His Majesty the late King Hassan II who, in the same vein, worked for the consolidation of this orientation, inaugurating in March 1987 Dar As-Sikkah so that our country could ensure the minting of its currency and print its notes. Finally, to His Majesty King Mohammed VI who wanted to establish and consolidate the full independence of the institution through its new statutes of February 20, 2006. - 2 . I would also like to pay tribute to the various finance ministers of the Kingdom, who have always been the privileged partners of the Central Bank, citing in particular the one who was at the side of His Majesty Mohammed V for the launch of Bank Al-Maghrib, the late Abderrahim BOUABID. Our gratitude is also addressed to all the governors who have succeeded each other at the head of the institution and who have served it with rigor and constancy, each bringing an important stone to the building. It is up to us to express our gratitude to the Bank's Executive Directors who, through their various mandates, have accompanied the institution through their availability, support and advice, while giving it the human, logistical and organizational resources necessary to accomplish its missions. A special mention to the current directors who, within the framework of the Bank's new statute, have undoubtedly enabled it to quickly climb into the various compartments of its action to the best international standards. Last but not least, it is a tribute to all the Bank's employees, men and women, who, throughout these decades, on the front of the stage or in anonymity, have served it with dedication, loyalty and self-sacrifice. Ladies and Gentlemen, Today's ceremony is one of the consecrations of all these efforts. The completion of this process is part of the three-year strategic plans that define the Bank's fundamental orientations and the actions it intends to carry out in the short and medium term. Bank Al-Maghrib thus becomes one of the few central banks to obtain global certification for all its activities. The process of obtaining the certification covered both governance aspects and business lines and support areas. It required a mapping of 26 processes led by improvement groups that mobilized more than 500 people over two years. The certification is thus the result of a general mobilization and a strong adherence that reflect the company's german culture and that honor all its agents. Our pride is that this certification was obtained from the first audit and in the absence of major or minor non-compliance. I would like to take this opportunity to thank Bureau Veritas, whose teams accompanied us with professionalism and efficiency. - . I would like to stress that for us, certification is not an end in itself and calls for a continuous effort on our part, of which we are aware. It is a step in our dynamic of improvement which calls us to prepare ourselves already for ISO 9001 standards according to the new version 2008 and to aim for the future at the objective of an integrated QSE (Quality/Safety/Environment) Management System. Ladies and Gentlemen, Our ambition remains, in an increasingly complex and difficult environment, while Morocco has made the strategic choice to be part of globalization, to make this institution a pole of rigor, transparency and modernity that participates, in the most efficient way, in the economic and social development of our country under the enlightened leadership of His Majesty King Mohammed VI. - .

Title: Message to the participants at the 32nd session of the Council of Arab Central Bank Governors
text: Praise be to God. Prayer and salvation on the Prophet, His family and Companions Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, We are pleased to send you this message on the occasion of this meeting of the Board of Governors ofcentral banks and Arab issuing institutions. This shows the esteem I have for these institutions in view of the avant-garde role they play in consolidating the good foundations on which the Arab economy is based, and in view ofthe contribution they make to the achievement of the comprehensive development to which our brotherly countries aspire, and which constitutes the solid foundation of joint, efficient and modern Arab action. Your forum is of particular importance because it is being held in a delicate international context. The global economy is facing an unprecedented crisis that threatens to slow the pace of growth and undermine the stability of the banking system and financial. This economic situation is also marked by the pressures induced by the strong demand for raw materials and basic foodstuffs, a situation which does not fail to accentuate the risks to growth and price stability. This crisis continues to be exacerbated by the worsening of disruptions in global financial markets following the collapse of the mortgage sector in the United States. As a result, a generalized crisis of confidence eventually set in as a result of the losses suffered by banking and financial institutions. Excellencies Notwithstanding this turbulent global economic climate, economic activity in the Arab region has continued to expand and stimulate the exponential growth momentum prevailing there, thanks to the increased pace of investment and consumption. This growth was accompanied by a consolidation of fundamental balances, despite the rise in the general price level due to the action of external factors. Just as the banking and financial sector of the Arab countries has experienced- thanks be to God - a stability that has enabled it to avoid the fallout of financial disruptions on a global scale. However, this should not obscure for us the need to be more vigilant, ensuring more efficient supervision of our financial markets and continuing to ensure their coordination, so as to make them a model for financial activity in terms of control and early warning. Like many brotherly Arab countries, Morocco has known, since the beginning of the current decade, rapid and sustained growth, resulting the structural reforms we have adopted, as well as the implementation of the works good economic policies. This growth translates into in particular by improving the business environment which has allowed, its turn, an increase in the volume of investment and an increase in the standard of living, both responsible for the development of the consumption. It is also due to the diversification of the production and emergence of new activities that have played the role of  locomotive of growth in the industrial and service sectors. We have also worked to control inflation, improve the state of public finances and external accounts, and preserve exchange rate stability. At the same time, we have focused on further developing the banking and financial sector and strengthening the supervisory and prevention systems. These combined actions have had the effect of promoting the development of financial markets and ensuring the diversification of financial instruments, a situation that has been made possible by Bank AI-Maghrib's practice of good governance, the exercise of strict control and the adoption of a sound strategy in this area. In addition to the rigorous autonomy and great professionalism of which it is credited, this institution has been able to carry out this conclusive approach thanks to the wisdom, know-how, determination and firmness recognized to Our faithful servant, the wali of Bank AI-Maghrib. In the same vein, I have ensured that Morocco continues to open up to its international environment through the conclusion of free trade agreements with the key poles of the world economy and the countries of the Mediterranean basin, in addition to Morocco's resolute adherence to the implementation of the agreement relating to the Arab Free Trade Area. 2 On the social level, !' National Initiative for Human Development,which We have launched and of which We are witnessing concretely the smooth running of the projects-has made it possible to combine, in all harmony, economic growth and social development, through medium and long-term projects. Similarly, the INDH has greatly contributed - with God's help and thanks to the adherence of all the living forces of the nation to its fruitful programs - to ensuring sources of stable income for the poor and to the creation of jobs. In order to give concrete expression to our desire to improve the social conditions of our citizens in general and to improve the situation of the middle classes in particular - to make them the broadest base of society and the focal point of public policies - measures have been taken with the aim of strengthening and developing consumption and thus stimulating investment. Excellencies Aware of the importance of the regional dimension for the development of the Arab economy, Morocco has actively contributed to the work of the regional symposia on trade liberalization, monetary integration and the role of the private sector in the five countries of the Maghreb Union. In this regard, the widening of the circle of projects and programmes with a regional scope is likely to strengthen economic integration among the Arab countries. Therefore, and in order to promote sustainable development in our Arab region, it is necessary to take advantage of all the potentialities and other energies that our countries have and to ensure coordination between our economic policies. In this context, I welcome the general Arab approach to speed in the implementation of structural reforms and the adoption of economic policies aimed at consolidating fundamental balances. We also welcome all initiatives aimed at enshrining the autonomy of central banks with regard to the tasks assigned to them, namely those of ensuring monetary stability and strengthening the soundness of the banking system, so as to promote the establishment of solid foundations for the economic development of n0 countries. 3 At the international level, I welcome the fact that agreement has been reached on the principles and practices relating to sovereign wealth funds. This agreement, which will be submitted to the Monetary and Financial Committee of the International Monetary Fund, will help to activate the role assigned to these funds by enabling them to help mitigate the fallout from the current crisis in the international financial system. We are convinced that the work of your important meeting will lead to convincing and concrete results by making it possible to achieve the objectives to which we all aspire, namely to strengthen the economic and social development of our countries and to ensure the development and well-being of our peoples. Title: At the third meeting of the National Credit and Savings Council
text: Third Meeting of the National Credit and Savings Council 28 July 2009 Rabat Speech by Mr Abdellatif JOUAHRI Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib Dear Minister, Dear Secretaries General, Dear Chief Executive Officers, Ladies and gentlemen First of all, I would like to welcome you to Bank Al-Maghrib on the occasion of the holding of the third meeting of the National Credit and Savings Council and especially to the members who are joining us for the first time. Our meeting is being held today at a crucial time. The global economy is experiencing an unprecedented economic collapse and there are still serious uncertainties about the return of growth in developed countries in particular. This trying economic situation does not fail to affect the national economy. That is why I would like to begin by returning to the main assets that have enabled the national economy to continue to show significant resilience in the face of the deterioration of the international economy. I would also give an overview of the actions taken by the central bank over the past twelve months, in the context of the conduct of its fundamental tasks, in the light of the events that have taken place. Finally, I would like to mention the challenges we face, in order to enable our financial system to increase its efficiency in financing the national economy. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, At the outbreak of the global financial crisis, the international environment was marked in particular by very high volatility in stock market indices, as well as by market tensions. monetary as evidenced by the abnormal level of spreads. Under these conditions, the international banking system has been weakened, leading to a phase of financial instability and prolonged economic recession. These developments have not failed to impact growth and macroeconomic management at the national level. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, The primary challenge today is for our country to face exogenous shocks linked, in particular, to growth in Europe, Morocco's main partner, and to the volatility of oil and commodity prices on international markets. Aware of the importance of macroeconomic stability and prudential supervision and regulation to support medium- and long-term growth, as well as for the development of national savings, the Moroccan authorities have worked to consolidate macroeconomic balances. First of all, the deepening of the structural reforms carried out by our country in recent years has considerably strengthened the fundamental macroeconomic balances. Thus, growth has clearly strengthened since 2000, thanks to the good results of the agricultural sector and the diversification of sources of growth, as shown by the sustained increase to more than 5% of non-agricultural GDP on average over the period 2001-2008, thus marking a break with the past trend. At the same time, the fiscal position has strengthened significantly despite the significant compensation expenditure linked to the increase in the price of oil, in connection with the good behaviour of tax revenues. In addition, it is important to stress the independence of the State budget from privatization revenues in recent years. With regard to price developments, it is important to point out that Morocco has been part of a global disinflationary movement, with an inflation rate that stabilized around 2% on average between 1997 and 2008. Similarly, inflation volatility has declined significantly, particularly for core inflation. At the same time, current transactions generated a surplus of around 2% of GDP on average between 2001 and 2007, while foreign exchange reserves consolidated to represent about 9 months of imports of goods and services during the said period. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, For several countries, the effects of the global crisis have led to a worsening of public deficits and debts, in relation to the need, on the one hand, to save the banking system by replacing it in its function of financing the economy and, on the other hand, to compensate for the insufficiency of private demand. In addition, the slowdown in economic growth has been characterized by a sharp decline in government revenues and a considerable increase in expenditure in view of the implementation of economic stimulus plans, which is bound to have an impact on public debt in the coming years. The successive downward sharp revisions to the global growth outlook and the major uncertainties that still weigh illustrate the downside risks that are expected to last longer than initially anticipated. The International Monetary Fund's latest growth projections show the world economy shrinking by 1.4% in 2009, before growing by 2.5% in 2010 instead of 3.1% in 2008 and 5.1% in 2007. The global economy also remains marked by significant volatility in commodity prices, which have risen in the recent period but remain well below the peak reached in 2008. On the financial front, while the risks of systemic collapse have diminished as a result of conventional and unconventional measures taken by major central banks, combined with government support, markets remain volatile. Although there is a renewed appetite for risk, confidence is far from being sustainably restored. However, the contraction of economic activity, particularly in Morocco's partner countries, is expected to continue during 2009, before a slight recovery in 2010. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, Like non-oil-exporting developing countries, Morocco has not escaped the impact of the international economic crisis. Its economy has been affected through the real channels of spread, mainly exports of goods and services and remittances from Moroccans residing abroad and direct investment abroad. This development has also been reflected in the growth figures. Excluding agriculture, growth returned to 1.9% in the fourth quarter of 2008, breaking with the average level of 5.5% observed in the first three quarters. In addition, the sharp contraction in export earnings, combined with the contraction in tourism receipts and repatriations of Moroccan residents abroad, resulted in a deterioration in the current account position at the end of 2008. The current account deficit represented 5.4% of GDP in 2008 and the level of foreign exchange reserves covers the equivalent of 7 months of imports of goods and services. We remain optimistic about the effects of the Government's actions to support productive sectors directly exposed to the collapse of foreign demand. The Strategic Intelligence Committee set up at the beginning of the current year ensures very close monitoring of the impact of such measures. However, as reflected in Bank Al-Magrhib's latest growth forecasts presented to its June Council, the sharp contraction in demand from our main partners is expected to continue to have a dampening effect on non-agricultural growth, which is expected to be between 2% and 3% in 2009. On the other hand, overall economic growth is expected to be between 5% and 6%, a level comparable to that observed in 2008, driven by a rebound in agricultural value added, which benefited from exceptional climatic conditions and whose rate of growth would reach 20% against 16% in 2008. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to recall, on this occasion, that Morocco has managed to resist the direct repercussions of the crisis on its financial system. The banking sector, which is its essential component, is stable, solid and shows good resilience in the face of changes in the international context. This soundness of the banking and financial system is the result of a long process of reforms carried out since the previous decade. The pace of these reforms has intensified over the past five years with a view to strengthening the prudential framework and the proactive risk detection and management framework. Since the outbreak of the crisis at the international level, banks have been required to be more vigilant in monitoring the quality of both the foreign assets held in their portfolios and their counterparties. The results of the investigations carried out in this direction show that the exposure of the banking sector to risk factors as well as the purely financial contagion channels of the crisis are very limited. The share of foreign assets is low, banks do not hold so-called "toxic" products and risks to foreign counterparties are controlled. In parallel, work is underway to set up a macro-prudential supervisory framework, based both on stress tests to assess the resilience of the banking system to different shocks and on the conduct of systemic stress tests, in consultation with the regulatory and supervisory authorities of the financial sector. The purpose of this work is to ensure the effectiveness of current mechanisms and to identify areas for their improvement, with a view to establishing, on solid foundations, coordination between regulatory authorities in the event of a systemic crisis and ensuring a global watch on the stability of the financial system. Thus, although decelerating, the growth of bank loans remains strong. After an increase of 23% at the end of December 2008 instead of 29% a year earlier, credit growth increased again by 17.1% at the end of May 2009. The overall stock of bank loans, stimulated by demand from both households and businesses and dynamic interbank competition, reached 519.3 billion dirhams in 2008, and represented 78% of GDP against 69% a year earlier, a level remaining well above that posted by the countries of the MENA region which stands at an average of 58%. Approached by the share of credit granted by the banking system in GDP, the weight of the banking sector in financing the economy has steadily increased, from 53.8% in 1980 to 60% in 1990 before exceeding 90% in recent years. Similarly, the evolution of the liquidity ratio, an indicator of the degree of deposit mobilization by the banking sector, shows that the share of M2 in GDP, which averaged 42.6% during the years 1980-1990, is close to 80% during the period 2000-2008. The soundness of the banking system also seems to be in line with international standards. Thanks to better risk management, outstanding receivables are part of a downward trend. Representing 8% of the total outstanding loans at the end of 2007, they experienced a further contraction to stabilize around 6% at the end of May 2009. Similarly, the ratio of coverage of receivables by provisions has improved significantly and the solvency ratio has been satisfactory from the point of view of international standards. At the same time, in order to meet the new regulatory requirements, banks have strengthened their capital, which has increased by 22% to 55 billion dirhams. In this regard, we have adopted a set of measures aimed at consolidating the banking system and financial stability. Thus, additional provisions on country risk management were enacted in 2008 and the minimum level of the solvency ratio was raised to 10%. Similarly, the rules for reporting interest rate risk have been defined in order to standardize the reporting sent by banks and facilitate its processing, while the conditions under which credit institutions must publish their financial statements under IFRS have been set. At present, eight banks have adopted international accounting standards and published according to these standards for the financial year 2008. For the micro-credit sector, specific rules for the classification of overdue receivables and provisions have been laid down. It is important to note in this respect that the activity of this sector did not develop significantly in 2008. The outstanding amount of assistance distributed by microcredit associations was almost at a similar level as in 2007, i.e. 5.7 billion dirhams, after an increase of 57% compared to 2006. Finally, I would like to point out on the same note that the entry into operation of the central financial information centre next September will make it possible to improve the credit information system in Morocco. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, On the monetary policy front, the Bank has focused on ensuring price stability over the medium term in recent months. Faced with the increase in inflationary pressures observed during the first half of 2008 and in a context characterized by rising inflation prospects, the central bank's key interest rate was first raised by 25 basis points in September, to 3.50%, with the aim of preventing the second-round effects associated with the rise in commodity prices internationally. With the downward orientation of risks and a central inflation forecast in line with the objective of price stability, the key interest rate was lowered again to 3.25% in March 2009. At the same time, given the magnitude and sustainability of the need for liquidity on the money market and the forecasts for the evolution of liquidity factors, the central bank has reduced the monetary reserve rate twice: from 15% to 12% from January 2009 and to 10% from 1 July. Minister, Ladies and Gentlemen, Recent developments in the economic environment and the implications of the global crisis are prompting us to improve Morocco's macroeconomic management. We must therefore learn the lessons of this crisis without depriving our economy of the benefits of liberalisation and financial innovations. As the challenges facing macroeconomic policy will therefore intensify, the quality of macroeconomic management is of particular importance in this regard. The monetary policy framework will therefore need to be continuously adapted to be able to accompany these economic changes. Thus, for Morocco, the need to shift the objective of monetary policy towards inflation targeting in the medium term stems from the process of the country's integration into the world economy. This dynamic is accelerating, in particular due to the deepening of tariff dismantling with the European Union and the signing of free trade agreements with new countries. The commitments made by Morocco, within the framework of these agreements, will further deepen financial and trade openness. At the same time, the cumulative effect of the process of gradual easing of foreign exchange regulations is beginning to have an impact on the country's financial integration. In this context, we have accelerated the process of putting in place the elements necessary for the adoption of the inflation-targeting strategy. This should be done in parallel with the deepening of the money and foreign exchange markets, as well as the strengthening of the capacity of economic operators to manage foreign exchange risk. Thank you for your attention

text: INTERNATIONAL WORKING GROUP UNDER THE THEME "Strategic management in central banks" SPEECH BY Mr. Director General Rabat Monday, May 4, 2015 Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a real pleasure for me to welcome you today to the Bank Al-Maghrib Training Center, to this meeting dedicated to strategic planning, a major concern for the central bankers that we are. I would like to thank all the participants and speakers present here, from Europe, Asia and Africa, for the interest they are giving to this meeting. My thanks go in particular to the Banque de France team for the support and support given to the organization of this event, which is the result of more than a year of efforts and cooperation between our two institutions. As you know, the recent financial and economic crisis has profoundly changed the world of central banks. It has fundamentally impacted their roles and responsibilities, making them more extensive and complex. From the very first manifestations of the turbulence, central banks pursued very accommodative monetary policies, resulting in significant cuts in their key interest rates. As the floor levels were quickly reached, they turned to the implementation of new "unconventional" measures, involving the injection of large amounts and the broadening of the panel of counterparties. The size of their balance sheets has increased, their composition has increased. diversified, and financial and reputational risks have intensified in consequence. Central banks have thus assumed tasks that have sometimes gone beyond what their price stability mandate requires. For the most part, they have been given macroprudential responsibility, which clearly introduces financial stability into their prerogatives and translates into the need to take preventive measures to combat the formation of systemic risks. For some, responsibility for supervision has been transferred to them, as is the case with the ECB, which is becoming the sole supervisor of banks in the Euro area, marking a change in the trend of separation of the different supervisory bodies. For others, they are in the process of initiating reforms, according to institutional models appropriate to their economic and political contexts. Ladies and Gentlemen The use of new monetary policy instruments, the reinterpretation of mandates in terms of financial stability and the expansion of the supervisory powers of central banks raise questions about the ability of these banks to carry out their tasks, while avoiding conflicts of objectives and interests. This question is all the more important since, at the same time, the Central banks carry out other equally important activities, which have also been affected by the fallout from the crisis, such as the management of gold and foreign exchange reserves and the issuance of money. These developments require a review of the governance and functioning of central banks, while enhancing transparency and communication to meet increased requirements in terms of the reissue of accounts. They also involve constantly adapting human resources management models and taking into account the opportunities offered by the development of new technologies. These are all challenges that we, as central bankers, should face, even though the resources we have are generally limited. While it is true that our existence is not threatened by financial difficulties, our ability to meaningfully carry out our missions could be compromised, as could our independence. It is in this particular context that we should place our meeting today. Central banks are multifunctional institutions and the expectations placed on them are very high. Many projects must be planned and carried out to effectively and efficiently manage all the complexity of our activities. The questions that arise are: By what means? And according to what modalities? Before providing some answers, I would like to make a small analogy with the private sector, for which the imperative of planning for the future is a condition for existence, success and sustainability. Indeed, planning is rooted in the practices of private organizations because they generally operate in a competitive environment. The generalization of planning practices in the private sector has also been accompanied by numerous research works and academic publications, promoting the dissemination of good practices in this area. Certainly the world of Central Banks is different: we carry out singular missions, of general interest, set out in our statutes and not subject to any form of competition. However, over the recent period, central banks have begun to converge towards strategic management models that are more compatible with their specificities, due to many challenges, including those I mentioned at the beginning of my speech. My conviction is that strategic management in central banks is likely to provide a useful framework for leading and succeeding in structuring institutional and operational changes:  on the one hand, it makes it possible to conduct an in-depth reflection on the impacts of the environment, but also to provide solutions; it also makes it possible to prioritize the initiatives to be carried out and to allocate the necessary resources to them.  on the other hand, it promotes the monitoring and evaluation of the objectives set, through the implementation of a dedicated steering approach based on the evaluation of the achievement of concrete and measurable results. I am convinced that such an approach is a tool for good governance. At a time when our activities are expanding, its appropriation will improve the quality of our services and meet our mandates. For our part at Bank Al-Maghrib, we have adopted a strategic planning approach since 2004, which allows us to set our priorities within the framework of three-year plans. We are now in our 4th planning cycle and we began work last January to develop our 2015-2018 plan. We have also set up and strengthened our process of managing our strategic plans, which is based on a dedicated governance framework and appropriate reporting. These are drawn up on a quarterly basis and are reported to the Government and the Bank's Board. They make it possible, through the evaluation of the results of the indicators and the progress of the projects, to monitor the achievements, to detect the possible difficulties and to adopt necessary corrective actions, while allowing a good control of strategic risks. As you can also see, there is no specific theoretical framework, or even enough space for sharing and dialogue in strategic planning between central banks. I have no doubt that our meeting is likely to help fill this void, through the creation of a rich program that covers all the dimensions related to strategic planning. Thus, as an introduction to the work, the first session of the programme will provide an overview of the processes of the central banks present here. Subsequently, round tables will deal with topics ranging from the design of strategic plans and their operational declination, to their implementation and evaluation, including the modalities of their communication. Similarly, workshops will be held to allow participants to test the tools and different practices, enrich exchanges and compare experiences. In conclusion, let me say that it is a pleasure for Bank Al-Maghrib to convene for two days a group of experts from important institutions such as yours. My sincere hope is that this meeting will lead to the establishment of a permanent channel of exchange on various issues related to strategic planning. The creation of a club of experts, belonging to the institutions present here and to those who could possibly join us, would be the ideal framework, in my opinion, to formalize and ensure the sustainability of exchanges between our institutions. While wishing your work every success, I dare to hope that the organizers and animators show leniency by giving you a little time to enjoy a little of your stay in Rabat and appreciate the millennial richness of this imperial city listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Thank you for your attention.

text: PUBLIC IORWG CONFERENCE International Operational Risk Working Group Rabat, from 24 to 26 April 2013 SPEECH BY MR. WALI Ladies and Gentlemen, I am pleased to welcome you to Morocco and to express to you, on behalf of all the staff of Bank Al-Maghrib, my sincere thanks for your participation in this conference which, as you know, takes place in an international context marked by the financial crisis where risk management has never been brought to the forefront. It is indeed a key element of good governance, particularly for central banks whose main asset is their credibility and the confidence they must inspire at all times and in all circumstances. The holding of your conference in Morocco gives me the opportunity to underline the importance I attach to risk management. Indeed, the development of a risk map according to a structured and concerted approach and its availability to management, as a tool for managing and steering activities, allows a better control of major risks that can impact the achievement of our objectives both strategic and operational. In my opinion, it is important for central banks, in their capacity as regulators, to be at the state of the art in this area in order to set an example for the banking sector and the financial centre as a whole. PUBLIC Thus, since 2005, I have personally ensured the introduction of the risk-based approach within Bank Al-Maghrib, as part of the restructuring of our internal control system, provided for in our first strategic plan which covered the period 2004-2006. To this end, we have adopted, in accordance with international standards and best practices, a participatory risk management approach with an appropriate organization with the required skills in this area. Also, I have closely followed the dynamics of continuous improvement of the "risks and internal control" process, in the same way as the Bank's other business processes, as part of the implementation and maintenance of our quality management system, certified since 2008 against the ISO 9001 standard. I believe that, in its continuous improvement cycle, the risk management process must fully integrate with the overall control environment of the organization and contribute to the overall improvement of performance. In addition, in view of the strengthening of the Bank's strategic framework and the importance of the structuring projects undertaken since 2004, our risk management framework has been extended to include strategic risks and project risks. At the same time, and due to the changes brought about by the international crisis context, the financial risk management framework has been improved through, in particular, the improvement of performance and risk indicators, thus contributing to better governance. This dynamic of improvement, established for some years now, will be continued as part of the current strategic plan (2013-2015) in order to strengthen risk management as part of an integrated vision for the efficient achievement of our objectives. The efforts made and the progress made have convinced us to subject the risk management process both to internal evaluations (self-assessment and internal audit engagement) and to external reviews (peer review) carried out by organizations whose experience is recognized in this area, and whose presence among you today at this conference I welcome. I also encouraged our Institute's membership of your group in 2007, with a view to promoting exchanges and cooperation in the field of risk management, a key factor in this dynamic of improvement. Your conference is, in fact, a platform for the exchange of experiences, the strengthening of partnership, and the development of cooperation. PUBLIC north-south, but also south-south, in the interest of the community of central banks and member institutions. Moreover, in terms of cooperation, we are also regularly asked by central banks, particularly on the African continent, to share with them our experience in risk management. Your conference aims to deal with current topics that challenge decision-makers in more ways than one. This is the case with the themes of "measuring and assessing central banks' reputational risk", "advanced approaches to operational risk assessment" and "risk tolerance and appetite". These themes are of particular importance in the current context, especially since our institutions, which in some cases have had to take non-conventional measures, are undergoing significant changes both in their roles and responsibilities and in their organization. It is essential that risk management, as a central element of the governance framework as I had to mention at the beginning of my speech, accompanies these changes to help us meet the challenges we face. Thanks to your exchanges and the quality of the speakers who will not fail to share with you their know-how, the expectations for the results of the conference are becoming greater and greater. I remain convinced that they will be treated with great interest by our various institutions. I wish you every success in your work and reiterate my thanks for your presence. Finally, I am pleased to invite you and your companions to take advantage of your stay in Morocco and Rabat, an imperial city recently inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, to discover its heritage and its millennial wealth.

text: STUDY DAY ON DATA FROM NON-FINANCIAL BUSINESSES: INTERNATIONAL EXPERIENCES CENTRAL BANK CROSSINGS SPEECH BY THE GOVERNOR DE BANK AL-MAGHRIB ABDELLATIF JOUAHRI RABAT MARCH 30, 2012 Mr President of the CGEM, representatives of central banks, representatives of public and private bodies, It is a great pleasure for me to welcome you on the occasion of this study day organized by Bank Al-Maghrib on the theme: "Data companies: cross-border international experiences of banks power stations' , welcoming and addressing my thanks to our privileged partners, present here, whether they are central banks, public administrations or private bodies for have agreed to exchange experiences and deepen their reflection around this theme. As an introduction to our work, I would like to recall the importance of company data for all economic actors and share with you the experience of Bank Al-Maghrib aimed at strengthening the informational device used for the conduct of its missions while ensuring its convergence with international standards. Ladies and gentlemen Business data is increasingly being solicited by different economic actors, governments, private sector actors or central banks. For governments, business data contributes to the assessment of the potential of the economic fabric and thus make it possible to design economic policies and coherent sectoral development. For the private sector, business information is a fundamental instrument for making strategic investment choices and is a key indicator for assessing the business climate. For central banks, corporate data, whether from surveys or accounting statements, make it possible to deepen the analytical arrangements underlying monetary policy and to strengthen those concerning banking supervision or macro-prudential policy. By their availability, at high frequencies and in a short time, survey data supplement national accounts indicators with more detailed information and contribute to the assessment of economic conditions in real time and even to the preparation of short-term forecasts. Such data also provide information on the rate of capacity utilisation of enterprises, a relevant indicator for measuring demand pressures on prices that central banks necessarily integrate into the monetary policy framework. For their part, the data extracted from the so-called "balance sheet data" accounting statements are of great use to central banks in several respects:  They provide an assessment of the impact of monetary policy on corporate balance sheets and net wealth and deepen the understanding of monetary policy transmission channels.  They offer the possibility of assessing the financial soundness of companies and their level of indebtedness. Ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to highlight the significant progress made by Morocco in recent decades in building and consolidating the national statistical apparatus. As evidenced by the various evaluations of international institutions, the statistical system Is comprehensive, reliable and transparent and today aligns with international best standards and practices. This is an opportunity for me to salute here today the efforts undertaken by all stakeholders which constitutes to advance the process of modernization and deepening of the national statistical and information system, and in particular the Office of the High Commissioner for Planning (HCP). I remain convinced that the progress made will continue to meet the requirements of rigour and consistency, in order to consolidate the effectiveness of our statistical and information apparatus.
