Title: At "The Euromoney Morocco Conference"
text: The Euromoney Morocco Conference Building a new economic paradigm Speech by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 19 February 2019 Ladies and gentlemen I feel a real pleasure to take part with you this morning in this first Euromoney conference in Morocco. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the organizers, in particular Mr. Richard Banks, for the completion of the project of this meeting, but also for the chosen theme "Building a new economic paradigm". There is currently a broad debate in Morocco on public policies and on the development model as a whole. His Majesty the King called for a rethink and invited stakeholders to contribute. There have certainly been many reports and conferences on this issue in recent months, but in view of the quality and diversity of the speakers, I am sure that the conclusions we will reach today will bring added value to the construction of this new economic paradigm. I know that the morning is busy, I will try to respect the time allotted to me while apologizing in advance if I exceed it. I cannot therefore claim an exhaustive coverage of Morocco's economic strategy, as proposed in the conference programme, but rather to some of its aspects. I would also like to share with you some ideas about challenging our development model. My purpose is not to give a roadmap, but rather to highlight some considerations that I think are important for the shaping of this model. Ladies and gentlemen Morocco is a middle-income country that aspires to accelerate its economic and social development. It certainly faces many challenges common to developing countries, but has two fundamental strengths. It enjoys political stability thanks to a monarchy that guarantees the unity of the country and respect for the rules of democracy, and has since its independence made the constant choice of openness and the market economy, alongside a policy of support for purchasing power. After an ambitious expansionist orientation that led it in the 80s to one of the most difficult periods in its modern economic history, the country managed to stabilize its economy with the implementation of a structural adjustment program. In the 90s, he launched a new generation of reforms, consolidating his choice of openness and liberalization and laying the foundations for a modern financial sector. In the early 2000s, the country initiated major institutional, societal and economic reforms, alongside a major infrastructure development program. For greater diversification of its economy and an improvement in its competitiveness, it has also put in place numerous sectoral development strategies and concludes several free trade agreements as well as strategic partnerships, particularly with the countries of the continent. Thanks to its choices and a prompt and judicious reaction at the highest level of the state, the country managed to get through the turbulence of the Arab Spring. In this wake, it undertook a major constitutional reform, enshrining the primacy of conventional international law, expanding the power of the executive and constitutionalizing the bodies for the protection of rights and freedoms, regulation and good governance. The projects launched since the beginning of this millennium have produced tangible results, with a significant acceleration in growth, a trend a slowdown in unemployment and a catch-up on several aspects of human development. Morocco has also been able to strengthen its position on the global map of car manufacturing, set itself up as a reference in the development of renewable energies and establish itself as a gateway to the continent, with in particular a banking system present in 26 African countries and a CFC pole confirming itself as a regional financial hub. That said, it is clear that over the past five years, despite continued efforts, the economy has seen a deceleration in growth and job creation, as well as resistance to falling inequality. This situation is amplified by social networks in the perception of the population which sometimes expresses a certain mistrust of the political class and intermediate bodies. These findings suggest that the development model is beginning to reach its limits and have led His Majesty the King to call for a rethinking and improvement. Putting the country back on a higher and sustainable development path depends on strengthening the resilience and adaptive capacity of the economy. This certainly presupposes a continuation of reforms but with a greater requirement in terms of efficiency and efficiency and a better consideration of a volatile and uncertain international environment. I would like to elaborate further on this last point before presenting some reforms that we are putting in place in this direction in Morocco. Ladies and gentlemen A decade after the advent of the 2008 crisis, its aftermath still persists and will certainly continue for a few more years. I am referring in particular to the worsening of the indebtedness of companies and States whose levels are approaching those of the crisis of the 80s, to the high rates of youth unemployment, widening social inequalities and erosion of trust in public and political institutions in particular. These developments, as well as the resurgence of migratory flows, linked in part to the multiplication of armed conflicts, have resulted in a rise in populism and the coming to power of extremist parties in several countries. The eurozone, Morocco's main trading partner, is among the most affected regions. The difficulties of uniting states around the common policy, the multiplication of identity claims, the twists and turns around Brexit, and the demographic ageing experienced by several large countries, limit the chances of strong and sustainable growth. The hope of solid expansion since 2017 has quickly given way to growing concerns about rising protectionism and the questioning of multilateralism and the rules governing global trade. Globalization, which has led to a remarkable rise in global value chains and an unprecedented reduction in poverty, is giving way to a new era that some call "slowbalization". It is these uncertainties in the global economy that explain the orientation of central banks in some advanced economies to slow the pace of normalization of their monetary policies. We hear the ECB reiterate the wording "as long as necessary" and the Fed recently announce that its committee will be patient in adjusting its target range of its rate. In addition, other profound changes are reshaping traditional patterns of production, consumption and exchange. These include the digital revolution whose implications are uncertain and complex, especially in the financial sector. The development of crypto-assets, the reflections around the creation of a central bank digital currency and the risks of cybercrime are some examples. The difficulty of apprehending them led the IMF and the World Bank to launch what is now known as the Bali Fintech Agenda. Global warming remains another concern that dominates international agendas, but the alarming reports that follow one another suggest that its pace is much faster than that of action. Ladies and gentlemen The challenge today for the public decision-maker is to integrate this given of persistent uncertainty and a volatile and unpredictable environment into the development and implementation of public policies. It is to face this context that Morocco initiated in January 2018, a transition to a more flexible exchange rate regime that aims to strengthen the capacity of its economy to absorb external shocks and support its competitiveness. Thanks to careful preparation and a broad consultation process, it is now taking place in good conditions, with appropriation by the banking system, a gradual adaptation of operators and a continuous deepening of the market. The evolution of the exchange rate within the fluctuation band without intervention by the Central Bank confirms, in accordance with our assessments, that the value of the dirham remains aligned with the fundamentals of the economy. While we welcome these developments, we remain vigilant and continue to support stakeholders and communicate in a targeted manner on the reform. In the perspective of the transition to the phases Bank Al-Maghrib continues to develop an inflation-targeting framework to be put in place at the appropriate stage of transition. This new framework should strengthen the autonomy of monetary policy and enable it to better anchor expectations and ultimately improve the transmission of its decisions. As the international financial crisis has clearly demonstrated, the resilience of the economy depends largely on the resilience of its financial system. In this area, Morocco has made significant progress in recent years thanks to regular work to deepen and diversify, but also to strengthen regulations in line with the best international standards. Like several central banks, Bank Al-Maghrib, in collaboration with other regulators, has set up a macro-prudential supervision framework including the establishment of a Committee dedicated to monitoring and evaluating the financial stability of our country. We also remain vigilant to the risks associated with technological innovations and money laundering and terrorist financing activities. In this regard, we are continuing our efforts to ensure compliance with the standards required in this area, particularly those of the FATF and FATCA, and to strengthen the resilience and security of our information systems. Thanks to these efforts, the FSAP carried out in 2015 as well as the assessments conducted by the IMF as part of the Article IV consultations and the reviews of the precautionary and liquidity line that Morocco has enjoyed since 2012, now confirm the soundness of the banking system. At the same time, special attention is paid to the most fragile or excluded segments of the system. I am referring to very small, small and medium-sized enterprises, but also to certain sections of the population, particularly young people, women and the rural population. It is in this spirit that we have jointly finalized with the Ministry of Finance the national strategy for financial inclusion, with the objectives of reducing the deficit and reducing inequalities in this area. The recent introduction of participatory finance, payment institutions, mobile payment, microcredit reform as well as the many ongoing projects relating in particular to microfinance and crowdfunding should contribute to the achievement of the objectives set out in this framework. In a situation where activity is operating below its potential, it is important that financing is accessible and incentive to invest. This is what led us at Bank Al-Maghrib to pursue an accommodative monetary policy and resort to unconventional measures. In this sense, and since 2013, we have in particular set up a specific mechanism for the financing of MSMEs and a dedicated observatory. Today, the results are encouraging, but efforts must continue, as this problem, it must be recalled, is global and recurrent. Ladies and gentlemen Ensuring the balance and soundness of public finances is also a key factor in the resilience of the economy. I will not dwell on this point, I will simply recall that in this area, important progress has been made and many projects are underway to introduce greater efficiency, visibility and transparency into the public financial management. I would mention in particular the reforms of subsidies and pension funds, the Organic Finance Law, not to mention the major overhaul of social policy focused on the establishment of a single social register that will allow better targeting of the population and optimization of resources. In addition, Morocco is working to ensure favourable conditions for investment, including a major reform of the judiciary, the development of an anti-corruption strategy and several measures to improve the business climate. The results in this area are certainly encouraging, as evidenced by the evolution of the country's position in various international rankings such as Doing Business, Economic Freedom Index, Corruption Perception Index, but significant room for improvement still exists and efforts must continue. Finally, I would like to stress once again the central role of human capital as a determining factor in economic and social development. Our country certainly has many challenges to meet in this area, but there is a strong will and awareness of stakeholders of the importance and scale of this project, as evidenced by the establishment of the Higher Council for Education, Training and Scientific Research. With this mobilization, the development of the 2030 vision and its declination into a framework law, Morocco hopes to make up for its deficits and offer better chances of integration to its youth. Ladies and gentlemen Questioning oneself outside the regular exercises of finance laws and electoral appointments is a salutary practice adopted by many countries, both developing and advanced. Often Dedicated commissions are set up to draw up roadmaps for accelerating growth or job creation. In some countries, it is during the development of strategic long-term visions that discussions take place both on the objectives to be achieved and on the means to achieve them. In Morocco, a debate similar to the one we are having today took place during the drafting of the fiftieth anniversary report fifteen years ago, and more recently during the preparation of the report on Morocco's wealth by the EESC and Bank Al-Maghrib on royal instructions. This questioning should be established as an ongoing requirement in the process of developing public policy on the basis of neutral and objective assessments. It is in this way that the country will be able to restore credibility to public action and political institutions. With the regular questioning of its choices, perseverance and courage in the pursuit of structural reforms, the strengthening of good governance at the various levels of the Administration, the consolidation of fundamental balances and the improvement of the resilience of the economy, the country preserves all its chances of being able to achieve its ambition of emergence. The ultimate goal is to be able to meet the aspirations of its population and youth in particular, to reduce inequalities and to strengthen social cohesion. Thank you.

text: Please find attached the presentation by the Governor on the occasion of the International Finance and Business Forum held in Casablanca from 2 to 5 December 2003. PRESENTATION BY THE GOVERNOR On  THE MODERNISATION OF THE LEGAL FRAMEWORK BANKING ACTIVITY IN MOROCCO  Ladies and gentlemen It is a great pleasure and honour for me to address such a distinguished audience on a subject of importance that has challenged the Moroccan authorities for at least two decades and in which Bank Al-Maghrib plays a central role, namely "the modernization of the legal framework of banking activity in Morocco". If this modernization is today at the heart of the financial news of our country, since two important projects relating respectively to the Banking Law and the Statutes of Bank Al-Maghrib will be presented to Parliament shortly and should be approved fairly quickly, it should be emphasized that the process relating to them was started in the 1980s and that it concerned both banks and specialized financial organizations as well as the methods of intervention of the central bank and the conditions for financing the economy. The reforms introduced gradually from the 1980s onwards were aimed at changing the financial system as a whole to support an increasingly open economy and were carried out as part of a vast structural adjustment programme supported by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. This programme aimed to reduce the serious internal and external imbalances resulting from the expansionary policy of the 1970s through the consolidation of public finances, economic liberalization, particularly of prices and foreign trade, and the introduction of far-reaching sectoral reforms. Morocco had to deal at the time with public finance deficits and double-digit inflation rates as well as heavy external debt maturities in the context of a virtual drying up of foreign exchange reserves. Having participated, within the framework of my responsibilities at the time, in the considerable recovery and reform efforts of the early 1980s, I am able to appreciate the progress made since then by Morocco, without underestimating the challenges we still have to face, particularly in terms of deepening structural reforms and consolidating fundamental balances, with a view to perfecting the modernization of the Moroccan economy and financial system and achieving their international integration. The role to be played by the central bank at all these levels is paramount and it intends to assume it fully. In this regard, it is encouraging to note that the new legislation that will be submitted to Parliament provides Bank Al-Maghrib with the necessary tools for its various tasks, whether in terms of achieving macroeconomic stability or strengthening the domestic banking sector, which are essential conditions for the pursuit of structural reforms and the opening up of the economy. In addition, the convincing results of previous reforms and the lessons learned from international experience, particularly in the wake of the Asian and Latin American crises, allow the central bank, which is itself called upon to carry out its own upgrade in terms of organization, supervision and style, to approach this new stage with cautious optimism. Ladies and gentlemen In order to highlight the contributions of the new laws concerning the role of Bank Al-Maghrib and banking activity, it seems to me useful to briefly retrace the developments that our country has experienced in this regard as well as the national and international contexts in which they are situated. Let me first recall that during the first years of independence, the Moroccan intermediation system was very similar. Indeed, to ensure the financing of the economy, the public authorities had created or reorganized specialized financial institutions such as the C.D.G. and the Caisse d'Epargne Nationale for the mobilization of savings, the B.N.D.E. for the financing of industrial investments, the C.N.C.A. for the financing of the agricultural sector and the C.I.H. to support the development of real estate and tourism. They had also entrusted specific tasks to the B.M.C.E. for the financing of foreign trade and credit Populaire for the financing of crafts and small and medium-sized enterprises. In addition, economic developments have led, over the years, to the establishment at the banking level of administered operating and management rules: the introduction of the credit framework (from 1969 to 1972 and again from 1976 to 1990) and the establishment of compulsory jobs to ensure the financing of the Treasury and the economic sectors considered to be priorities. In addition, lending and payable interest rates were also administered. Such a system prevented the emergence of competition and the functioning of market mechanisms and ultimately proved incapable of mobilizing financial resources and ensuring their optimal allocation. Under these conditions, the financing of the economy was all the more hampered by the marginal role of the capital market, with an almost non-existent monetary compartment and sluggish stock market activity. The reforms begun in the early 1980s were already aimed at modernizing the Moroccan financial system as a whole by gradually addressing these handicaps and its archaism, with a view to enabling it to better fulfil its function of mobilizing resources and adapting its structures and modes of operation to the requirements of international openness. In the banking sector, the reform resulted in the decompartmentalization of the sector and the generalization of universal banking, the liberalization of interest rates payable from 1985 and lending rates from 1990 and the deregulation of banking activity, which resulted in the lifting of the credit framework in 1991 and the elimination of compulsory jobs between 1992 and 1998. The first revision of the Banking Act in 1993 consolidated the liberalization orientation of the sector, leading banks to make new products available to their customers and to adopt new credit techniques inspired by those in force at the international level. This period saw a remarkable development of deposits and credits, an extension of electronic banking, a significant increase in atMs and bank account openings and the development of international operations. In parallel with the modernization of the banking system, the government has proceeded to renovate the capital markets through the implementation of a series of reforms that have led to the emergence of a money market and a complete overhaul of the institutional framework governing the financial market. The measures taken in this regard concerned, inter alia, . the adoption by the Treasury of the technique of auctions for the financing of its deficits and the gradual opening of this market to financial institutions and insurance companies as well as to companies, natural persons and non-residents, . the creation of a secondary market for treasury bills that ensures the liquidity of government securities, . the opening of the market to the issuance by the private sector of negotiable debt securities (certificates of deposit, finance company bills and commercial paper) and finally, . the restructuring of the stock market with the constitution, on the one hand, of the Casablanca Stock Exchange as a private law company responsible for the management and development of the securities market and, on the other hand, of stock exchange companies with a monopoly on trading on this market and providing customer services. The reform of the stock market has also led to the creation of Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS), with a view to channelling household savings to this market, as well as to the establishment of a supervisory body, the Securities Ethics Council and a central depository (Maroclear). The objective of these reforms was to promote the construction of a large capital market, prior to financial disintermediation, with a view to allowing all participants to arbitrate between short and long securities within a framework of free market mechanisms. Thanks to these various reforms, the Casablanca Stock Exchange experienced a tremendous expansion during the 1990s, also favored by the success of the privatization program of public companies. In many emerging countries, the liberalization of the financial sector has been accompanied by a weakening of certain credit institutions, and even of the banking system as a whole. In order to contain such a risk, the monetary authorities have put in place strict prudential regulations, based on international standards in this area (minimum capital, Cooke ratio, liquidity and risk division coefficients, classification and provisioning of overdue claims, etc.). This system has been supplemented more recently by the alignment of the accounting of banking institutions with international standards and by the introduction of audit and internal control rules aimed at further informing, and thus making accountable, the governing bodies of these institutions. With regard to Bank Al-Maghrib, in addition to the consecration of its responsibilities for the supervision and organisation of credit institutions, the amendment of its own Statute in 1993 made it possible to significantly strengthen its role in the definition and conduct of monetary policy, affirming its tasks relating to the stability of the national currency and the regulation of the money market and making available to it the instruments required to this effect. In this regard, Bank Al-Maghrib had initiated indirect regulatory instruments in the form of money market advances in 1981, which in 1988 became the main means of allocating "central money" to banks. Indirect adjustment instruments have developed further within the decompartmentalized and deregulated framework organized by the Banking Act of 1993. They allow the central bank, in accordance with its monetary objectives, to act on bank treasuries and therefore on the level of interest rates on the interbank market, which themselves impact the evolution of all interest rates and, ultimately, the behaviour of lenders and borrowers. The efficiency of these instruments has also been enhanced by the significant reduction in Treasury's recourse to central bank financing, at the same time as the consolidation of public finances and the substantial development of its auction issues. Ladies and gentlemen It is undeniable that the Moroccan monetary and financial sector has undergone remarkable developments over the past ten years in an international environment marked by currency fluctuations and financial crises. Despite a growth rate that remains below Morocco's development needs, significant progress has been made in terms of macroeconomic stability and the consolidation of the situation of the banking system, thanks in particular to a control of public finances and the establishment of a rigorous monetary policy and an adequate exchange rate policy, and also thanks to the modern legal framework of banking activity. These results were achieved within a framework of liberalization of the exchange rate regime that accelerated after 1992, a year that marked the end of Morocco's cycle of rescheduling of external debt and recourse to IMF financing. In 1993, for example, the government declared the convertibility of the dirham for current transactions and introduced almost total convertibility for non-resident transactions. They also liberalized foreign loans to finance investment and foreign trade, set up a foreign exchange market, and allowed Moroccan banks to invest their foreign currency holdings abroad. Similarly, if the control of public finances has been facilitated by the revenues of privatizations, it should be emphasized that it is also due to an improvement in the yield of tax revenues, achieved in addition in the context of the tariff dismantling required by our accession to the WTO and by the free trade agreement with the European Union. It is clear that the prospects for the opening up of the national economy and financial markets are forcing all sectors to modernise and complete their upgrading. With regard to the banking system, the need to further modernize its structures and instruments stems as much from the constraints of openness as from the adoption at the international level of new standards concerning its management and the conditions of its supervision. These standards, which also concern the role of the central bank in macroeconomic stability, relate to the governance and supervision of credit institutions as derived from Basel II, as well as to the prevention of financial crises, as well as the fight against the laundering of illicit funds and the financing of terrorism. It is these developments and considerations at the national and international levels that have led the public authorities to modernize the legal and regulatory framework resulting from the 1993 reform. This action has led to the plans to revise both the Banking Law and the Statutes of Bank Al-Maghrib, the main innovations of which I would like to highlight before concluding with some reflections on the new responsibilities of the central bank. With regard to the draft banking law, the following elements should be noted: 1- the extension of the scope of the law: the provisions on supervision and accounting will be applicable to any body with a banking or para-banking activity, such as the C.D.G., the Caisse d'Epargne Nationale, the C.C.G., offshore banks and micro-credit associations. The law also makes the exercise of operations related to financial engineering, wealth management and intermediation for the transfer of funds subject to approval, 2- the redefinition of the powers of the monetary authorities and the advisory bodies, including a strengthening of the powers of Bank Al-Maghrib, 3- the strengthening of prudential supervision of credit institutions, 4- the redefinition of the mission of the auditors, 5- the establishment of cooperation between Bank Al-Maghrib and the other supervisory authorities of the financial sector (insurance and capital market), 6- the establishment of a specific procedure for the treatment of the difficulties of credit institutions, with in particular a derogation from the procedures of amicable settlement and judicial reorganization provided for by the Commercial Code to adapt them to the conditions of the banking activity, 7- the strengthening of the customer protection rules of credit institutions and 8- the strengthening of transparency rules, including the obligation for Bank Al-Maghrib to justify its refusal decisions, the notification to the boards of directors and auditors of the results of on-the-spot checks and customer access to services of common interest such as the central service for payment incidents or the central balance sheet service. The draft banking law aims to ensure that Morocco is part of the recommendations and standards adopted at the international level, with a view to developing a sound, solid and profitable banking system capable of meeting the challenges facing the country, contributing to its economic development and supporting the process of opening up. The Bank Al-Maghrib project is a fundamental revision of the Statutes of the Issuing Institute. It aims to establish a new framework for its organization, management and control. It also enshrines the principle of the separation of executive and monetary functions. Title: During The Meeting Of The African Advisory Group With The Director General Of The IMF
text: MEETING OF THE AFRICAN CONSULTATIVE GROUP MEETING WITH IMF MANAGING DIRECTOR Speech translation of Mr. Abdellatif Jouahri Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib Washington, April 23, 2017 - 1 - Mr. Chairman, Ms. Lagarde, In accordance with its statutes, the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real incomes are fundamental objectives of the IMF. In this regard, we welcome the IMFd5s increasing commitment to inclusive growth and job creation, which became increasingly important in the surveillance and lending policy to member countries. As you know, while many advanced countries are facing the challenge of an aging population, Africa is experiencing high population growth, due to lower mortality and improved life expectancy. The demographic window opens a unique opportunity to accelerate growth and improve the well-being of citizens. However, many of our countries are struggling to develop appropriate policies in order to effectively benefit from this dividend. Many are unable to integrate newcomers into the job market, leaving them more prone to social exclusion and poverty. Such difficulties are likely to increase in the future, owing to the digitalization and technological changes that will make millions of jobs disappear. The least qualified workers who make up the majority of the labor force in Africa today are particularly at risk. While it is clear that sustained and inclusive growth is essential for generating employment and income, investing in quality education and training systems and the implementation of effective labor market policies are crucial for reducing unemployment and boosting growth. In this respect, a study carried out in Morocco shows that an improvement in some indicators of education leads to a significant rise in GDP in the medium and long terms. Ms. Lagarde, There remains one important factor, that relating to freeing women from all obstacles, discrimination or prejudice. This should considerably increase their participation in the labor market, enlarge the scope of skills available and increase the potential for growth and job creation. I can testify to that starting from our own experience at Bank Al-Maghrib where we have highly qualified and trained women who, from a technical point-of-view, match the skills of their male counterparts. In addition, they are generally more engaged and more dedicated. We call on the IMF to continue to make available to our countries relevant analyses and advice in this field and to ensure regular monitoring of the policies implemented to this end. Thank you

Title: During The G-24 Ministerial Meeting
text: CO-OPTATION OF MOROCCO TO THE INTERGOVERNMENTAL GROUP OF TWENTY.FOUR ON INTERNATIONAL MONETARY AFFAIRS AND DEVELOPMENT Speech translation of Mr. Abdellatif Jouahri Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib Washington DC, April 20, 2017 - 1 - Mr. Chairman, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, World Bank Group President, Fellow Ministers and Governors, Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great privilege for me to participate today in this G-24 ministerial meeting, in which Morocco is taking part for the first time as a member country. I would like to thank the Chairman, the Bureau and all the G24 members for having co-opted Morocco to such a dynamic and influential group. We believe the Groupd5s expansion is a wise and timely choice in an ever-changing international environment. For more than 30 years, Morocco has regularly participated in the G24 as an observer. It has always shared the Groupd5s principles and positions, and continuously supported its proposals and recommendations, whether in terms of policies to promote growth and macroeconomic stability on a global scale and in developing countries in particular, the support provided by the Bretton Woods institutions to our countries, the governance reforms of these institutions for a more equitable representation of developing countries, the strengthening of the global financial safety net, and last but not least in terms of the concessional support to low-income countries. The uncertainty that characterizes the international economic situation and the many risks and challenges we face require more than ever the combination of our efforts to strengthen international and regional cooperation. Morocco has made co-development within the African continent a fundamental axis for its foreign policy. Its membership to the G-24 reflects this willingness to strengthen South-South cooperation. I also would like to seize this opportunity to confirm Moroccod5s commitment to step up efforts in the context of the Global Development Agenda and the fight against climate change. Morocco will continue to work towards the implementation of the commitments made at COP 22 which the Kingdom organized in Marrakech last November and which it currently chairs. I cannot miss this opportunity without commending Ms. Lagarde and Dr. Kim for their active participation in the proceedings of our Group and the special attention they pay to its analyses and recommendations. The institutions they head provide considerable support for our efforts to ensure stronger and more inclusive growth for the well-being of our peoples, and we look forward for an even stronger support. Thank you.

Title: During The Meeting Of Mena Finance Ministers And Central Banks Governors With The Director General O...
text: MEETING OF MENA FINANCE MINISTERS AND CENTRAL BANK GOVERNORS WITH IMF MANAGING DIRECTOR d2THE IMPACT OF GLOBAL UNCERTAINTIES ON THE MIDDLE EAST AND NORTH AFRICA REGIONd3 Speech translation of Mr. Abdellatif Jouahri Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib Washington, April 23, 2017 - 1 - Managing Director, Fellow Ministers and Governors, Good afternoon, I would like to thank Ms. Lagarde and through her the Fund for this biannual meeting which has become a well-established meeting point to discuss the challenges specific to our region. The theme chosen for this meeting is very topical. Indeed, the global economy has gained momentum but is becoming increasingly uncertain. We are witnessing rising protectionism and populism which we consider to be the consequences of the crisis and heightened inequalities. Such an increase in uncertainty only exacerbates the loss of confidence and the wait-and-see attitude of economic operators. In this regard, I want to congratulate you and the IMF staff for the excellent quality of the background paper which covers the challenges we face in the MENA region. Let me now focus on the situation of Morocco. Considering the impact of the crisis and its surrounding uncertainties on our traditional partners, particularly in the euro area, we decided to broaden our integration, mainly with African sub-Saharan countries as part of win-win strategies. In recent years, Morocco has increasingly become a refuge for sub-Saharan immigrants. The Moroccan authorities responded through a humanitarian approach, by regularizing the situation of the first waves of illegal immigrants who became full-fledged residents. The uncertainties arising from the trend in commodity prices, particularly oil, and its impact on macroeconomic balance prompted us to implement rather quickly a major reform of subsidies. This reform, together with other reforms which concerned mainly public finances, the justice and pension schemes, has provided us with some fiscal space to increase public investment and strengthen social safety nets. I should highlight here that the instruments which the Fund made available to us have provided us with effective support, as an insurance against external shocks. In a further measure aimed at mitigating the impact of uncertainties and external shocks on the economy, we have initiated a gradual transition to exchange rate flexibility. Preparations are nearing completion and we will start implementation at the beginning of the second half of this year. As you pointed out in the background paper, communication about reforms is very important in order for the citizen to embrace the reforms. I would like to take this opportunity to commend the quality of the Fundd5s teams who worked with us during this preparatory phase. I think there is another source of uncertainty that weighs on our economies, particularly on the financial sector. It is about digitization that calls for fundamental changes and adaptations of our market and regulatory institutions. In this regard, the IMF may need to establish a roadmap to accompany the countries of our region in developing and implementing effective policies. However, I would like to conclude with a certainty, which is the joint organization by the IMF and Morocco in 2018 of the Second High-Level Conference on reinforcing inclusive growth in the region, after the one that was held in Jordan in 2014. This is an additional manifestation of the Fundd5s interest in our countries. Thank you.

Title: Insurance Meeting: Inclusion in Insurance & Pandemic Resilience
text: Rendez-Vous de Casablanca de l'Assurance Inclusion in insurance & resilience to pandemics Speech by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Casablanca, 31 March 2021 Dear Minister of Economy, Finance and Administrative Reform, Mr Secretary General of the Insurance and Social Security Supervisory Authority, Mr. President of the Moroccan Federation of Insurance and Reinsurance Companies, Ladies and gentlemen First of all, I would like to thank the organizers and in particular Mohamed Hassan Bensalah, President of the Moroccan Federation of Insurance and Reinsurance Companies, for inviting me to this meeting. I am delighted that they have maintained it even if it is in a semi-virtual format, it is a sign of optimism that a gradual return to normality is beginning. I would therefore like to congratulate them on this decision, but also on the choice of theme, which could not be more relevant in the current context. I have no doubt that the debate will be rich and profound, with the list of speakers being impressive both in terms of quality and diversity, an observation to which this forum has accustomed us since its inception. As far as I am concerned, I would like to share with you some thoughts on the chosen theme and the implications of the paradigm shifts induced or accelerated by the crisis. In my opinion, the latter pose real challenges that should be addressed, but at the same time there are immense opportunities to be seized. Ladies and gentlemen Like everywhere else, we have just experienced a year unlike any other, marked by a multifaceted crisis of rare depth. While the aftermath of this pandemic would certainly continue in the years to come, one year after its onset, we better appreciate its economic impact. and social, and we are able to draw the first lessons. In particular, the crisis has enabled us to measure the extent of the vulnerability suffered by large parts of the productive fabric but also of the population, in particular that occupied in informal activities. She reminded us of the need to strengthen economic and social resilience in our country. An imperative that we made bank al-Maghrib the main message of the introductory speech of the Bank's latest annual report. It is also one of the most recurrent recommendations in international forums and debates in recent months. At a meeting last July hosted by the Paris Forum and the Saudi Presidency of the G20, the Managing Director of the IMF called resilience "the new religion of the IMF." Investing in resilience is part of a long-term forward-looking approach. It is a question of moving from a mode of action that I will call "firefighters", acting retrospectively, to another based on anticipation and prevention. It should be generalized to all areas and benefit all categories of the population. This is what will ensure the inclusiveness of our development. The concept of inclusion was first put forward at the macroeconomic level to draw attention to the fact that economic growth is not automatically synonymous with improved living standards and reduction of inequalities. It is only when it benefits all strata of the population, that is, when it is inclusive. This concept was subsequently transposed to several areas, including finance with the development of microfinance and inclusive insurance. The latter, which is based on new approaches to enable low populations Revenues from protecting themselves against risks, are now attracting growing interest from public and private actors in the financial ecosystem. In our country, the development of inclusive insurance is one of the priority objectives of the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion that the Ministry of Finance and Bank Al-Maghrib developed together with stakeholders and launched in 2019. The roadmap of this strategy provides for three axes for this component. The first is to design innovative offers adapted in particular to low-income populations, micro-enterprises and MSMEs, with the mobilization of new distribution channels such as microcredit associations and payment institutions. The other two are to strengthen the supply of insurance in the agricultural sector as well as financial education and communication. In this regard, the Foundation for Financial Education that we set up in 2013 is called upon to play a central role. In collaboration with ACAPS and the Moroccan Federation of Insurance and Reinsurance Companies, it is already working on the development of an education program on inclusive insurance whose objective is to raise awareness among individuals of the importance of protecting property and people. At the legal level, the draft law on microfinance aims to extend the activity of this sector to micro-savings as well as to the offer of micro-insurance products. In the same vein, we are working, ACAPS and Bank Al-Maghrib, for the implementation of the "Takaful" Insurance, a product that conditions the development of participatory finance and is being finalized with the coordination and mobilization of all stakeholders. Ladies and gentlemen I would now like to address the implications of the paradigm shifts induced or accelerated by the crisis on the insurance sector, but first, recall the role of the latter in the economy because I think it is not often highlighted. Indeed, insurance as an industry contributes significantly to the mobilization of savings, especially long-term savings, which are crucial for investment and development in a country like ours. Monetary statistics compiled by Bank Al-Maghrib show that the financial investments of insurance and reinsurance companies are around 180 billion dirhams. Of this amount, 40 billion is invested in debt securities, including nearly 23 billion in the form of treasury bills. This shows the high level of participation in the financing of the economy. They also contribute to the dynamism of the stock market and asset management activity, with an investment of nearly 123 billion dirhams in the form of shares and shares. These data show that it is clearly a central component of the financial sector, contributing to its development and stability. Moreover, ACAPS, regulator of the sector, is a member alongside the Ministry of Finance, the AMMC and BAM of the Committee for the Coordination and Supervision of Systemic Risks. That said, the sector's development margins remain significant. Indeed, the penetration rate measured by the ratio of premiums written to GDP stands at 3.9%, a figure that is certainly among the highest in the region, but which remains below those observed in advanced economies where it reaches in particular 9% for OECD countries. In addition, data from the "Financial Capacities" survey conducted by BAM and the World Bank in 2013 show that only 2% of Moroccans said they had subscribed to non-compulsory insurance products. Several factors explain this observation, the poorly adapted offers, the limited geographical coverage of the distribution network, the low level of financial knowledge and skills, but also and above all low levels of income. Ladies and gentlemen The insurance sector, like other activities in finance and the economy in general, is now facing paradigm shifts and profound changes, some of which began long before the crisis and others, the crisis was the catalyst. One of the major challenges facing the insurance industry today is low interest rates. It is often forgotten or ignored, but a rate cut does not only have positive consequences. It certainly helps to boost demand and investment, but also has a negative impact on savings, especially small savings. It could weigh on the balance of pension funds and on the profitability of insurance undertakings, and thus on financial stability. Unfortunately, the "low and long-term interest rate" environment is a new reality that industry players are called upon to take into account in their strategies and decisions. Indeed, the secular stagnation of the global economy and the disinflationary movement induced by structural factors such as technology and demography would likely maintain pressure on rates in the coming years. In the national context, low interest rates combined with the narrowness of the stock market constitute a real challenge for the development of savings and certain segments of insurance, issues of which we at the Central Bank are well aware, and which are part of the criteria for formulating monetary policy decisions. The second challenge is that of climate change, the consequences of which are obvious, floods, droughts, fires... An increasingly widespread awareness of this issue is leading public and private decision-makers to take this into account in their decisions. In the financial sector in particular, greening is a growing trend with a trend towards its gradual integration into regulatory and supervisory norms and standards. In this sense, insurance players are called upon to adapt and appropriate this trend instead of suffering it in the years to come. For them, it is a double challenge that it is, to take into account the impact on the environment in their investment decisions, but also to develop an offer to protect themselves or to hedge against climate risks. The latter are often systemic and coordination with public actors in the context of Public-Private Partnerships would be the most appropriate framework for their management. The other mutation that never ceases to surprise by its speed as well as by the breadth and depth of its implications, is the digital transformation. It is a revolution at work for a few years now but has accelerated with the crisis which has been an opportunity to appreciate the immensity of the opportunities it offers. I am thinking of teleworking, online schooling, e-commerce, e-Banking and many other areas where technology is disrupting the modes and habits of production and consumption. Insurance, of course, is not on the margins of this revolution. It is called upon to apprehend it in order to adapt its organization, improve its products and its marketing methods. The deluge of data generated by this transformation allows the industry today to better assess risks and design personalized offers at a fair price. Unfortunately, this transformation not only has positive implications, but it is also at the root of one of the most important risks currently and the most difficult to combat. This is cybercrime that threatens private companies, public institutions, governments, individuals... It also poses a major challenge in terms of the protection of personal data, one of the most required conditions in the regulation of economic and social activities. For insurers, it is once again a question of protecting themselves against these risks but also of working to design and propose insurance offers, which represents a potential market that remains to be developed. Ladies and gentlemen It is all of these mutations and certainly many others that are already shaping the post-covid world into which we are gradually entering. While the national insurance industry is working to keep pace with these changes and paradigm shifts, the speed with which they are evolving requires scaling up investment in both technology and human capital. In the latter area in particular, it is becoming increasingly difficult to attract and especially to keep certain profiles, as competition on both the national and international markets is very fierce. Finally, all these developments do not only concern operators, but also regulators such as ACAPS, Bank Al-Maghrib or AMMC. Their role is to anticipate and allow sufficient flexibility while ensuring resilience and stability. For us, it is often a difficult exercise to find this right balance, especially as we suffer another deluge, which is that of increasingly binding international standards. Ladies and gentlemen Today, our country is experiencing a major new situation that is likely to transform the social landscape. The project recently launched by His Majesty the King to generalize social coverage is a real revolution that should allow our country to make a qualitative leap in terms of human development and thus reduce the structural deficit it has recorded in this area since its independence. In this regard, we are all, government, regulators, operators, called to mobilize for the completion of this project. I am convinced that the insurance sector, which has always taken care to make its contribution to actions and policies aimed at the development of our country, will not fail to resolutely subscribe to this royal vision and work for its full realization. Thank you.

Title: At the colloquium on the reconsideration of the development model of Morocco
text: Second International Symposium on the Theme The reconsideration of the development model in the light of the evolutions that Morocco is experiencing Speech by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Skhirat, October 19 , 2018 Dear Head of Government, Dear Ministers, Dear President of the Fez-Meknes region, Dear President of the CGEM, Ladies and gentlemen First of all, I would like to thank the organizers for inviting me and congratulate them on this second meeting and on the theme to which it is dedicated. The debate around the question of our development model responds to the wish of His Majesty the King and is now at the center of the concerns of public decision-makers. I am convinced that many reflections have been carried out since Her Majesty's call and will contribute, each on its own, to shaping the foundations of this new model. At my level, I would like, in the time allotted to me, to place more emphasis on the conditions and factors that will ensure that this new model, whatever the choices made, has the best chances of success and good performance. Ladies and gentlemen The questioning of economic and social policies or the development model as a whole is not specific to Morocco. This is an issue that concerns many countries, both developing and advanced. It often responds to a need to adapt these models to the increasingly rapid changes in the internal and external environment. This is the reality that emerged during the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank held in Bali, Indonesia last week. What we can remember is that profound changes and emerging challenges are taking on worrying dimensions and are challenging everyone, governments, regulatory authorities, international institutions, businesses and civil society. It can be said that digital transformation was one of the issues that captured the most attention during these meetings. Two fundamental observations are almost unanimous today. The first is that this evolution is much faster, deeper and more diffuse than one might think. The second is that there is a lot of uncertainty about its implications and consequences. What is even more worrying is that we do not know so far how to do it. We observe developments, we grope, we look at what others are doing... It is precisely this situation that led the World Bank and the IMF to develop what is called the Bali Fintech Agenda, and which is ultimately a set of general principles to guide everyone's action to make in the face of this revolution, exploit the opportunities it offers and manage the risks it entails. Among the latter, the most important is undoubtedly cybercrime, which generates annually, according to the figures put forward, 1500 billion dollars in illicit revenues. The other major concern is related to the rise of protectionism and populism. Globalization, which until recently had great opportunities, is now being questioned by many countries and large sections of the population. Multilateralism and international cooperation, which make it possible to establish mutually acceptable rules and standards, are also under strain. Obviously this has consequences for all countries, large or small, advanced or developing. Everyone wonders about the impact, the consequences and the strategy to adopt. Geopolitical tensions, migratory movements, climate change, demographic dynamics (ageing of the population for some and strong growth for others), as well as inequalities, including gender inequalities, are other factors that are no less important and are sure to have a significant impact on the economic and social performance of the countries concerned. Ladies and gentlemen In the same context of discussions within the international community, there was also unanimity on a number of common considerations and prerequisites for development models, whatever their nature and orientation, to produce satisfactory results. First of all, it is a question of the development of human capital, the level and quality of which are decisive for the development process. Obviously, this observation challenges us at the level of our country. Morocco's ranking according to the Human Capital Index published by the World Bank on the occasion of these annual meetings reminds us once again of the backlog we have accumulated in this area and the magnitude of the challenge ahead. Certainly, a major project has been launched, with the development of the 2030 vision and its declination into a framework law, but what must be emphasized is that this reform is the last chance to develop our human capital, enhance it and hope to place our country on the path of emergence. This means that we no longer have the right to make mistakes. The second requirement that has also emerged is the need for the development model to be inclusive. That is to say, growth must benefit the vast majority or according to the formula consecrated in English, that no one must be left behind. In addition to the creation of quality jobs, this requires the establishment of redistribution mechanisms, social safety nets to guarantee everyone what can be called a "social SMIG", i.e. decent living conditions (housing, water, electricity and sanitation) and access to education and health. The third fundamental prerequisite is good governance. The aim is to establish a framework for the development and implementation of public policy that is effective and efficient at all levels of the State, to work for a business environment conducive to investment through, in particular, the strengthening of the fight against corruption and the impartiality and fairness of the judicial system. These criteria have recently been incorporated into the IMF's assessments, particularly in the context of Article IV consultations. Such an environment must primarily benefit the company, but the company must in turn ensure its tax transparency and social responsibility alongside its quest for competitiveness and profit. On this aspect of governance, we have, at the level of the Central Bank, called for the establishment of a strategic planning framework that would ensure this overall coherence and create the missing synergies within the framework of a development vision that brings together all stakeholders. The search for this coherence also calls for the need to monitor the implementation of reforms and public policies. In the case of Morocco, several projects and reforms have been launched in recent years, but many have not yet been completed. despite long delays. We can talk about the reforms of pensions, subsidies, the labour code and the law governing the right to strike, to name but a few. The reason for this finding lies precisely in the absence of a monitoring and evaluation framework. This aspect, including sanctioning, is also one of the necessary conditions for the success of the new development model. Ladies and gentlemen If I have stopped and listed the necessary conditions for any development model, it is because in our case it is even more obvious, because while it is true that we have certainly made significant progress in several areas, it is clear that our economic and social performance has weakened in recent years. Indeed, since 2013, non-agricultural growth has returned to a lower level and the downward trend in unemployment has reversed in a particularly worrying way for young urban dwellers. Private investment remains weak despite the incentives granted and macroeconomic balances are fragile. What is still worrying is that this situation is amplified in the perception of the population. The latter expresses in different ways its concerns about unemployment that it perceives to be worsening sharply, a standard of living that it considers to be deteriorating and inequalities that it sees increasing. It is enough to analyse the data from the HCP's quarterly survey of households to realise how negative households are in their assessments. This negative perception is further accentuated by the openness and connectivity that social networks offer today. The latter make it possible to spread messages on a large scale and to have a significant impact on public opinion. Public. We have experienced several such examples recently in our country. What I would like to say is that, here again, communication is a fundamental component in the implementation of reforms to which we unfortunately do not attach the importance it deserves, although it is essential to ensure the proper understanding and support of stakeholders and thus increase the chances of success of these reforms. Ladies and gentlemen The adjustment of our development model, which is the subject of our debate today, is a long-term undertaking that requires significant and continuous efforts. The results of this repositioning cannot all be expected in the short term, while as I have just mentioned, expectations are important and pressing. As a result, the State needs to free up margins and prioritize actions to meet urgent needs, particularly in the social field. For this reason, and in view of the means at our disposal, the optimization of resources and the rationalization of expenditure are permanent imperatives in the management of public finances. However, as we all know, the tax base is narrow due, in part, to the relatively high weight of informal activities, the return on public spending is low and the relevance of the many tax incentives remains to be demonstrated. In other words, my point is that such reforms do not call for sacrificing macroeconomic balances. On the contrary, for an economy like ours, high levels of deficits and public debt are quickly sanctioned by rating agencies. and international institutions and question the attractiveness of the country and the confidence of operators. Above all, we must not find ourselves in the situation of the 80s and the structural adjustment plans. In the same vein, the conditionalities imposed on certain countries in the region or even on advanced countries such as Greece remind us that the best way to preserve the sovereignty of its decision is to ensure its balances and that there is no sustainable growth and development without macroeconomic stability. Ladies and gentlemen The reflection around our development model as desired by His Majesty the King is a collective effort that requires the mobilization of all stakeholders. Each should make its contribution according to its field of intervention, its experience and the challenges it faces. This is the logic behind Her Majesty's call in her last speech. From my personal experience of more than 55 years in the public service, I can say that we often manage to make good diagnoses and we manage to formulate appropriate solutions, but what we often lack is to have "the long breath" to complete the projects and make them succeed. That being said, we must remain optimistic because, given the magnitude of the challenges and constraints in the difficult context we are going through and especially to respond to the successive calls of His Majesty the King, the burst will have to come at the level of the political elite, the officials and executives of the Administration as well as public and private operators, mobilized that we will be to ensure our country and its population the best possible future. Thank you.

Title: International Seminar on the National Information System and Modelling
text: International Seminar National Information System and Modelling Theoretical foundations and development issues Speech by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 21 January 2020 Dear Perpetual Secretary of the Hassan II Academy of Science and Technology, Dear Minister, Mr. Wali Director General of Local Authorities, Dear Secretaries General, Eminent researchers and professors, Honorable Assistance, It is a real pleasure for me to take part in this seminar dedicated to the national information system and economic modelling. A little over two years ago, I was invited to speak on the role of mathematics in the economic and monetary field and I have excellent memories of the enriching exchanges we had in this very Chamber. I am convinced that it will be the same at this meeting, which is part of the continuity of the efforts of the Hassan II Academy of Sciences and Techniques on themes related to economic development. In this regard, I would like to congratulate Professor Omar Fassi-Fehri on this initiative, to which Bank Al-Maghrib has not hesitated to make its contribution. For the time allotted to me, I would like to share with you some ideas from the perspective of the head of an institution that is both a producer and a major user of data, but also that makes intensive use of economic modelling. I will articulate them around three conditions that seem to me essential for economic modelling, focusing on that relating to data. Like all central banks and many institutions represented here, Bank Al-Maghrib has developed over the years a set of models and statistical tools that allow it to meet its needs in terms of forecasting, simulations and impact analyses of public policies, stress tests, etc. I am not likely to be mistaken in saying that there is unanimity on the contribution and added value of these tools, which are in many cases almost unavoidable, but they require a certain number of prerequisites that seem essential to me. First, as we all know, modeling consists of formalizing economic relations in the form of mathematical equations in order to measure the correlation or causality between the variables considered. This presupposes that these relationships are governed by market mechanisms with a certain depth or by dynamics that are preparing for identification and quantification. However, not all of these conditions may be fully met. This is particularly the case when the economy lacks depth or when the variables considered are subject to recurrent and significant shocks. Formalization may lose its relevance and may not make it possible to understand the behaviors and interactions of agents and markets. Examples abound in this direction, because in our country, for example, could we claim to produce a forecast of agricultural growth with a reasonable level of accuracy in September? Is it possible to predict even over a horizon of a few weeks the evolution of the prices of food products such as fresh vegetables? At a more global level, what credit should be given to the oil price forecasts published by international institutions? Frequent and sometimes large-scale revisions remind us of the need for caution in their use. Second, an important problem that is often overlooked is that of measuring variables. The latter refer to theoretical concepts that can be difficult to grasp in practice. For example, how reliable are microeconomic data on household incomes even in countries with developed tax collection systems? GDP, one of the best-known economic aggregates, suffers in its measure from several limitations, particularly in terms of coverage, both in developing and advanced economies. This explains in particular the regular changes in the basis of national accounts, which generally result in upward revisions to the estimates of this aggregate. Another illustration that is particularly relevant for central banks is the measurement of inflation. This is a problem that remains complex as evidenced by the recurrent debate on what to consider as inflation (GDP deflator, consumer prices, core inflation, etc.). Added to this are other difficulties such as the measurement of rent, or more recently, the choice of points of sale in view of the growing weight of online commerce. The example of Amazon and its impact on price dynamics has become a textbook case that is being researched at the most prestigious academic institutions in the world. Even more enlightening, there is a broad consensus that the measures we have today overestimate inflation, contrary to the general perception of the population. The reasons are known and widely documented in the literature. These include the increasingly important substitution effect, the failure to take into account the improvement in the quality of many products... Ladies and gentlemen The third point I would like to raise is that of the availability of data. Of course, I know that it is not at the hearing that I have before me that we have to explain the importance of information for decision-making, but I am afraid that there are not so many who appreciate the magnitude of the task of statistical production and its requirements in terms of human and financial resources. Official statistics are obtained only after a rigorous process of collection, processing and reliability according to known and recognized methodologies. Once available, it is then used for the determination of needs, the monitoring and evaluation of public policies and the prediction of economic and social developments, often through sophisticated models. The latter are generally very demanding in terms of data. Could we claim to have enough for an appropriate formalization of the national economy. I think if you ask that question at such a hearing in any country, you will be told that we would like to have even more. On this same note, and contrary to what the recurrent controversies over the figures would suggest, Morocco enjoys, in comparison with its peers, a good position in terms of the development of its statistical system. It should be remembered in this sense that we are among the first countries in the Africa and MENA regions to adhere to the IMF's Special Data Dissemination Standard. Certainly, there are always margins to do even better. If I have to mention an axis of reform, I will prioritize as a central bank the improvement of the production of infra-annual quantitative economic data. On the other hand, from a broader perspective, I think there is an urgent need to review the legal framework of the national statistical system. It remains governed by texts dating back to 1968, more than half a century. For a system as decentralized as ours, it is necessary to put in place a framework and bodies capable of ensuring greater coordination of its various components, to establish priorities in terms of operations to be carried out and to establish clear rules and policies in terms of production, dissemination and accessibility. In short, it is a question of ensuring that users have the most reliable service in the field of official statistics. Ladies and gentlemen The questioning of approaches and modes of organization is in itself a healthy practice, I would even say essential in view of the profound changes that the ecosystem of official statistics is experiencing. The predominant role of the latter as the main source of information is, with the digital revolution, challenged by new players who provide huge amounts of more detailed, up-to-date and often less expensive data. While official statistics continue to stand out for its methodological rigour and transparency, which facilitate its use and international comparability, the opportunities offered by unstructured data cannot be ignored. The exploitation of the latter allows, thanks to the development of technologies and new professions such as data scientists, to draw useful lessons that bring an increasingly important added value. For empirical research in particular, these data are now presented as a new Eldorado for innovation and experimentation. That said, caution must remain in order, especially when it comes to public decision-making, which often has significant impacts on the economy and the population. "How should official statistics understand this new situation?" remains a question asked and whose exploration is only in its infancy. The fact that an entire session of this meeting is dedicated to big data testifies to the growing interest in it. Ladies and gentlemen, The questions we raise in this meeting are not country-specific and should not be one-off. Remember in the aftermath of the 2008 global crisis, there was a questioning of the models used for forecasting and questions about the availability of the data needed to predict economic downturns with reasonable accuracy. It is these questions that have led institutions like the IMF to reflect on how to rethink macroeconomic policy. This is also what prompted the G20 member countries to launch the Data GAPS Initiative in 2009 with a particular focus on the financial sector, paradoxically the field most abundant in high-frequency data. One of the major lessons of this crisis is the need to remain cautious and modest in the face of the complexity of human behavior and the uncertainty surrounding the implications of the profound changes shaping our environment. One only has to note the frequency and especially the extent of the revisions of the forecasts of such prestigious institutions as the IMF or the World Bank to realize the difficulty of apprehending economic developments. Opportunities such as the one offered to us today allow us to exchange and debate the challenges we face and the opportunities to be seized to ensure the availability of reliable data for better decision-making and ultimately for the benefit of the citizen. Thank you.

Certes, je sais que ce n<d5>est pas <88> l<d5>audience que j<d5>ai devant moi qu<d5>il faut expliquer l<d5>importance de l<d5>information pour la prise de d<8e>cision, mais je crains qu<d5>ils ne soient pas si nombreux ceux qui mesurent l<d5>ampleur de la t<89>che que constitue la production statistique et de ses exigences en termes de ressources humaines et financi<8f>res. La statistique officielle n<d5>est obtenue qu l<d5>issue d<d5>un processus rigoureux de collecte, de traitement et de fiabilisation selon des m<8e>thodologies connues et reconnues. Une fois disponible, elle est alors utilis<8e>e pour la d<8e>termination des besoins, le suivi et lvaluation des politiques publiques et la pr<8e>vision des <8e>volutions <8e>conomiques et sociales, souvent par le biais de mod<8f>les sophistiqu<8e>s. Ces derniers sont en g<8e>n<8e>ral tr<8f>s exigeants en mati<8f>re de donn<8e>es. Pourrions-nous pr<8e>tendre en avoir suffisamment pour une formalisation appropri<8e>e de lconomie nationale. Je pense que si vous posez cette question <88> pareille audience dans n<d5>importe quel pays, on vous r<8e>pondra qu<d5>on aimerait en avoir encore plus. Sur ce m<90>me registre, et contrairement <88> ce que laisserait croire les pol<8e>miques r<8e>currentes sur les chiffres, le Maroc jouit, en comparaison avec ses pairs, d<d5>une bonne position en mati<8f>re de d<8e>veloppement de son syst<8f>me statistique. Il est <88> rappeler dans ce sens que nous sommes parmi les premiers pays des r<8e>gions Afrique et MENA <88> adh<8e>rer <88> la Norme Sp<8e>ciale de Diffusion des Donn<8e>es du FMI. Certes, il y a toujours des marges pour faire encore mieux. Si je dois <8e>voquer un axe de r<8e>forme, je prioriserai en tant que banque centrale l<d5>am<8e>lioration de la production des donn<8e>es <8e>conomiques quantitatives infra-annuelles. Par contre, dans une perspective plus large, je pense qu<d5>il y a urgence de revoir le cadre l<8e>gal du syst<8f>me statistique national. Celui-ci reste en effet r<8e>gi par des textes qui remontent <88> 1968, soit plus d<d5>un demi-si<8f>cle. Pour un syst<8f>me aussi d<8e>centralis<8e> que le n<99>tre, il est n<8e>cessaire de mettre en place un cadre et des instances <88> m<90>me d<d5>assurer une plus forte coordination de ses diff<8e>rentes composantes, dtablir les priorit<8e>s en mati<8f>re d<d5>op<8e>rations <88> r<8e>aliser et d<d5>instaurer des r<8f>gles et des politiques claires en termes de production, de diffusion et d<d5>accessibilit<8e>. En bref, il s<d5>agit d<d5>assurer pour les utilisateurs le service le plus fiable en mati<8f>re de statistique publique. Mesdames et Messieurs, La remise en question des approches et des modes d<d5>organisation est en soi une pratique saine, je dirai m<90>me primordiale eu <8e>gard aux mutations profondes que connait lcosyst<8f>me de la statistique officielle. Le r<99>le pr<8e>dominant de cette derni<8f>re comme principale source d<d5>information se trouve, avec la r<8e>volution digitale, concurrenc<8e> par de nouveaux acteurs qui fournissent des quantit<8e>s <8e>normes de donn<8e>es plus d<8e>taill<8e>es, <88> jour et souvent moins co<9e>teuses. Certes la statistique officielle continue de se distinguer par sa rigueur et sa transparence m<8e>thodologiques qui facilitent son utilisation et sa comparabilit<8e> internationale, mais on ne peut ignorer les opportunit<8e>s qu<d5>offrent les donn<8e>es non structur<8e>es. L<d5>exploitation de ces derni<8f>res permet, gr<89>ce au d<8e>veloppement des technologies et de nouveaux m<8e>tiers tels que les data scientists, d<d5>en tirer des enseignements utiles qui apportent une valeur ajout<8e>e de plus en plus importante. Pour la recherche empirique en particulier, ces donn<8e>es se pr<8e>sentent aujourd<d5>hui comme un nouvel eldorado pour l<d5>innovation et l<d5>exp<8e>rimentation. Ceci-dit, la prudence doit rester de mise surtout quand il s<d5>agit de prise de d<8e>cision publique qui a souvent des impacts importants sur lconomie et sur la population. <c7> Comment la statistique officielle devrait-elle appr<8e>hender cette nouvelle donne ? <c8> reste une question pos<8e>e et dont l<d5>exploration n<d5>est qu ses d<8e>buts. Le fait qu<d5>une session enti<8f>re de cette rencontre soit d<8e>di<8e>e aux big data t<8e>moigne de l<d5>int<8e>r<90>t grandissant qu<d5>elles suscitent. Mesdames et Messieurs, Les questionnements que nous soulevons dans cette rencontre ne sont pas sp<8e>cifiques <88> un pays donn<8e> et ne doivent pas <90>tre ponctuels. Rappelez-vous au lendemain de la crise mondiale de 2008, il y avait une remise en cause des mod<8f>les utilis<8e>s pour la pr<8e>vision et des interrogations sur la disponibilit<8e> des donn<8e>es n<8e>cessaires pour pr<8e>voir avec une pr<8e>cision raisonnable les retournements de conjoncture. Ce sont ces questions qui ont amen<8e> des institutions comme le FMI <88> entamer une r<8e>flexion sur comment repenser la politique macro<8e>conomique. C<d5>est <8e>galement ce qui a pouss<8e> les pays membres du G20 <88> lancer en 2009 le projet Data GAPS Initiative avec un focus particulier sur le secteur financier, paradoxalement le domaine le plus fourni en donn<8e>es <88> haute fr<8e>quence. L<d5>un des enseignements majeurs de cette crise est la n<8e>cessit<8e> de rester prudent et modeste devant la complexit<8e> du comportement humain et l<d5>incertitude entourant les implications des mutations profondes qui fa<8d>onnent notre environnement. Il n<d5>y a qu constater la fr<8e>quence et surtout l<d5>ampleur des r<8e>visions des pr<8e>visions d<d5>institutions aussi prestigieuses comme le FMI ou la Banque mondiale pour r<8e>aliser la difficult<8e> d<d5>appr<8e>hender les <8e>volutions <8e>conomiques. Des occasions comme celle qui nous est offerte aujourd<d5>hui permettent dchanger et de d<8e>battre des d<8e>fis auxquels nous faisons face et des opportunit<8e>s <88> saisir pour assurer la disponibilit<8e> d<d5>une donn<8e>e fiable au service d<d5>une meilleure prise de d<8e>cision et in fine au b<8e>n<8e>fice du citoyen.
