text: MOROCCO FACING THE CRISIS AND THE POST-CRISIS PERIOD Mr Abdellatif JOUAHRI Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib Hassan II University Faculty of Legal, Economic and Social Sciences LINKS - Centre for Legal, Economic and Social Research Casablanca, 26 November 2009 I-Introduction The current financial crisis, which began in August 2007, has been characterized by its brutal nature, its magnitude and its speed of diffusion. This crisis, initially limited to the US real estate market, gradually affected the entire global financial system before affecting the real sector of the various economies. Despite the stimulus packages put in place by governments and the measures adopted by central banks, the confidence of economic agents has not fully recovered and a climate marked by high uncertainties still persists. The outcome of the crisis thus remains heavily compromised. Morocco, like the emerging countries, has suffered since the second half of 2008 the repercussions of the global crisis, which have been felt mainly through the macroeconomic channel, the financial system, due to its low exposure to international financial markets, having been relatively spared the effects of the crisis. The real channels of spread have mainly impacted exports of goods and services, tourism receipts, remittances from Moroccans living abroad and foreign direct investment. The significant progress made in recent years by the Moroccan economy and the soundness of the banking sector, combined with a fixed exchange rate regime, have made it possible, for their part, to significantly mitigate the impact of the crisis on Morocco. Beyond its direct repercussions on certain sectors, the current crisis has highlighted structural deficiencies in the Moroccan economy, mainly linked to the room for manoeuvre of fiscal policy, the weak competitiveness of the economy, the worsening of the trade deficit, the narrowness of the internal market and the major dysfunctions of certain sectors of the economy. Strategic reflection on the post-crisis period is therefore necessary in order to identify problems and plan appropriate responses. Morocco must consolidate the gains made over the last two decades, at the same time it must begin and accelerate the implementation of urgent projects, able to enable it to ensure healthy and sustainable growth. This document briefly recalls, at first, the nature of the international crisis and its multiple repercussions on the financial and real levels in the various countries before assessing its impact on Morocco. In a second step, the factors of resilience of the Moroccan economy that have made it possible to mitigate this impact will be developed. Next, the sources of fragility that the international crisis has helped to highlight will be addressed, as well as the short-term responses of governments and monetary authorities to the crisis. In a third step, the strategies for preparing for the post-crisis period will be presented by first outlining the new architecture of the global economic and financial framework induced by the crisis and then by exploring some avenues for reform for the Moroccan economy in the years to come. II-Morocco in the face of the international financial crisis The current financial crisis has been brutal and of considerable magnitude. Unfolding in three phases to successively affect the markets, the banks and the real economy, this crisis was characterized by an extreme rapid spread, taking both public authorities and central banks by surprise. In the Market, the mechanisms for transmitting the effects of the crisis have taken the real channels of trade and direct investment rather than the flows to purely financial character because the Moroccan financial market has not yet reached a sufficiently significant level of integration with international markets. As a result, the exposure of the financial sector has been relatively limited. A- A global financial crisis unprecedented since that of 1929 The current crisis differs from previous financial crises in its global dimension, its magnitude and its speed of diffusion. Indeed, confined at the beginning to a specific segment market (the subprime mortgage sector in the United States), the crisis quickly spread to the financial sphere. and banking, causing the failure of many institutions, turbulence on the financial markets and a generalized crisis of confidence, before subsequently generating multiple macroeconomic repercussions. 1- Genesis of the crisis Appearing in the United States in the summer of 2007, the crisis, initially called the "subprime" crisis, has its origin in the downturn in the real estate market and the soaring interest rates. to the UnitedStates. As a result of these two factors, borrowers' defaults had multiplied and mortgage companies were faced with serious financial difficulties, triggering an acute crisis in the sector. The effects of the subprime crisis quickly spread beyond the U.S. housing market and subsequently disrupted global financial markets. Initially manifested in the form of a liquidity crisis, the crisis materialized in severe tensions on the interbank markets. These disruptions have resulted in a surge in spreads, a reduction in maturities and a significant decline in credit. Other segments of the financial markets were also affected. This crisis also emerged as a securitization crisis. The collapse of the most generous forms of securitisation has revealed that financial innovation in recent years has served not to better manage and spread risk, but to increase credit through leverage. The collapse of the investment bank Lehman Brothers in September 2008 marked a turning point in the crisis. It has triggered a climate of widespread mistrust in all financial markets characterized by a sharp increase in volatility, a significant risk aversion and a blockage of money markets as well as a deep breakdown of confidence in the solvency of financial institutions (see Appendix 1). The turbulence in the financial sphere eventually affected the real channel, leading to the paralysis of a large number of economic sectors and a remarkable decline in world activity and trade. Figure 1: Deterioration of international economic activity Source: Datastream The financial crisis can thus be schematized as a market problem that occurred at the beginning in subprime, which generated a financial crisis in the short-term refinancing market which, in turn, caused an acute crisis in the banking sector before inducing severe implications for the real economy and employment, as evidenced by the evolution of the unemployment rate which has particularly exploded in the main advanced economies. Figure 2: Evolution of the unemployment rate Source: Datastream The crisis quickly took on an international dimension, since after affecting all developed countries, emerging economies were in turn caught up by the crisis from the summer of 2008, a year later after it triggered on the American market. Such a degree of international contagion suggests that the current crisis can be described as the first crisis of globalization. For most experts, this is one of the most severe seizures ever. In this regard, the IMF recorded more than 120 banking crises between 1970 and 2007, but the recent financial crisis is of unprecedented magnitude and complexity. As for the explanatory elements put forward, it seems that the current crisis has its origin in several factors, namely monetary policy in the United States, the analytical framework of central banks and finally the supervision of banks and markets. Credit rating agencies and accounting rules have also played a significant role. Reflecting the very strong magnitude of the crisis, the global growth outlook has been subject to successive downward revisions due to the rapid deterioration of the international economy. According to the IMF's most recent growth projections, advanced economies will experience a decline in growth of around 3.4% in 2009 before returning to growth of 1.3% in 2010. The United States will suffer a contraction in growth of 2.7% in 2009 followed by a rebound in activity of 1.5% in 2010, while the Eurozone will record a decline in growth of 4.2% before starting a timid recovery estimated at 0.3% in 2010. For their part, emerging economies that have been much more resilient to financial turbulence will see their growth rate grow by 1.7% in 2009 and 5.1% in 2010 (see Annex 2). While there are signs of recovery in economic activity at present and financial markets are relatively improving, the prospects for recovery vary from country to country and there are still great uncertainties about a definitive exit from the crisis. The global economy also remains marked by significant volatility in commodity prices, which have risen in the recent period but remain well below those reached in 2008. On the financial front, while the risks of systemic collapse appear to have been reduced as a result of crisis management policies, markets remain volatile. And while risk appetite has rebounded, confidence is far from being sustainably restored. 2- Crisis management policies With regard to the responses to the crisis, it must be noted that at the beginning, given the resulting general instability and panic in the markets, the actions deployed to deal with it were not concerted, particularly in Europe. Countries were not unanimous on the choice of mechanisms to resolve the crisis, in particular on the priority to be given to urgent measures to be adopted. Uncertainties included the need to prioritise liquidity on the interbank market, to secure operators and, consequently, the capitalisation of banks, or to provide the necessary guarantees with regard to toxic claims. However, it soon became clear that the deepening of the crisis and the awareness of the inefficiency of certain measures taken individually made it necessary and crucial for global consultation. As a result, two types of stimulus have declined, namely fiscal and monetary stimulus. It is the combination of these two instruments that has been instrumental in averting a systemic crisis, sustaining confidence and creating the conditions for recovery. To this should be added the action of the G20 and international organizations, including the IMF, which have also played a leading role in the recovery process. These measures were primarily aimed at restoring confidence in the markets with a view to ensuring financial stability. With regard to the heavy programmes deployed by the public authorities to stimulate demand, rescue weakened banking institutions and reduce uncertainty on the financial markets, Governments have disbursed colossal sums to counter the fallout from the crisis and help their economies (see Annex 3). As a result of this large-scale expenditure, fiscal balances in these countries have deteriorated sharply. At the same time, public debt ratios are expected to deteriorate significantly in 2009 to worrying levels. This situation of widening of the budget deficit and worsening of the debt raises questions about the conditions of repayment. Will these take place through a revival of inflationary pressures? With the resumption of economic activity, will budgetary revenues be sufficient or will it be necessary to provide for an increase in the tax rate? The situation is all the more worrying as it occurs in a current context of disinflation and even deflation in some countries. For their part, central banks, as soon as the financial turbulence appeared, reacted quickly and flexibly. To stem the effects of the crisis, conventional and non-conventional measures have been widely used. In terms of conventional measures, rates have been lowered substantially, reducing to zero rates in advanced economies. In addition, in the face of the deepening crisis and the scarcity of interbank operations, central banks have also resorted to unconventional measures to inject liquidity and support credit. However, like fiscal policy measures, the exit from monetary policy measures also raises concerns in the event of a recovery in economic activity. Chart 3: Evolution of key central bank rates The third type of action concerns the coordinated response within the framework of the G20 and the role of the IMF. Through their extensive action, these bodies have worked hard to restore confidence and revitalize the money market, which will inevitably promote the recovery of credit activity. As a result, imf financial assistance to a large number of countries and the allocation of SDRs have helped restore confidence. The Flexible Credit Line (FCL) in particular has provided significant support to several emerging countries. At the same time, the increase in concessional lending has expanded the room for low-income countries to pursue countercyclical policies. For its part, the G20, at its meeting in London on 2 April 2009, reached a number of commitments on fiscal and monetary stimulus, strengthening financial regulation and promoting international trade. These commitments include restoring growth and jobs, strengthening the supervision and regulation of the financial system, strengthening the international financial institutions, and combating protectionism and promoting international trade. On the other hand, it appears that the World Bank, as an important player in international organizations, has not played a significant role in this recovery dynamic, as the international community has not provided it with adequate resources. It has focused more on addressing the difficulties of the international financial system than on trying to address the problems of growth. Ultimately, concerted fiscal and monetary stimulus policies have succeeded in controlling systemic and severe recession risks, although fragilities still persist. Unprecedented interventions by central banks and governments around the world have succeeded in stabilizing the financial situation of credit institutions, easing funding and counterparty risks, and supporting aggregate demand. All the measures put in place have generally led to a normalization of financial conditions in recent months and a stabilization or even a recovery of economic activity in the world. On the financial front, bank debt markets and interbank markets have restarted. Uncertainties about counterparty and liquidity risks in the banking sector are less pronounced, as reflected in the narrowing of LIBOR-OIS spreads and contract spreads at risk of default. Stock market indices have also begun to recover. At the real level, there have also been early signs of recovery, as confirmed by the first positive growth rates in the second quarter of 2009 observed since the beginning of the crisis in some advanced economies such as France, Germany and Japan. However, overall financial conditions remain tense. The growth of bank credit to the private sector has not yet regained momentum in advanced economies, securitization markets are still stalling, except for those that receive government support, and borrowers with lower quality signatures have little access to capital markets to finance themselves. Government interventions, which have been decisive in reducing private sector risks, have also led to increased risks for the public sector and represent a growing burden on the sustainability of public finances. However, the global recession is expected to continue until the end of 2009, before giving way to a partial and gradual recovery in 2010, the extent of which remains dependent on the effectiveness of stimulus measures and the dynamics of credit markets. Overall, what conclusions can be drawn from the current crisis and the recovery measures at the international level? It can be argued that the crisis, by its magnitude and the speed of its spread, has revealed serious dysfunctions that profoundly characterize the international financial system. Moreover, it can be seen that the mistakes made during the 1929 crisis have not been reproduced, such as a return to protectionism in the areas of trade, finance, investment and labour services, competitive devaluations or orthodox reactions on the part of central banks. In the medium term, major risks to the economic recovery continue to weigh, mainly in advanced economies. On the financial front, the major challenge is to restore lasting confidence in a financial system that has been badly battered by the crisis. At the macroeconomic level, the most significant risk relates to the deterioration of fiscal positions, particularly as a result of measures taken to support the recovery. B- The impact of the crisis on Morocco: a marked slowdown in economic activity In terms of the impact of the crisis on Morocco, the approach adopted is not necessarily comparable to that followed at the international level, as the financial sector has remained relatively sheltered from the turbulence observed at the international level. Like emerging countries, the effects of the crisis have been felt more through macroeconomic transmission channels. Indeed, the slowdown in economic activity in our main partners has had a significant impact on the real sector. The spread of recession factors to the real sector has impacted the Moroccan economy through four main transmission channels, namely exports of goods, remittances from Moroccans living abroad, travel receipts and foreign direct investment flows. 1- The decline in trade in goods with foreign countries Although exports increased by 23% in 2008, the increase was mainly due to an exceptional increase in the prices of phosphate and its derivatives, while the increase in exports excluding phosphates and derivatives was limited to only 0.5%. An examination of the data for the first nine months of 2009 shows that exports fell significantly by 34% compared to the same period of the previous year to 83.6 billion dirhams, driven by the slowdown in foreign activity and consumption in the main partner economies. Imports of goods, after recording an increase of 23% in 2008, largely in line with the sharp rise in international prices of commodities and raw materials, fell by 23.4% at the end of September 2009 compared to the same period of the previous year to 193.5 billion dirhams. As a result, the overall trade deficit, which had increased in 2008 to 167.4 billion dirhams, already reached 109.8 billion at the end of the first nine months of 2009, although down compared to the same period of the previous year. Figure 4: Evolution of the trade balance (in billion dirhams) 2- The impact on the tourism sector The sustained dynamism of tourism activity in recent years was interrupted in 2008, following in particular the slowdown in growth in the euro area, the main source market for tourists. Under these conditions, travel revenues contracted to 55.4 billion dirhams, a decrease of 5.6% instead of an increase of nearly 11% in 2007 and 30% in 2006. At the end of the first nine months of 2009, tourism receipts, despite an increase in arrivals of 5.3% to total 6.5 billion visitors, returned to 40.5 billion dirhams, a decrease of 8.8% compared to the same period of the previous year. Similarly, overnight stays recorded in classified establishments decreased by 2.5% to 12.8 million. The decline in tourism receipts is due to the decline in household spending in the issuing countries as well as to the increased competition from other countries. Figure 5: Evolution of travel receipts (year-on-year) 3- The slowdown in transfers from Moroccans living abroad In recent years, the repatriation of Moroccans living abroad fell steadily in 2008 from 55 billion dirhams in 2007 to 53 billion dirhams. Data available at the end of September on financial flows abroad indicate a year-on-year contraction of 9.7% in transfers from Moroccans residing abroad, which amounted to only 37.6 billion dirhams. This contraction in remittances from Moroccans living abroad, which is the result of a reduction in their income, is due to the decline in activity and unemployment, particularly in the construction and automotive sectors where foreign labour is very represented. Figure 6: Evolution of transfers of Moroccans living abroad 4- The contraction of foreign private investment and loans After being reduced by 21.5% in 2008 to 32.5 billion dirhams, foreign private investment and loans at the end of September 2009 amounted to only a modest amount of 17.4 billion dirhams, down significantly by 35.9% year-on-year. The contraction in foreign investment is due to continued uncertainties and financing difficulties at the international level. Figure 7: Evolution of foreign direct investment (year-on-year) III-The factors of resilience of the Moroccan economy In the deteriorated context of the international crisis, it can be argued that the Moroccan economy has shown a proven resilience, as demonstrated by the importance of the progress made in recent years. Its strengths are the result of a continuous process of reforms that has accelerated since the beginning of the current decade. A- Mechanisms for cushioning the crisis 1- A sound macroeconomic framework The deepening of our country's structural reforms in recent years has considerably strengthened fundamental macroeconomic balances, as reflected in long-term data on growth, fiscal position, inflation and external accounts. Thus, growth has clearly strengthened (5% per year on average over the last five years) and has become less volatile, thanks to the process of diversification of the economy, as shown by the sustained increase to more than 5% of non-agricultural GDP on average over the period 2000-2008, thus marking a break with the past trend. Figure 8: Evolution of GDP and non-agricultural value added Non-agricultural VA GDP At the same time, the fiscal position has strengthened significantly thanks to the good performance of tax revenues and despite the significant compensation expenditure linked to the increase in the price of oil. The budget deficit on average over the period 2000-2008 thus represented 3.7% of GDP. In addition, it is important to stress the independence of the state budget from privatization revenues in recent years. Chart 9: Evolution of the budgetary balance as % of GDP With regard to price developments, it is important to point out that Morocco has been part of a global disinflationary movement. Inflation and core inflation rates remained on average limited to 2% and 1.9% respectively between 2000 and 2008, which helped in particular to preserve the internal value of the currency and prevent any misalignment of the effective exchange rate of the dirham in real terms. Bank Al Maghrib's forecasts for the coming years also indicate an inflation rate of 1.2% for 2009 and 1.6% for 2010. At the same time, the current account balance of the balance of payments showed a surplus of around 2% of GDP on average between 2001 and 2007 (before turning negative in 2008), while foreign exchange reserves consolidated to represent about 9 months of imports of goods and services during the said period. Finally, the acceleration of structural reforms and those of sectors in which Morocco has comparative advantages, as well as the significant increase in investment in infrastructure, have contributed to the significant consolidation of macroeconomic stability. 2- A solid banking system Alongside the positive results of the reforms adopted by our country, the soundness of the national banking and financial system has strongly contributed to Morocco's resilience to the crisis. The banking sector, which is its essential component, was judged by the FSAP mission, carried out in 2007 jointly by the World Bank and the IMF, as stable, solid, and showing good resilience in the face of changes in the international context. In this respect, it can be considered as the benchmark of the MENA region. At the credit level, even though in several countries there has been a collapse of the interbank market, as well as the interruption of credit operations to companies and individuals, credit activity has remained vigorous in Morocco. Thus, after increasing by 29% in 2007, bank loans in 2008 increased by 23% to reach 519.3 billion dirhams, stimulated by demand from both households and companies and by very sustained competition. Relative to GDP, this outstanding amount represents 75% against 69%, a level that remains well above that posted by the countries of the MENA region, which stands at an average of 58%. In addition, the share of the banking sector in financing the economy has steadily increased from 53.8% in 1980 to 60% in 1990 before exceeding 90% in recent years. Similarly, the evolution of the liquidity ratio, an indicator of the degree of deposit mobilization by the banking sector, shows that the share of M3 in GDP, which averaged 42.2% during the years 1980-1990, exceeds 95% during the period 2004-2008. The forecasts made by Bank Al Maghrib, in this respect, show a growth rate of bank loans of 12% at the end of 2009. While this may seem modest compared to the growth rates recorded in previous years, in reality it corresponds more to a phase of downward adjustment after successive periods of credit boom. It is important to note that the slowdown in bank credit that has been observed is mainly related to the slowdown in the growth rate of real estate loans and consumer credit, the latter two categories having experienced a strong expansion over the recent period. This sharp increase in bank credit took place in a context of risk control. Indeed, the average rate of outstanding loans has continued to fall to represent only 6% of all loans, this rate being reduced to 4.3% for banks with a majority private capital. Similarly, the ratio of coverage of receivables by provisions has improved significantly to 75.3% and the solvency ratio has been satisfactory from the point of view of international standards. The domestic banking sector also remains particularly profitable, confirming its strength and adaptation in a difficult and constantly changing international environment. In fact, in the first half of 2009, the banks achieved a cumulative net profit of 5.3 billion dirhams, up 5.6% compared to the end of June 2008. As for the exposure of the banking sector abroad, the results of the investigations carried out by Bank Al Maghrib at the outbreak of the crisis at the international level have shown that this exposure to risk factors as well as the purely financial contagion channels of the crisis are very limited. The share of foreign assets is low, banks do not hold so-called "toxic" products and risks to foreign counterparties are controlled. 3- A financial market with little international exposure With regard to capital market activity, the financial market has been the subject of a multitude of reforms and several regulatory texts have been adopted. These reforms, combined with a favourable economic situation, have favoured a significant increase in stock market activity, with Casablanca showing the second largest capitalization of the stock markets in North Africa and the Middle East, behind the Egyptian market. The capitalization of the Casablanca Stock Exchange increased from 75 billion dirhams in 1996 (42.2% of GDP) to 531.7 billion dirhams, or 79% of GDP in 2008. The volume of transactions reached more than 244 billion dirhams in 2008 instead of 20 billion dirhams in 1996 while the number of listed companies increased from 44 to 78 during the same period. The Casablanca market index recorded remarkable performances of around 71% and 34% respectively in 2006 and 2007. Another considerable development is that of asset management with net UCITS assets exceeding 160 billion dirhams at the end of 2008 and a constantly increasing number of market players (260 funds in operation in 2008 against 22 in 1996). With regard to the recent evolution of the Casablanca Stock Exchange, stock market indicators experienced a relative contraction in 2008 and during the first nine months of 2009. After five successive years of exceptional performance, MASI fell by 13.5% in 2008 and recorded increased volatility in the first nine months of 2009. In this regard, analysts attribute this decline to psychological factors rather than a sign of weakness in the Moroccan market. Casablanca's stock exchange, unlike other markets, has not experienced erratic sales movements. The fundamentals of listed companies are solid with real growth prospects, while the weight of foreign investors in the stock market, limited to 2.3% at the end of 2008, remains insignificant overall. This downward phase corresponds more to a market correction movement caused by a readjustment after previous valuation levels abnormally high and totally disconnected from the evolution of the fundamentals of listed companies. Concerning the insurance sector, it is also not impacted by the financial crisis, since it is essentially a domestic market and with little exposure to the outside world, adding, in this context, that the regulation limits to 5% the share of total insurance assets that can be placed abroad. 4- A partially closed capital account The authorities have favoured a gradual opening of the capital account. The main measures adopted in 2007 concerned the authorisation of UCITS and insurance companies to invest a share of their assets abroad subject to certain conditions and the relaxation of the conditions for banks' investment abroad. Other measures relate to:  The expansion of hedging instruments against exchange rate risks that should enable exporters and importers to immunize themselves against any undesirable fluctuations in the exchange rate,  The possibility for companies to freely invest up to 30 million dirhams per year in productive projects related to their sector of activity.  The possibility for importers to prepay up to 40% of the value of imports for goods and 20% for services.  The possibility for exporters to grant credits that can reach up to 85% of the agreed amount for the benefit of their customers.  The increase in the share of export earnings that can be kept in foreign currency or convertible dirham accounts from 20% to 50%. It is important to stress at this level that the resilience of the Moroccan economy in this phase of crisis is largely attributable to the maintenance of the fixed exchange rate regime and the low foreign exchange exposure of economic agents. In this area, Morocco has opted for a cautious and gradual approach. B- Sources of fragility to monitor Despite developments in recent years, however, the Moroccan economy remains weakened by a number of structural factors that hinder its development process. Indeed, the Moroccan economy continues to face internal constraints, including the impact of weather conditions on the level of growth, low export competitiveness and the deterioration of the current account balance of payments, risks to the control of the budget deficit and numerous social deficits. 1- The volatility of agricultural growth The agricultural sector, despite the significant efforts undertaken, remains characterized by low productivity and is still dependent on climatic hazards, as shown by the volatility, although significantly decreasing, of the growth of its value added. Despite its relatively small share of overall value added (13.4%), the agricultural sector remains a determining factor in overall growth due to the sharp fluctuation in output from one year to the next. 2- Risks to the budgetary position The satisfactory results achieved at budgetary level were driven more by actions at the revenue level and not by the control of expenditure. Tax revenues increased by more than 7 percentages of GDP between 2000 and 2008, while recurrent expenditure averaged 24% of GDP per year over the same period. More fundamentally, expenditure on the wage bill and the compensation system, which was further reflected in 2008, has not been reduced. In this respect, the weight of the wage bill in GDP and total expenditure, which in 2008 represented 10.2% and 34.9% respectively, remain well above the average of the countries of the MENA region whose level is 8.1% and 25.2% respectively. The evolution of public finances as a result of both the reduction in tax revenues (at the end of September 2009, tax revenues fell by 9.9% compared to the same period in 2008) and the increase in investment spending to revitalize the economy could jeopardize the control of the budget deficit in the future. 3- The deterioration of the current account balance of the balance of payments The insufficient productivity of industrial enterprises combined with a structure that is still dominated by low value-added goods are largely responsible for the lack of dynamism in exports. Indeed, the structure of exports continues to be dominated by products with low technological content and suffers from limited diversification, concentrated for almost two-thirds on the markets of the European Union. This situation, aggravated by ever-increasing imports, contributed to a sharp widening of the trade deficit, which amounted to 25.1% of GDP in 2008. For their part, receipts from tourism and transfers made by Moroccans living abroad, whose fluctuations have just been demonstrated by the recent crisis and which have declined by 5.6% and 3.4% respectively, have not managed to make up the deficit. As a result, current transactions showed a deficit of around 5.2% of GDP instead of an average annual surplus of around 2% of GDP over six successive years. Finally, foreign exchange reserves represent only 7 months of imports of goods and services against about 9 months a year earlier. 4- The persistence of social deficits Despite the progress made in recent years in the field of education and training, many challenges remain, which hinder the development of human capital and hinder Morocco's competitiveness. The handicaps identified relate to the persistence of illiteracy, high school dropout rates and the low quality of learning. The labour market also remains under severe stress. Although the unemployment rate fell slightly in 2008, the rate of 9.6% remains high, particularly in urban areas and among the graduate population. The gradual extension of the economic slowdown to all sectors could exacerbate the difficulties on the labour market. Under these conditions, the risks of precariousness and exclusion in urban areas, poverty in rural areas and social instability would become even more worrying. Finally, although poverty has been considerably reduced in recent years, it remains very significant (more than 9% of the Moroccan population lives in conditions of poverty and 17.5% in conditions of vulnerability) and is therefore likely to worsen in the absence of adequate social policies. In short, despite its appreciable performance, Morocco must remain vigilant in the face of the difficulties encountered by our economic partners in Europe, which represent our main market and which record a decline in their growth of 4.2%. The negative consequences of this situation are beginning, as we have seen, to have an impact on Morocco. Indeed, as can be seen from Bank Al-Magrhib's latest growth forecasts, the sharp contraction in demand from our main partners is expected to continue to have a dampening effect on non-agricultural growth, which is expected to be between 2% and 3% in 2009. On the other hand, overall economic growth is expected to be between 5% and 6%, a level comparable to that observed in 2008, driven by a rebound in agricultural value added, which benefited from exceptional climatic conditions and whose rate of growth would reach 20% against 16% in 2008. C- The first responses to the crisis Responses to the crisis have consisted of several government actions to support productive sectors directly exposed to the collapse of foreign demand. For its part, Bank Al Maghrib has taken the necessary steps to assess and consolidate the soundness of the banking sector and to ensure the liquidity of the banking system with a view to boosting economic activity. 1- Government support measures In order to support demand and provide support to businesses affected by the crisis, the Government has set up a mechanism to monitor and evaluate the impacts of the crisis. As soon as the first signs of a slowdown in economic activity appeared, a Strategic Intelligence Committee composed of all the ministries concerned, Bank Al Maghrib, the OCP and professional associations and federations was set up in February 2009. The committee's mission is to monitor the developments of the crisis, its impact on the national economy and to propose to the Government appropriate support measures for the sectors affected by the crisis. The Committee's work focused in particular on the establishment of several support plans for the textile, leather, automotive equipment, electronics and tourism sectors. The measures are intended to safeguard market shares in the sectors affected, to strengthen the competitiveness of enterprises, to improve their conditions of access to credit and export markets and to avoid job losses within these enterprises. The measures adopted by the Committee are structured around three components: a social component aimed at maintaining employment, a financial component aimed at improving the cash flow of the affected companies, and a commercial component in support of the diversification of outlets and markets. Measures relating to the tourism sector have focused on strengthening promotion and institutional communication. They also focus on stimulating package sales, consolidating air transport, launching new products and supporting domestic tourism. With regard to transfers from Moroccans living abroad, the measures recommended are aimed at supporting and encouraging the investment of MREs. As such, an adjustment of the "Dammane Assakane" scheme has been envisaged to better support the acquisition of housing for the benefit of this category, in parallel with other support actions at the level of their host countries. Export sectors weakened by the decline in foreign demand have also benefited from Government assistance to improve their competitiveness and support their cash flow. At its seventh working meeting held on 4 November 2009, it was decided to strengthen the missions of the Strategic Intelligence Committee and to adopt a new strategic approach, based on the choice of themes related to a better post-crisis positioning. Despite encouraging signs of recovery in the sectors directly affected by the crisis, the Committee recommended continued vigilance and mobilization in order to continue to correct the structural deficiencies revealed by the crisis. At the same time, the Government's policy has been to take direct measures in favour of sectors most vulnerable to foreign demand. Several "structural" measures aimed at sustainably reducing the vulnerability of the national economy within the framework of a 2009-2015 Programme Contract on the National Pact for Industrial Emergence were adopted on 13 February 2009. As part of the continuity of the Emergence Plan, this Contract aims to implement a long-term strategy aimed at the development of Moroccan Industry. Other support measures by the government, in consultation with the private sector, have directly targeted exporting companies. These measures are mainly aimed at maintaining jobs and skills within exporting companies and should enable them to strengthen their competitiveness by improving the conditions for access to credit and markets. Thus, an agreement was signed between the State and the CGEM on February 24, 2009 in and relate to an amount of 3.24 million dirhams, resulted in direct support to exporting companies in their trade promotion activities through the assumption by the State of 80% of the costs relating to promotional activities, the reorganization of premium rates and guaranteed quotas for export insurance and finally the launch of sectoral communication campaigns targeted by Maroc Export. An agreement has also been signed between the Government and the Electronics Sector Association in favour of the electronics sector. These measures are structured around three components: a social component aimed at maintaining employment through the reimbursement by the State of employers' contributions of companies in the electronics sector for low wages, a financial component through provisions aimed at improving the cash flow of companies and a training component aimed at maintaining jobs and skills and preserving the positioning of these companies internationally. In addition, to counteract the decline in transfers, the State has set up actions in favor of Moroccans living abroad. These actions include free remittances until the end of 2009 for MREs and a state subsidy for investment projects. In addition, in view of the direct effects of the international situation on tourism, an action plan "CAP 2009" has been launched, with an envelope of 100 million dirhams. This plan aims to consolidate market shares at the level of the issuing countries and to boost tourism activity in the main cities visited. Finally, the 2010 finance bill adopted on 17 November includes a budget envelope of 160 billion dirhams devoted to investment, up 20% compared to 2009. This amount will be used to promote growth to limit the effects of the crisis, support purchasing power, accelerate the pace of reforms initiated in Morocco and finally strengthen social cohesion. 2- The action of Bank Al-Maghib For its part, Bank Al Maghrib, faced with the difficult international context, has adopted a set of measures aimed at consolidating the banking system and financial stability. Thus, additional provisions on country risk management were enacted in 2008 and the minimum level of the solvency ratio was raised to 10%. In addition, the central bank recommended that banks provide more detailed and frequent reporting on direct and indirect exposures related to subprime loans. It also invited the management of banks to raise the level of vigilance and to show greater involvement in the risk management of their institutions, particularly those related to international activities. In order to ensure regular monitoring of the effects of the crisis on the banking sector and to prevent future developments, a permanent monitoring unit has been set up within Bank Al Maghrib and the GPBM. At the same time, exchanges of information with other financial sector supervisors have been intensified, within the framework of the Coordination Commission, with a view to taking the necessary actions in good time and ensuring the necessary efficiency of the measures adopted. In the same vein, Bank Al-Maghrib has taken a series of measures to ensure an adequate level of liquidity for the banking sector and, consequently, to support economic activity. Indeed, as soon as the situation became difficult, Bank Al Maghrib proceeded to inject liquidity into the market of more than 22 billion since the beginning of 2009 against 5 billion dirhams in 2007 and 13 billion in 2008. The Central Bank has thus undertaken to make available to the interbank market all the necessary means for banking institutions to enable them to finance economic activity in a sound and rigorous manner. At the same time, Bank Al Maghrib recommended that banks relax the conditions for granting credit to economic operators, especially in the sectors most affected by the crisis. In addition, in order to improve the liquidity of banks, the Board of Bank Al Maghrib has reduced the monetary reserve rate three times. The latter, which stood at 15% until the end of 2008, was reduced to 12% in January 2009, then to 10% from July of the same year and finally to 8% in October 2009. Through this monetary instrument, which aims to mitigate the liquidity needs of banks, the Central Bank thus contributes to increasing the supply capacity of the national banking system and thus to supporting growth. Of course, if the situation requires it again, the level of this rate will be reviewed. In addition to credit and the reserve rate, Bank Al-Maghrib has spared no effort to use its key interest rate as an indispensable tool for reviving domestic demand and economic activity in general. This rate was revised downwards in March 2009 to 3.25%, a reduction of 25 basis points. It should be noted that this measure does not affect the central bank's mandate in terms of price stability, as the decision was taken after noting a decline in current and future inflationary pressures. In this context, Bank Al-Maghrib's overall vision is to closely monitor recent economic and financial developments, thus committing to take all necessary measures to revive national economic activity, in parallel with fiscal and fiscal instruments. At the same time, work is underway to establish a macro-prudential supervisory framework, based both on stress tests to assess the resilience of the banking system to different shocks and on the conduct of systemic stress tests, in consultation with the regulatory and supervisory authorities of the financial sector. The purpose of this work is to ensure the effectiveness of current mechanisms and to identify areas for their improvement, with a view to establishing, on solid foundations, coordination between regulatory authorities in the event of a systemic crisis and ensuring a global watch on the stability of the financial system. IV-Post-crisis preparedness strategies The current period is crucial. It poses major challenges for countries facing several problems of reviving their economies. Above all, it is an opportunity to work towards a reshaping of the global economic and financial framework to ensure solid, sustained and balanced growth for the years to come. The current situation must make it possible to bring the world economy out of the crisis and to bring about the necessary and adequate changes in the interest of the international community. It is imperative to learn from the crisis and avoid repeating the mistakes that have led to the current difficulties. In this respect, the modern financial model, which has provided countries with a certain development for many years, must be maintained, provided that the necessary adjustments are made to it and that its operating conditions are improved. Current concerns about economic recovery and market restoration must contribute definitively to building a new global architecture based on this same model, but this fois.ci accompanied by new, more binding provisions and more appropriate rules in terms of safety, efficiency and transparency. A- Towards a new configuration of the global economic and financial framework 1- The major challenges of the post-crisis period The global landscape has been profoundly disrupted by the damage caused by the financial crisis. Asset markets have been seriously disrupted, causing colossal losses for savers. Economic activity and trade have been severely affected and are experiencing a sharp slowdown. Unemployment has exploded in most economies, with around 15 million people reportedly losing their jobs as a result of the effects of the crisis. Poverty and precariousness have increased significantly, particularly in low-income countries. The crisis has, in fact, revealed deep malaise in the economic system. On the financial front, latent dysfunctions continue to characterize the markets. At the real level, because of the drastic drop in demand, the productive apparatus has been undermined, causing the bankruptcy of many companies and blocking economic activity. At the same time, financial intermediation has been severely hampered. In almost all countries, the colossal sums spent by States to help their economies have increased the burden on public finances. In recent months, a recovery movement seems to be beginning. However, questions remain about the sustainability of this movement and in particular about its degree. The most significant risks are that growth will not be sustainable, particularly if demand from advanced economies is too weak to support economic recovery. Other risks to the volatility of international financial markets persist. Finally, worrying risks linked to the rise in unemployment remain relevant despite the measures adopted by some countries in favour of the labour market. Faced with this problem of exit strategies, the G20 group considered, at its meeting on 6 and 7 November 2009, that the economic and financial conditions of the world economy have improved following the coordinated measures of their countries against the crisis. However, the recovery is uneven and remains dependent on the support of economic policies and the high level of unemployment is a major problem. To restore the health of the global economic and financial system, the Group is committed to maintaining economic stimulus measures until the global economic recovery is assured. In this regard, seven principles have been laid down to design and implement exit strategies:  The timing of exit strategies should depend on the state of the economy and the financial system and should lean more towards supporting demand and restoring stability to the financial system;  With a few exceptions, fiscal consolidation should be a top priority in the implementation of exit strategies. Monetary policy can adjust flexibly when normalization is needed;  Fiscal exit strategies should be transparent, comprehensive and clearly communicated with the aim of reducing public debt to moderate levels in clearly specified deadlines;  Strengthening the primary balance should be the key driver of fiscal adjustment policies, starting with actions to ensure that crisis-related fiscal stimulus remains temporary;  Unconventional monetary policy does not necessarily have tobe cancelled before traditional monetary policy is restrictive;  The economic situation, the stability of financial markets and the basic mechanisms of markets should determine when and how financial assistance should be phased out;  Coherent exit strategies will need to improve the performance of all countries. Coordination does not necessarily imply synchronization, but the lack of policy coordination could create negative spillovers. 2- The strategic orientations of the new global framework Post-crisis preparedness strategies could take five major paths, namely, the need for better international dialogue, the improvement of regulatory systems, the need to overcome the shortcomings of private demand, the need for better integration of developing countries and the strengthening of the international monetary system. With regard to international dialogue, this strategy would result in close collaboration on the policies implemented. The effects of the crisis have been mitigated through joint measures taken as part of this collaboration. Fiscal stimulus, combined with central bank measures, has helped restore confidence in the financial system and support output. This collaboration is all the more necessary during this post-crisis period to ensure strong and balanced growth. In particular, it should decide whether to withdraw the support measures adopted to deal with the crisis. It is also useful for promoting increased but robust and healthy financial integration, given the interdependence between different markets and financial actors. The second main axis is the improvement of regulatory and supervisory systems to ensure financial stability. In view of the failure of the regulatory bodies in the outbreak of the crisis, there is an urgent need for a thorough reform of the mechanisms for supervising and controlling financial systems. In parallel with recent progress on several aspects such as prudential supervision, risk management and market security, the challenge now is to put in place international rules on strengthening banks' capital, improving derivatives markets and reforming remuneration practices. In addition, sustained attention should be paid to the consolidation of bank balance sheets and the regulation of securitisation markets. The application of new rules on the regulation and supervision of the financial system is the condition for a return to healthy and sustainable growth. A third axis is to overcome problems on the demand side. Current forecasts point to a resumption of growth in countries for the coming quarters. Nevertheless, this recovery will be insufficient to sustainably reduce unemployment, which the crisis has considerably increased. Moreover, the recovery is largely based on fiscal stimulus policies and corporate rebuilding of inventories, not on the strength of private consumption. This situation is likely to create a marked increase in countries' indebtedness. It is necessary to put in place now the necessary measures to stimulate private spending in order to support investment in a healthy way, especially since uncertainties will continue to weigh on a real recovery in household demand until the issues related to unemployment are resolved. As far as developing countries are concerned, emerging economies have collectively weathered the crisis relatively well, and several of them have been among the very first to initiate a recovery that has reinvigorated global economic activity. However, the crisis will continue to wreak havoc in the developing world. The sharp contraction in world trade, the decline in remittances and the decline in tourism, as well as the continued tightening of credit, have led to a sharp slowdown in growth, massive job losses, increased poverty and social tensions in many countries. In this disrupted environment, it is essential to continue to pursue coordinated countercyclical fiscal and monetary policies and to take measures to revive credit, promote job creation and the establishment of safety nets. In this context, special attention should be paid to low-income countries. These countries, already weakened by the food and oil crisis and facing severe instability in aid flows, have been hit hard by the financial crisis. The final focus is on strengthening the stability of the international financial system through the existence of a global lender of last resort. Increased financing requirements in times of crisis such as the one we have just experienced have demonstrated the need for a lender of last resort, represented by the IMF, who would play this decisive role in distributing funds to fragile economies and provide them with the assurance of protecting themselves against a decline in capital flows in times of crisis. In Morocco, as soon as the first effects of the crisis appeared, the authorities implemented, in a concerted and rapid manner, the necessary measures to help the affected sectors. But beyond the start of the recovery, it is already a question of implementing and accelerating exit strategies from the crisis aimed at remedying the structural shortcomings of the economy that the crisis has helped to highlight, as well as to ensure strong and sustainable growth in the future. B- Structural reforms to be carried out by Morocco Recent developments in the international environment and the implications of the global crisis on the Moroccan economy raise several major questions: what positioning for Morocco on the international scene? What are the strategic paths to be favored within the macroeconomic management of our country? Several challenges await us in the coming years. First of all, and without further delay, it is a question of putting in place the reforms necessary to accelerate growth on a sustainable basis. These reforms, which are already lagging behind in their implementation, are made all the more necessary and urgent as the crisis has highlighted the structural problems affecting the Moroccan economy. Another challenge concerns the governance and efficiency of economic policies in our country. The crisis has indeed clearly demonstrated the importance of mechanisms for coordinating and ensuring coherence of economic policies, as well as the need for efficient monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. In this respect, the most important risk is to ensure cohesion in the various public policies. The proliferation of sector-wide approaches must not take precedence over the macroeconomic vision. Social issues should not be minimized. Reducing unemployment is a major challenge for our economy. As such, labour market flexibility could be a fruitful measure in the future. Deficiencies in national education and health must be addressed quickly. Nor should the problems associated with the fight against poverty be overlooked in this post-crisis period. Finally, we must learn the lessons of this crisis without depriving our economy of the benefits of liberalisation and financial innovations. In order to successfully meet the challenges it faces, our country must now focus on solving the structural problems whose critical nature has been exacerbated by the current crisis and prepare with determination for the post-crisis period. To this end, several major reforms must be considered quickly. 1- Preserving macroeconomic balances and increasing the competitiveness of the economy In order to ensure healthy growth, the preservation of the acquis of macroeconomic stability is essential. The need to respond to current challenges requires the maintenance of an appropriate balance in economic policies. In the budgetary field, the consolidation of budgetary sustainability is an essential achievement that must be maintained in the medium term in order to be able to carry out actions aimed at reducing social deficits. Morocco achieved a surplus of 0.4% in 2008 and forecasts for 2009 and 2010 suggest a return to a deficit of 2.7% and 4% respectively, in particular in connection with the increase in investment spending. In addition, operating expenses remain extremely high and will have to increase by 11% compared to 2008. In this respect, efforts to rationalize this expenditure deserve to be undertaken as soon as possible. In addition, it is necessary to strengthen revenue dynamics through the absorption of the informal sector and tax reform. Similarly, and in view of the systemic risk they entail, particular attention must be paid to the financial balance of pension funds, in the light of the increase in life expectancy. In addition, the problem of the current account deficit in the balance of payments needs to be considered. Far-reaching measures to enhance the competitiveness of enterprises and thus boost the export sector must be adopted. In this respect, the ways to be favoured include improving the business environment, deepening the fight against corruption, progress in education and training, and labour market flexibility. In addition, in addition to the measures taken to increase the transfers of THE MREs, actions likely to strengthen external assets must be given priority in order to avoid the unfortunate consequences observed during the period that prevailed before the implementation of the Structural Adjustment Programme in the years. 80. 2- Adjustments in monetary and exchange rate policy In order to be able to sustain economic changes, the monetary and exchange rate policy framework must be continuously adapted. Thus, the need to shift the objective of monetary and exchange rate policy towards a more flexible inflation and exchange rate targeting regime in the medium term stems from the process of the country's integration into the world economy. This dynamic is accelerating, particularly due to the deepening of tariff dismantling with the European Union and the signing of free trade agreements with new countries. The commitments made by Morocco, within the framework of these agreements, will further deepen its financial and trade openness. To do this, our country must consolidate the elements necessary for a successful transition to the strategy of inflation targeting. These prerequisites are mainly based on the preservation of macroeconomic stability, the continuation of progress in monetary policy transparency, the soundness of the financial system and the strengthening of the technical and operational analytical capacity of the Central Bank. At the same time, the cumulative effect of the process of gradual easing of foreign exchange regulations is beginning to have an impact on the country's financial integration. It is now a question of preparing for future developments in order to succeed in the transition to a more flexible exchange rate regime, more consistent with the degree of openness expected of the Moroccan economy. 3- The further consolidation of the banking sector and the modernization of the financial system The consolidation of financial stability must continue with the convergence of banking sector standards with international standards. In recent years, indicators of the soundness and activity of the banking system have continuously improved as a result of the strengthening of the prudential framework and the proactive risk detection and management framework. These efforts must be maintained in the coming years and the banking sector must continue its evolution on a sound and solid basis and according to the most rigorous asset management possible. In addition, there is an urgent need for further banking of the population. The penetration of financial services remains extremely modest and below its potential, and is expected to be a major objective for the banking sector in the coming years. With regard to the modernization of the financial market, it is important that the Casablanca Stock Exchange regain its dynamism so that it can effectively fulfill its role in the economy. The rules on integrity and transparency must also be strengthened. In addition, financial products such as the Housing Savings Plan or the Equity Savings Plan must be launched as soon as possible in order to promote long-term savings and boost the financial market. Finally, important draft laws such as the full autonomy of the regulatory authorities (CDVM and DAPS) as well as the creation of a futures market for financial products must be quickly adopted. 4- Deepening the integration of the Moroccan economy internationally In parallel with the monetary and financial reforms, it is necessary to capitalize on the progress made to strengthen the attractiveness of our country and ensure the success of its transformation into an international financial platform. This large-scale project, which will certainly contribute to the successful integration of the Moroccan economy into its global environment, nevertheless requires deepening the reforms initiated compared to other financial centres because competition in this area is extremely strong. Moreover, given the weak growth prospects in the euro area, Morocco would benefit from moving towards integration into regional areas which, as international experience shows, are likely to act more broadly. In this regard, Maghreb integration could be an effective vector of growth for all countries. In the short term, financial rapprochement with certain countries could represent a first phase to be developed. 5- The overhaul of social policies At the social level, the strategic direction will be to consolidate the social bond through a profound overhaul of social policies. For this, a reorganization of the national landscape of social development actors must be undertaken. This reorganization would result in several actions. First of all, it is a question of consolidating the social bond and emphasizing human development, without which no economic growth is sustainable in the long term. Actions to combat poverty and precariousness must be considerably strengthened. In this regard, Morocco has organized its social policy strategy within the framework of the INDH. There is a need to deepen these social programmes, including through access to better and better social services, faster pace of job creation and regular evaluation of programmes to identify and address shortcomings. Secondly, social policies should be thoroughly reformed through an evaluation of the effectiveness of human development programmes and an overhaul of the compensation system with a view to ensuring greater social equity for the most disadvantaged and vulnerable groups. Finally, there is a need to accelerate and deepen reforms in the areas of national education and justice. V-Conclusion In the light of recent developments in the international crisis, it can be seen that while our country has been able to overcome the financial effects of the crisis relatively and limit its consequences on the real sector, the challenges facing macroeconomic policy have intensified as a result of the deterioration of the global economy. Consequently, the quality of macroeconomic management and the choice of responses are of particular importance in this context. On the economic front, the overarching challenge today is for our country to strengthen its capacity to cope with exogenous shocks. In addition, growth in Europe, Morocco's main partner, is expected to remain weak in the coming years, coupled with continued volatility in oil and commodity prices on international markets, which is expected to pose significant challenges. In order to successfully meet the challenges it faces, Morocco must continue to pursue sound macroeconomic policies while enhancing overall coherence and efficiency. To this end, it is crucial to deepen and broaden the fields of reforms, in particular those related to increasing competitiveness in order to improve the productivity of companies and the quality of human capital, to maintaining fundamental balances, to continuing the necessary adjustments in monetary, financial and exchange rate matters, to a better integration of our economy into the international environment or those aimed at providing a response. appropriate to social deficits. While there is a need to focus on sectoral plans and assess their contribution to improving growth, attention should also be paid to strengthening the coherence of reforms by integrating them into an overall macroeconomic vision that maximizes the impact of these reforms on the level of growth and poverty reduction. In this respect, the strategic challenge for the coming years will be to constantly adapt the orientation of public policies to fluctuations in economic activity. The improvement of the governance of public policies can only result from a continuous and close monitoring of the actions carried out. In this sense, a strong and regular responsiveness of the public authorities is the essential condition for adapting the reforms undertaken to changes in their environment. To ensure sustainable and equitable growth, Morocco should also accelerate the pace of reforms in the social fields, including education, health and justice. At this level, it is important to address the rigidity of labour regulations that restrict employment prospects and to reorganize the social protection system. The health sector also needs to be significantly improved, while education reform needs to be accelerated and further refocused in line with the changing needs of the economy. The functioning of justice must finally be reviewed in order to consolidate the rule of law and promote the improvement of the business climate. The new configuration of the post-crisis global economic and financial framework finally imposes new constraints on Morocco, linked in particular to the positioning of its economy in the international environment. The current crisis has highlighted the decisive nature of strong and integrated regional groupings. In this regard, regional integration should be a way forward, particularly within the Maghreb and with other African countries, with a view to a sustainable acceleration of growth and the improvement of the standard of living of the population. Title: At the symposium organized by the HCP on World Statistics Day
text: WORLD STATISTICS DAY BETTER STATISTICS AT THE SERVICE MONETARY POLICY AND FINANCIAL STABILITY Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 20 October 2015 Ladies and gentlemen First of all, I would like to say that it is a real pleasure for me to join you in celebrating World Statistics Day together. In this regard, I would like to express my sincere thanks to the High Commission for Planning, which brings us together today and offers us the opportunity to exchange and share our ideas and experiences for the benefit of the development of statistics and ultimately for the benefit of the citizen, as indicated in the theme of this day "Better data for a better life". There is, of course, no need to go back over the importance of statistical information for decision-making, monitoring and evaluation. For my part, I would like to share with you the challenges in terms of data availability and quality in the context of our missions as a central bank and the solutions we provide to them. Ladies and gentlemen The international financial crisis has reminded us of the gaps between the need for and the production of data inevitably resulting from the development of markets, institutions and risks. Efforts must therefore be ongoing to support the increasing complexity of economic and financial systems and to enable efficient policy-making. This is the framework of the initiative launched by the G20 in April 2009 to identify gaps and develop proposals to strengthen data collection. Discussions under this initiative have focused in particular on the importance of enriching bank data, strengthening the monitoring of systemically important institutions and cross-border financial activities. They also highlighted the importance of standardizing information through the adoption of common methodologies and standards and the development of cooperation at the international level, particularly in terms of data sharing. In the same vein, the IMF has introduced a new dissemination standard, called the Special Data Dissemination Standard Plus (SDDS), which is more demanding in terms of data coverage and publication times and is now a real challenge for our national statistical system. Ladies and gentlemen Bank Al-Maghrib, as an actor in the national statistical system, has long worked for the continuous strengthening of its statistical capacities. The aim is to have the necessary information base for decision-making in the context of its fundamental tasks, in particular the conduct of monetary policy and, more recently, that of financial stability. In this context, we have developed a macro-prudential supervision system, including the development of a global risk map and a stress-testing system to assess the degree of resilience of financial institutions. To this end, the Bank has worked to broaden the coverage of the data collected, in particular to the indebtedness of economic agents and the related risks. At this level, I would like to recall that the Bank has been involved for several years in the establishment of financial information centres, which it continues to improve and strengthen, in particular by extending their coverage to data relating to bank accounts, unpaid bills of exchange and information concerning non-financial suppliers. In the same vein, and also to meet monetary policy decision-making needs, the Bank has in recent years adopted a gradual approach to upgrading the production of monetary statistics. Thus, as a first step, in 2010 the Bank aligned the development of money and credit aggregates with the IMF methodology. Work continued thereafter to ensure comprehensive coverage of financial companies. After the integration of finance companies, microcredit associations and offshore banks in 2012, data from non-money market UCITS and CDG were taken into account in 2013 and those of insurance and reinsurance companies in 2014. The Bank expects to complete the entire process by the end of the year with the integration of pension funds. Bank AL-Maghrib has also enriched its statistical system by launching two new surveys. The first, in 2012, focuses on the inflation expectations of financial experts and academics with the aim of measuring the degree of anchoring of economic agents to the inflation forecast announced by the bank. The second, in 2013, addresses the conditions for granting bank credit and provides qualitative indicators to better understand the transmission of monetary policy. In addition, the Bank is currently working with the National Agency for Cadastre and Land Conservation to extend the coverage of its real estate asset price index to new properties. This strengthening of data collection was accompanied by the development within the Bank of a decision-making information system with advanced tools to optimize the processing of statistical data from collection to dissemination. Ladies and gentlemen These efforts have earned us the recognition of international institutions such as the IMF or the Bank for International Settlements. Together with those of other national statistical producers, they have enabled us to raise our national statistical system among the best in the region. However, we must all work to consolidate our gains, close current gaps and meet future needs. Indeed, despite the efforts made, a fairly important need remains in terms of information. Several areas still need to be covered, in particular concerning household wealth, economic and balance sheet data of enterprises and financial flows between the various economic agents. In particular, some of this information will be of great use to us for our policy of supporting very small, small and medium-sized enterprises. A category of companies for the benefit of which we are in the process, with our partners, of setting up a dedicated Observatory. In addition, the move towards gradual flexibilization of our exchange rate regime and the transition to an inflation-targeting framework require the availability of detailed and detailed data. This data will allow us at the Bank level to further refine the integrated forecasting framework and the economic policy impact assessment framework that we are finalizing as we prepare for this transition. To this is obviously added the need to monitor the new post-2015 development agenda, which must be remembered is much more demanding in terms of data than the previous one. Ladies and gentlemen The need for information is not static, it is growing with complexity and economic and social changes. The right response requires an appropriate legal framework that allows these developments to be taken into account, efforts to be coordinated and the use of resources to be rationalised. In our view, the current legal framework needs to be renovated, in particular to strengthen the coordination of data production and exchange. Finally, I would like to acknowledge the valuable contribution of the units that provide the data at the base, especially businesses and households. It is through this cooperation, which I hope will continue and strengthen, that we can have better data that contributes to a 'better life' for citizens. Thank you for your attention.
