Title: During the celebration of International Savings Day
text: International Savings Day Saving, a necessity to build the future Speech by Mr Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Rabat, 31 October 2018 Dear Minister, Dear Directors General, Ladies and gentlemen It is a real pleasure for me to join you in celebrating International Savings Day and I thank the organizers for their invitation. I would like to congratulate them on this initiative to organize the debate around this important topic. I think we often talk about the problem of financing, but we hear much less debate about savings, even though it is a prerequisite for it. The importance of savings for investment and growth is not to be demonstrated. Its level and structure affect the cost of financing and therefore the dynamics of investment. Its insufficiency can lead to the use of monetary or external financing and in both cases to the increase in the country's indebtedness and therefore to the vulnerability of its macroeconomic balances. The episodes experienced in the 80s by several developing countries, including Morocco, are the illustration of such a situation. In the longer term, saving is the variable that determines the intergenerational distribution of wealth. Ladies and gentlemen The concept of saving is complex and multidimensional. It can be approached on several levels and from several angles. Over the years, we have seen many paradigm shifts itself. One of the most important is certainly the introduction of the concept of adjusted net saving, also known as real saving. The latter was first developed in order to take into account the sustainability of the development by deducting from gross savings, the depreciation of capital and the depletion of natural resources. It was then adjusted by integrating education expenditure, which was thus considered as an investment, instead of its usual accounting as consumer expenditure. It is this last vision that underpins the concept of human capital, enshrined in the economic literature and which the World Bank has just highlighted once again with the publication of its new Human Capital Index on the occasion of the last annual meetings of the IMF/WB held in Bali earlier this month. It should be recalled in this regard that the application of these concepts to the case of our country is among the issues widely addressed in the report on the evolution of Morocco's wealth that Bank Al-Maghrib produced in collaboration with the EESC on the instructions of His Majesty the King. During the time allotted to me, I will focus my speech on a segment of savings, that of households, particularly in its microeconomic dimension. This choice is in line with the spirit of the celebration of this day and its initiators, the savings caisand the retail banks. I would like to share with you some thoughts on the challenges facing the development of this savings in our country and the solutions recommended to overcome them. . In Morocco, according to the annual national accounts published by the HCP, household savings are around an average of 14% of their gross disposable income. This rate is high in comparison with several emerging and developing countries such as Brazil, Chile or Tunisia (around 10.5%) or South Africa (1.3%) and is close to the levels in some developed countries such as France (14.6%) or Belgium (13.9%). This observation should be qualified, however, for two main reasons related to the weights of certain components of household income. The latter is marked, in the case of our country, by the low contributions, in international comparison, and especially by the relatively large weight of transfers from Moroccans residing abroad which represents on average nearly 15%. Excluding these transfers, the savings rate would be much lower, a finding in line with the available microeconomic data. Indeed, the latest results of the HCP business survey for the third quarter of 2018 indicate that only 3.8% of households say they save part of their income. Similarly, data from the World Bank's 2017 FINDEX survey show that the proportion of the working-age population that saves is half the average of countries in its income class, i.e. middle-lower. These levels would be even lower if we were limited to financial savings, that is, those made with a financial institution. The challenge is therefore twofold: to promote savings on the one hand and to channel them into formal channels on the other. In this regard, and in order to act better, we first need to understand the reasons behind these findings. Ladies and gentlemen At the level of a household, building up savings presupposes that it has an income and therefore a job. However, data from the national survey on the employment carried out by the HCP shows that the activity rate in Morocco is low, not exceeding 47%, with more than half (53%) of the population of working age being excluded from the labour market. In addition, more than 10% of the working population cannot find a job and of those who do, more than three out of five people are unpaid. In total, only 35% of the adult population has a paid job and therefore potentially able to save. Taking into account the nature of the job, which provides a large amount of information on the level of remuneration, the proportion would be even lower. Indeed, nearly four out of ten jobs are concentrated in agricultural activities, for the rest, more than 36%, according to data from the HCP survey on the informal of 2013/2014, has an informal activity. These findings are in line with the results of the Findex survey, which show that 70% of Moroccans who do not have a bank account cite a low level of income as a reason. In addition, the still high level of illiteracy and other cultural factors mean that savings are only weakly channelled into the financial system, with 90 per cent, according to national accounts data, invested in non-financial assets, including real estate and land. Financial savings are not only low, but mobilized mainly in the form of liquid assets, which represent 80%, an investment that is not very adapted to the financing needs of the investment. Such data would be explanatory factors for the relative preponderance of cash in our country both in terms of payment of transactions and hoarding. That said, it should be noted that our knowledge of these microeconomic aspects of saving remains insufficient. Indeed, despite the level Of development achieved by our statistical system, there is always a great need for information on certain economic characteristics of households which are, it should be recalled, difficult to apprehend (income, savings, wealth ...). Ladies and gentlemen While the level of savings remains dependent on the dynamics of economic activity, adequate and well-targeted policies can encourage savings and channel them into formal channels. I will not go back over the many reforms implemented in our country, especially since the early 90s. What we could conclude is that Morocco can now claim a financial system among the most developed, both regionally and in comparison with emerging countries, with mainly a solid and resilient banking system, present in more than thirty countries, particularly in Africa. In terms of offering financial products and services, I think there has been significant diversification, with the development of investment funds and the proliferation of dedicated savings instruments (life and non-life insurance, education savings plans, housing, shares, etc.), and even more recently, the entry into activity of participatory finance. Finally, I would like to point out that in the conduct of our monetary policy mission, the impact of our decisions on savings is one of the important factors we take into consideration. These efforts must obviously be continued in order to respond more adequately to the needs of the different segments of the population and to go beyond the persistent weaknesses in the financial system. It should be recalled in this regard that the banking sector remains predominant in our financial system and that disintermediation is still weak, although it can be an important channel for mobilizing savings, as is the case in many both advanced and emerging countries. Our stock market in particular suffers from a lack of depth and structural liquidity. It is a double challenge that he faces, attracting the company on the one hand and the saver on the other. For those who want more details on these issues, I invite you to consult the public report of the last evaluation of the Moroccan financial sector carried out in 2015 jointly by the IMF and the World Bank. Ladies and gentlemen It is a kind of paradox that we see today between a developed financial system and a limited demand for financial services. So one of the big challenges we face is getting Moroccans back to using financial services and putting their savings at the service of the economy. Achieving our goals in this direction requires a multidimensional approach. First and foremost, this means improving our education system. An educated person is better able to use financial services than an illiterate person. Aware of these challenges, we initiated at Bank Al-Maghrib in 2013 a whole program for financial information, training and education, especially for the benefit of young people and MSMEs. To this end, we have created the Moroccan Foundation for Financial Education which, for us, should be one of the pillars of the financial inclusion strategy, which I will come back to in a few moments. Another important area we have invested in is strengthening public confidence in financial services. That is why we have taken many actions to strengthen consumer protection, several of them in the banking system, but the time I have does not allow me to go back on this. I believe that these dimensions, education and awareness,are often not taken into account in the development of our strategies and in their implementation. The most striking example is the low presence of individuals today at the stock market level. Indeed, during the phases of enthusiasm that accompanied certain privatization and IPO operations, very little effort was made to make them aware of the benefits, but also and above all of the risks inherent in stock market investment. As a result, there has been mass speculation that has led to valuation levels that are out of step with fundamentals and has led to significant stock market falls and a loss of investor confidence, particularly individuals. Beyond traditional financial channels, including banking and insurance, the development of alternative options, a path on which our country has so far lagged behind, should contribute significantly to improving financial inclusion. These offers are based on models that make them less expensive, better adapted and therefore more accessible to excluded populations. The digital revolution now offers us immense opportunities to move forward in this area. To mention just a few, I would like to mention the entry into operation of a new category of institutions, the payment institutions to which we have given the opportunity to collect small savings. In addition, the implementation of mobile payment, the revision of the legal framework for microfinance and the development of microinsurance are all other initiatives to mobilize small savings. However, success and adherence to these new services also require tax incentives that can make them as cheap as possible and therefore more attractive, both on the supply and demand sides. Ladies and gentlemen It is to consolidate all these efforts and federate all stakeholders around a common vision that the Ministry of Economy and Finance and Bank Al-Maghrib are joining forces to finalize the implementation of the national financial inclusion strategy. Its ambition is to ensure that all individuals and companies have access to financial products and services adapted to their needs and means, thus contributing to an inclusive development of our country. Its objectives are to reach and then exceed the level of penetration relevant to Morocco and to reduce the most significant inclusion gaps, particularly for the benefit of women, young people, the rural population, as well as very small businesses. With this ambitious strategy and the commitment of all stakeholders, it is a profound transformation of the financial sector that we wish to carry out both qualitatively and quantitatively, in line with this more global Royale vision of the redesign of our development model. Thank you.

text: KEY ROLE OF THE STATISTICAL INFORMATION SYSTEM IN THE CONDUCT OF BANK AL-MAGHRIBd5S CORE MISSIONS SPEECH OF THE GOVERNOR OF BANK AL-MAGHRIB MR. ABDELLATIF JOUAHRI WORLD STATISTICS DAY RABAT, OCTOBER 20, 2010 Mr. Speaker of the House of Representatives, Mr. Speaker of the House of Councillors, Dear Ministers, Mr. High Commissioner for Planning, Ladies and gentlemen, First, I would like to thank the High Commission for Planning (HCP) for bringing us together on the occasion of the World Statistics Day to discuss a subject of topical interest. I seize this opportunity to laud the constant efforts it makes to upgrade the national statistics system. I will focus my comments on the role of statistics in the conduct of the central bankd5s core missions. But let me first say a few words about the major contribution of statistical information to the development process, and share with you my perception of the progress made by our national statistics system. Ladies and gentlemen, Increasingly seen as a public utility, statistical information today is crucially important to economic growth and helps to ensure the transparency and accountability of actors. Statistical information is, indeed, an essential tool for the design and assessment of public policies and socioeconomic programs. But it is equally important for corporations, as a decision-making tool. The increase in demand for statistics from the various economic policy actors, market participants and the general public implies permanent data credibility, comprehensiveness, reliability and timely availability. Alongside the tremendous efforts made by public authorities in this area, international institutions are working to promote the establishment of sound national statistical systems with standardized data to improve transparency and comparability. Moreover, the recent financial crisis has highlighted the need for countries to address deficiencies in data and improve the quality of statistics in order to prevent further systemic risks. Ladies and gentlemen, Nationally, we note with pride the significant progress accomplished in recent decades in building and strengthening the statistical system. As evidenced by the different assessments undertaken by international institutions, the national statistical framework is now consistent with international standards and practices. With this progress, Morocco occupies a distinguished position in the African continent and the MENA region. I would like to take the opportunity to acknowledge the substantial contribution of all statistics producers in our country, with particular reference to the HCP for the primary role it plays in developing a comprehensive, reliable and transparent statistical system. These efforts were rewarded years ago with Moroccod5s subscription to the IMFd5s Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS) as well as with the improved transparency of our information system through the release of methodological papers describing how statistical indicators are prepared. I remain convinced that the current progress will continue to further meet rigor and consistency requirements to strengthen the effectiveness of our national statistics system. Achieving a better match between statistics and the various user needs, combined with sustained improvement in data dissemination deadlines, must remain the keys to bolster our statistical system. This of course requires closer cooperation and exchange among the different producers of statistical information and smooth interaction with its users. Ladies and gentlemen, Recognizing the vital importance of statistical information for the conduct of its core missions, Bank Al-Maghrib has for several years now worked in a resolute and rigorous manner to develop its statistical capacity and collect new data. The powers of the central bank in the conduct of monetary policy, the preservation of a sound and stable banking system, the security of payment systems and more broadly the contribution to national financial stability require the bank to continuously strengthen its statistics and information system. In a bid to further satisfy the requirements of adapting and modernizing the analytical framework underlying monetary policy and financial stability, the bank has developed several high-frequency indicators with significant value added. In this context, it has mainly put in place a framework for monitoring and forecasting inflation in Morocco, in which the core inflation indicator constitutes an important tool for the general public. Today, the information system which provides the basis for the Bank Board decisions in monetary policy and other core missions of Bank Al-Maghrib includes more than 300,000 monetary, economic and financial series, covering both data produced by the bank and external data. While careful not to overlap with other statistical information producers, the central bank has conducted for some years now, and in compliance with the standards laid down by the Statistical Surveys Coordination Committee, the monthly business survey in the industrial sector. It also carries out, as part of its missions, surveys with credit institutions, mostly on lending rates. In the same vein, we recently concluded a partnership and data exchange agreement with the National Land Registry and Cartography Agency for the joint development of a quarterly real estate price index, the results of which were first released in the first quarter of this year. A contract was also signed with the Moroccan Industrial and Commercial Property Office in order to have access to balance sheet data of all corporations registered in the trade register. The bankd5s achievements in the area of statistics and information are the result of the exchange and interaction with our national partner data producers and providers. I wish here to pay tribute to the exemplary cooperation we have maintained over the years with the HCP and which keeps expanding both quantitatively and qualitatively. Ladies and gentlemen, The bank remains an important user of statistical information, but is also a statistics producer, especially of national monetary statistics. Since the adoption last June of the IMFd5s methodology, the bank has enlarged the analytical framework of monetary and financial trends by providing monthly detailed information on claims and liabilities of depositary corporations vis-88-vis all economic sectors. For the sake of transparency, the bank publishes on its website the new methodology for the preparation of monetary statistics and provides users with chained series dating back to 1985. Ladies and gentlemen, The current situation is fraught with many challenges for the conduct of the bankd5s missions, on top of which the need to adapt the monetary policy framework to the accelerating financial opening of the national economy. Indeed, with the increasing openness of our economy, constant tradeoffs must be made between assets on the domestic and international market. Investment decisions will hinge, among other things, on price ratios and interest rate differentials, thus requiring almost real-time availability of information on asset prices and interest rates. In view of this situation and in anticipation of the future, the central bank has worked for several years now to put in place a monitoring and evaluation framework for economic agentsd5 indebtedness and credit conditions, at the same time with the strengthening of the analysis framework of real estate asset prices. It has also launched a project for the development of a monitoring framework of nonfinancial corporationsd5 financial soundness. Ladies and Gentlemen, Ensuring the sustainability of good practices in the production of statistics requires further strengthening of coordination and cooperation between the different statistical data producers and users, while seeing to the independence of statistics producers d0 which is tantamount to data credibility. To this end, the current debate on a national strategy for developing statistics, which provides for the creation of a national council for statistics, should come to fruition very soon. Such a council, composed of all the concerned parties, will define the national strategy for the production and publication of statistics. In addition, the implementation of a modern dissemination policy, based on new technologies, will allow strengthening the transparency and credibility of data providers. Investment in information exchange platforms will therefore develop markedly. On the occasion of the World Statistics Day, I wish to assert that Bank Al-Maghrib will continue to work toward preserving, on a permanent basis, the compliance of statistics it produces with the international standards. It will make every effort to contribute to the success of all projects which Morocco is set to undertake in the field of statistics. Thank you.

Title: Opening remarks at the Global Forum on Financial Inclusion Policies (GDF) of the AFI
text: AFIl Inanciere (GPF) on Inclusion Policies FForum Mondia Under the theme: "Exploring Diversity, Promoting Inclusion" Opening remarks by Mr Abdellatif JOUAHRI Wali of Bank Al-Maghrib and Chairman of the 40th Session of the Board of Governors of Arab Central Banks 2017 September 14 . "Cultural diversity is a driving force for development and an indispensable asset for alleviating poverty and achieving sustainable development" - Unesco Your Excellency the President of the Arab Republic of Egypt; Your Excellency the Prime Minister; Madam Minister of Planning, Monitoring and Administrative Reform; Mr. Managing Director and Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Arab Monetary Fund; The Governor of the Central Bank of Egypt; Mr. Executive Director of the AFI; Distinguished Governors, Ladies and gentlemen members and partners of the AFI; Dear colleagues; Ladies and Gentlemen, I feel a great honour to participate today in the Global Forum on Financial Inclusion Policies, especially since it is being held, for the first time, in our Arab region and in our sister country of Egypt. First of all, I would like to congratulate the organizers, the Central Bank of Egypt and the Alliance for Financial Inclusion, for taking the initiative to gather around the theme "Exploring diversity, promoting inclusion", with a view to uniting and strengthening our efforts to establish inclusive finance that promotes the socio-economic development of our countries. This theme reminds us that the diversity of our countries is the strength and richness of our network and represents a major asset in the fight against poverty and achieving our common goals of sustainable development. Ladies and gentlemen As you know, financial inclusion has become an important factor in economic efficiency and social equity. Indeed, international organizations and standard-setting bodies, including the World Bank, the G20, the United Nations and the Bank. International Regulations, have for nearly a decade stressed the need for public authorities to adopt national policies and strategies to overcome exclusion factors and provide populations, individuals and businesses with a financially inclusive environment. They also highlighted the importance of alliances at national, regional and international levels to enhance the effectiveness of financial inclusion policies. The AFI, for its part, increasingly encourages and supports regional initiatives to transmit its values, which are increasingly asserted at the international level. This is how it has accompanied the birth of 3 regional initiatives: the African Initiative on Financial Services Policies via Mobile Telephony, the Pacific Islands Regional Initiative and the Initiative for Financial Inclusion in Latin America and the Caribbean. This model has proven its relevance, promoting the in-depth analysis of the barriers specific to each region and the development of effective policies adapted to the social and economic context of the populations. These regional initiatives have also made it possible to provide decision-makers and regulators with practical and tested policies and coherent and proportionate regulatory principles that make it possible to reconcile, in a complementary way, the objectives of financial inclusion with the mission of stability and financial integrity. Ladies and gentlemen According to the results of the latest FINDEX survey in 2014, only 29% of adults in the Arab world have access to formal financial services compared to 69% in East Asia and the Pacific as an example. This rate does not exceed 24% for women and is only 7% for low-income populations and young people aged 15 to 24. Not to mention migrants and refugees, whose numbers are constantly increasing in our region, and who seem to be excluded from the formal financial system. With regard to small and medium-sized enterprises, it appears that only one in five SMEs has credit even if they represent more than 80% of the economic fabric of the region and that their need exceeds by more than three times the supply of financing. These figures also mask significant disparities between the countries of the region. For example, while the rate of banking in some countries does not exceed 10%, this rate exceeds 70% in others. Faced with this alarming situation, central banks, often outside any explicit mandate at the level of the laws governing them and with the support of the Arab Monetary Fund, have erected financial inclusion as the main axis of their strategies with the aim of reducing poverty, promoting the transition from the informal sector to the formal economy, maintaining stability and financial integrity and stimulating economic growth. In this context, they have drawn up action plans specific to the different categories of the population and businesses, while ensuring their protection. In this sense, the Board of Governors of the Arab Central Banks decided, in October 2012 at its meeting held in Kuwait, to set up, within the FMA, a specific working group on issues relating to Financial Inclusion in the MENA region, and instructed it to propose measures that could contribute to improving access to and use of financial services, to support the implementation of international standards relating to this theme and to allow the exchange of experiences and expertise between Arab countries. In collaboration with our international partners, this group has focused its efforts on critical issues in the region including those related to financial inclusion data, women's financial inclusion, financial education, consumer protection and the legal framework for FINTECH. The conclusions of its work are presented at the annual meetings of our Council to approve the action plans to be adopted by the Arab countries and monitor their effective implementation. Thus, at its last meeting held in Rabat in 2016, the Council approved the adoption of 27 April each year as an Arab Day of Financial Inclusion with the aim of contributing to the raising awareness among all stakeholders in Arab countries of the importance of financial inclusion. This day became an opportunity to renew the region's commitment to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030. I am pleased to highlight here the support and support of the Arab Monetary Fund to accompany the efforts of our region in its quest to overcome the challenges it still faces. It is in this sense that the FMA has taken the initiative to join the efforts of the region with those of the AFI and GIZ within the framework of the tripartite initiative "FIARI", able to establish an inclusive model that will overcome barriers to access and use of formal financial services and strengthen partnerships. Such cooperation will be one of the key factors in supporting and accelerating the implementation of our policies and strategies while establishing a framework for the continuous exchange of best practices. Bank Al-Maghrib, being a member of the AFI since 2010, supports the "FIARI" initiative and considers that it will make available to our region the feedback of its members as well as the know-how of its experts to strengthen the effectiveness of our work. As such, I take the opportunity offered to me here to invite my fellow Arab Central Banks to join the AFI, alongside Egypt, Jordan, Palestine and Morocco. This membership will undoubtedly strengthen the position of our Region within this organization and make it more influential. Ladies and gentlemen In Morocco, financial inclusion has been erected as a strong commitment of Bank Al-Maghrib which has made it, since 2007, one of its major objectives and one of the main vectors of a global strategy for the development of the financial sector by 2020, and aimed at both the deepening of the national banking market, the development of capital markets and the positioning of our country as a regional financial hub. Moreover, our commitment to promote access to and use of quality financial services on a sound and solid basis was announced in 2013 through the Maya Declaration and reaffirmed in 2016 as part of the roadmap for aligning the financial sector with the Sustainable Development Goals at COP 22 held in Marrakech. In this context, our commitment has resulted in many actions that we have undertaken, with the involvement of public and private actors, and which have focused on all the dimensions of financial inclusion including the banking of different segments of the population, financial education, consumer protection, the financing of MSMEs and the promotion of innovation in the offers of financial institutions. These advances were highlighted by the World Bank and the IMF during their last FSAP financial sector assessment mission conducted in 2015 and demonstrated by the evolution of the banking rate, which reached 70% at the end of 2016 while it did not exceed 25% ten years earlier. That said, we must recognize that we still have challenges to overcome: the disparities between the rural and urban world, between genders, the improvement of data quality and the development of an effective impact measurement system. These challenges remind us of the need to continue to unite our efforts, at the national, regional and international levels, and to mobilize in a comprehensive and harmonized manner to provide an adequate response to all these challenges. Faced with this situation, we are committed to addressing these disparities, as part of a long-term national financial inclusion strategy, which we are finalizing with the Ministry of Finance and in collaboration with all public and private stakeholders. As part of this strategy and recognizing the critical role of women's financial inclusion in driving inclusive growth, we join the AFI in bridging the gender gap as part of the Denarau Action Plan. Ladies and gentlemen I remain convinced that this forum, given the theme it has chosen, the quality of its workshops and the cultural diversity of its members will generate new resolutions that will allow us all to achieve our goals of inclusive and sustainable development.

Title: At the BEAC Conference on "Central Banks in the face of exogenous shocks: exit strategies..."
text: BEAC High Level Conference Central banks in the face of exogenous shocks: Exit strategies from the crisis? Session 1: Impact of the crisis on developing economies Introductory remarks by Mr. Abdellatif Jouahri Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib Yaounde, 25 January 2017 Your Excellency, Head of Government of the Republic of Cameroon Dear Ministers, Dear Governors, Dear friends, dear colleagues, Ladies and gentlemen It is a real pleasure for me to respond to the invitation of my friend Lucas to participate in this debate on our contribution  as central bankers  to our countries' efforts to deal with the consequences of the crisis and external shocks. I have known Lucas for several years during which we have developed excellent relationships that have allowed me to appreciate both his professional and human qualities. I would like to congratulate him on all the work he has done at the head of BEAC1 for the benefit of the economies of the region. The presence of many eminent personalities here today is a testimony and recognition of all his peers. I remain convinced that, after his tenure at the BEAC, he will continue to make his contribution to the work of building and consolidating our continent. 1 (*)BEAC: The BEAC is an African international institution created in 1972 and headquartered in Yaounde. It is responsible for: the definition and conduct of the monetary policy of the Central African Monetary Union (UMAC); the issuance of banknotes and coins that are legal tender and discharge in the Union; the conduct of the Exchange Rate Policy of the Union; the holding and management of the official foreign exchange reserves of the Member States and the promotion and proper functioning of payment and settlement systems. The UMAC includes the following 6 countries: Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Chad. Ladies and gentlemen I think there is no need to recall the relevance and importance of the theme that brings us together today. Since 2008, the world has alternated between crises and shocks, all against a backdrop of economic, geopolitical, security and climate uncertainties. Every time a hope of a return to normalcy is announced, the situation becomes complicated and we understand that it is not yet over. Today, several countries are still struggling and while some seem to be recovering, the after-effects are likely to persist for some time to come. It is the potential for growth that has weakened, it is unemployment, especially among young people, that has worsened significantly, it is public debt that has become worrying, it is populism and protectionism that are gaining ground. It is also in the context of the ramifications of the crisis that commodity and oil prices, in particular, have been on a downward trend since June 2014. This development, which is putting a strain on exporting countries, including several from our continent, is precisely the subject of this first session of our meeting. We will focus on the impact of falling commodity prices on developing economies and perhaps also on the responses, although this will be the main focus of the next two sessions. Ladies and gentlemen Since its discovery in 1859, oil has been a precious resource but also a source of several shocks and the object of geopolitical conflicts in modern history. Let us remember, in this regard, the oil shocks of the post-war period: the Suez Canal crisis of 56-57, the OPEC embargo in 73-74, the Iranian revolution of 78-79, the Iran-Iraq war launched in 80, and the first Gulf War in 90-91. These shocks, exclusively supply-side shocks, have resulted in significant but temporary price increases. The situation we have been experiencing since mid-2014 is quite special. This is a significant and persistent fall in prices that has its origins in both supply and demand factors. Indeed, the 2008 crisis led to a sharp slowdown in global growth and, consequently, in oil demand. Initially, the decline in activity was more pronounced in advanced economies, notably the United States and the Eurozone, while emerging market and developing economies, notably the BRICS, played the role of engine of global growth. From 2011, the effects of the crisis eventually caught up with these economies mainly through trade and FDI. On the supply side, this drop is mainly due to the development of shale oil production. This has seen a significant increase in the United States and Canada, favoured by the high levels of the price per barrel, but also the gradual fall in the cost of production thanks to technological progress. The quest of some major conventional oil producers to preserve their market share has resulted in the volume of supply remaining at high levels, which has increased the downward pressure on prices. It was only recently, in September 2016, that the producing countries, notably those of OPEC, agreed to a reduction in production, which they subsequently concretized in November in Vienna. One of the lessons that can be drawn from these different shocks is that forecasting the price of this resource remains a difficult art. Let us remember that in 2008, experts were almost unanimous that the era of "cheap" oil was definitely over, so the threshold of 200 a barrel was imminent. Ladies and gentlemen The fall in prices since 2014 represented an opportunity that fuelled hopes for a faster recovery in activity globally and, in particular, in advanced economies. A July 2015 IMF study estimated that a 10% drop in the price of a barrel would translate into a 0.2% increase in global growth. Another World Bank study estimated the impact of a decline of the same magnitude for importing countries between 0.1 and 0.5 percentage points of additional growth, depending on the importance of imports of energy products in GDP. In practice, the positive impact on importing economies was less than the negative impact on exporting countries. The latter have experienced a significant contraction in their oil revenues, which has strained their external balances, put strong pressure on their reserve stocks and reduced their budgetary margins; especially for those whose economies are not very diversified, as is the case in several African countries. At the level of emerging importing countries, the combination of several factors, including the rebalancing of the Chinese economy, geopolitical conflicts and a weak international environment, has not allowed them to take full advantage of the fall in prices. These countries have certainly benefited from a reduction in their energy bills, which has allowed a recovery in macroeconomic balances and a strengthening of foreign exchange reserves; nevertheless, they faced several constraints. These are mainly the weakness of foreign demand and the tightening of monetary and financial conditions as a result of lower investment from oil-exporting countries. Similarly, importing advanced economies have not been able to take full advantage of lower oil prices. The exhaustion of monetary policy margins and its weak transmission have not allowed a revival of activity. In addition, the economic situation in these countries would have suffered from the uncertainties related to the normalization of monetary policy in the United States, the elections in several countries and BREXIT. All in all, it is certainly difficult to isolate the effects of this drop in oil prices, but overall the expected recovery in activity has not been at the rendezvous. This recovery in advanced economies remains slow and weak activity continues in several emerging markets. Thus, global growth decelerated to 3.2% in 2015 and would have been limited to 3.1% in 2016. It is expected, however, to accelerate again from this year, recording a rate of 3.4%. Ladies and gentlemen Before the fall in commodity prices, the economies of our continent, especially those of Sub-Saharan Africa, were globally resilient, despite an unfavorable and uncertain international environment. As a result, they have posted sustained and vigorous growth that has enabled them to reduce the vulnerabilities of their economies and even to build buffers. Several factors contributed to this performance, including high commodity prices, the inflow of capital and foreign investment, and the easing of financing conditions in international financial markets. In addition, these countries continued to benefit from external assistance and the support of international institutions. This economic performance has enabled them to make significant progress in terms of human development, including a marked improvement in access to schooling and a significant reduction in infant and maternal mortality. However, the reversal in commodity prices has resulted in lower incomes and weaker growth in several countries. In total, growth in Sub-Saharan Africa slowed sharply in 2016 to 1.4% after 3.4% in 2015, its weakest performance in more than twenty years. In terms of prospects, after the increases recorded following the agreement of the oil-producing countries, prices are expected to remain well below pre-2014 levels in the medium term, thus weighing on the growth prospects of the countries of the region. The latest IMF forecasts, dating from last October, indicate some improvement in activity in the medium term, but this would remain modest compared to the results recorded over the last decade. Growth in sub-Saharan Africa is expected to be limited to 2.9% in 2017 before rising to 3.6% in 2018, compared to an average of 5.3% recorded over the period from 2010 to 2014. In addition to the above-mentioned difficulties, the countries of the region are also expected to face other no less important challenges. First, Africa remains one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change. In 2016, parts of eastern and southern Africa experienced the worst drought in 35 years with a sharp decline in agricultural production, exacerbating food insecurity for millions of people. Second, terrorism and geopolitical conflicts threaten the economies and populations of several countries. To give just one figure, according to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, in 2014 there were 3.7 million refugees and 11.4 million internally displaced persons in sub-Saharan Africa. Faced with all these challenges, the priority is that the security and geopolitical problems be definitively ironed out. Second, to address development challenges, sound economic policies and structural reforms are needed to promote economic transformation and diversification, improve competitiveness and ensure sustainable and inclusive growth. African countries have certainly launched several initiatives and projects in recent years. Examples include programmes under the New Partnership for Africa's Development (NEPAD), including the African Agriculture Development Programme (CAADP) and the Infrastructure Development Programme (PIDA). The results have often fallen short of expectations, but most of the recommended paths remain relevant and require the will and means for effective implementation. So, there is a problem of resources that arises with insistence! It should be recalled here that the estimates provided in 2013 by Global Financial Integrity with the AfDB show that Africa, if we take into account illicit capital outflows, remains a net creditor of the rest of the world. There is therefore an opportunity to launch incentive policies to repatriate a good part of African capital abroad. I would like to mention, in this regard, the example of the tax amnesty operation launched by Morocco in 2014 and which gave quite convincing results since the figures reached represent nearly 3% of GDP. For their part, international institutions  in the current conjuncture  must make more efforts for Africa and also be more flexible in their requirements while ensuring quality technical support. Our representatives in these institutions can play an important role, but we must also unite our voices, through coordinating bodies such as the African Caucus. Moreover, strengthening integration at the level of our continent is now more necessary than ever. Despite the formation of several regional blocs and currency areas, trade integration is still weak. According to data from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), between 2007 and 2011, the share of intra-African exports in total merchandise exports averaged 11% compared to 50% in developing countries in Asia, 21% in Latin America and the Caribbean and 70% in Europe. However, it should be recalled that fiscal and monetary policies must also play an important role. We will have a debate on this in the next sessions of this day. Ladies and gentlemen With that, I stop to give the floor to our eminent speakers who will enlighten us on (i) the impact of the fall in commodity prices, in particular on net exporting economies, (ii) the lessons to be learned from such situations, and (iii) the reforms to be undertaken to limit the heavy dependence on oil and the export of raw materials.

Title: At the Regional Conference on Financial Education in the Arab World
text: Regional Conference on Financial education in the Arab World: Strategies, implementation and impact Opening address of Mr. Abdellatif JOUAHRI Governor of Bank Al-Maghrib and Chairman of the Board of the Moroccan Foundation for Financial Education October 20, 2016 d2Knowledge is the only treasure you can give entirely without running short of itd3 -Amadou Hampat8e B88 d2Upon the education of the people of this country the fate of this country dependsd3 -Benjamin Disraeli Honorable Ministers, His Majestyd5s Governor of Skhirat Temara, Honorable Governors, Mr. Director General of the Arab Monetary Fund, Mr. Executive Director at the Alliance for Financial Inclusion, Distinguished representatives of international and regional organizations, Ladies and gentlemen, It is my great pleasure to welcome you today in Rabat for this regional high-level conference on financial education, which we organize jointly with the Ministry of Economy and Finance. I would like to thank our partners, the Arab Monetary Fund (AMF), the German Corporation for International Cooperation (GIZ), the World Bank, the OECD and the SANAD Fund, for responding positively to the decision taken at the AMF Council of Central Bank Governors, held on September 13, 2015 in Cairo, to organize this conference in Morocco. I commend their contribution to its organization and funding. I wish also to thank the ministers for attending this conference despite their busy schedules, which reflects the support they provide to promoting financial education in our countries. The presence of the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI), represented by its Executive Director who has made the effort to take part in this conference, demonstrates all the interest that AFI has in financial inclusion and its various components. For the record, the AFI members adopted in 2011, at the Global Policy Forum held in Mexico, d2the Maya Declarationd3 under which they take measurable commitments to develop financial inclusion in their countries and monitor their implementation annually. This Declaration reflects the growing awareness and recognition among financial regulators and central banks of the role of financial inclusion in improving financial stability and integrity. Bank Al-Maghrib joined the AFI in 2010, a year after its creation. I take this opportunity to invite my colleagues in Arab central banks that are not a member yet to join us quickly. Ladies and gentlemen, In light of the increasingly complex global financial conditions, financial education has become a major factor of economic efficiency and social equity. In this regard, international organizations have stressed, for over a decade now, the importance and the need for public authorities to adopt national strategies for financial inclusion and education. To this end, they put under their disposal networks of experts and several analytical reports. OECD members and program of action have also recognized the importance of financial education. The World Bank also considers financial inclusion as a key factor for reducing poverty, which prompted it to set the goal of universal access to financial services by the year 2020. In this context, priority was given to twenty-five countries, including Egypt and Morocco. The G20 made financial inclusion and education among its key priority areas and created, in 2009, an experts group which developed the nine core principles for an innovative financial inclusion. In 2010, the G20 launched the Global Partnership for Financial Inclusion bringing together member and non-member countries, in cooperation with the AFI, the Consultative Group to Assist the Poor and the International Finance Corporation. Moreover, following the decision of the AMF council of central bank governors, in October 2012 in Kuwait, the AMF set up a working group on financial inclusion in the Middle East and North Africa region. One of the objectives of this group is to propose measures likely to contribute to the development of financial inclusion policies in Arab countries, and to help these countries implement international standards and facilitate the sharing of experiences and expertise among them. Ladies and gentlemen, In our region, public authorities, especially central banks, committed themselves to advancing the cause of financial inclusion, particularly financial education, albeit often without a clear mandate in this regard, starting from their deep conviction in the role it can play in the achievement of their main missions. Accordingly, many central banks prepared action plans that include financial education within the main axes of financial inclusion strategies, in consultation with all public and private sectors actors, and as part of a participatory approach which aims to identify the activities specific to each segment of the population. One of the first initiatives in the region was the organization of a Financial Education Week, which has become, since 2013, an annual event celebrated by many countries in the Arab world, such as Egypt, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Tunisia, Palestine, Yemen, Somalia and Morocco, in order to disseminate financial education among children and the youth. In 2015, the initiative benefited more than 1.7 million children and young people in the region out of a total of 5.6 million beneficiaries from 124 participating countries. In the same vein, the AMF council of central bank governors decided to adopt an Arab Day for Financial Inclusion on April 27 of each year, a date which marks the anniversary of the signing of the AMF Establishment Agreement in 1976 in Rabat. Ladies and gentlemen, At the start, several actors in Morocco took various initiatives to promote financial education. However, in response to the challenges this implies in the short and long run, we decided to coordinate our efforts at the national level, by involving the relevant government departments as well as the financial and banking sector. Hence, the Moroccan Foundation for Financial Education was created in 2013, with the mission of implementing the National Strategy for Financial Education. Endeavoring to achieve its goals aiming at (i) anchoring the principles and good practices related to financial education and (ii) raising public awareness as to financial services, the Foundation focused, as part of its first three-year plan 2014.2016, on the following five strategic areas: 1. Providing financial literacy training for youth; 2. Incorporating financial education as a component in economic and social development programs; 3. Conducting public awareness campaigns; 4. Supporting VSMEs awareness and financial education programs; and 5. Promoting national and international cooperation. To implement this strategy, the Foundation developed didactic tools and kits specific to each targeted category, based on pilot experiences to be rolled out throughout the country. With regard to children and young people, the Foundation worked together with the Education Ministry to incorporate financial education in school curricula. To this end, student and teacher textbooks were prepared, drawing on the educational tools provided by the international organization of financial education d2Aflatound3. Rabat was chosen as a pilot city for the implementation of this project. Concerning the target group of enterprises, more particularly VSMEs, the Foundation launched, together with the Ministry of Crafts, Social and Solidarity Economy, the National Financial Literacy Caravan to promote financial education among craftspeople and entrepreneurs. This initiative benefited over 4,000 persons across all regions of the Kingdom. The Ministry also integrated financial education as a compulsory module in the initial vocational training curriculum designed for craft apprentices. As such, the Foundation developed a special educational package and trained more than 80 trainers from the Ministry, who will, in turn, ensure training for the targeted artisans. At the university level, the Abdelmalek Saadi University of Tetouan was chosen as a pilot tertiary education institution to start implementing the programs intended for students. At the level of cooperation, the Foundation partnered with several public and private institutions, both nationally and internationally. In this regard, we will soon lead, in collaboration with the World Bank, a new survey, after the one conducted in 2013, on the financial capacity of households with a view to giving a clearer picture of the achievements and challenges lying ahead, in line with the aspirations and needs. Ladies and gentlemen, Our two-day high-level meeting, featuring plenary sessions and workshops, is an opportunity to share best practice in promoting financial education and developing financially capable communities. I am confident that this conference will make concrete proposals and recommendations that will undoubtedly contribute to establishing a regional cooperation framework in this field. Thank you for attention and I wish you a pleasant stay in Morocco.

Title: At the Conference on "the development of the private sector and investment in Morocco"
text: Rabat on December 8, 2017 Conference on "Strengthening Private Sector Development and investment in Morocco Opening Remarks Elements of intervention of Mr ABDERRAHIM BOUAZZA Managing Director of Bank Al-Maghrib Mr Vice-President of the EIB, Mr Vice-President of the CGEM, Honourable guests, ladies and gentlemen, I am very pleased to welcome you to BAM, here in its training centre and to welcome you to this conference organised by the EIB in partnership with CGEM and BAM under the theme "Strengthening private sector development and investment in Morocco". Let me begin by apologizing to Governor Jouahri, who was scheduled to deliver opening remarks at this conference, but commitments abroad prevented him from being with us today. I would like to express my deep thanks to the heads of the EIB and CGEM for their cooperation in organising this conference. My thanks also go to the various speakers and also to the leaders and heads of national and international institutions and to the representatives of the business world and the financial sector who kindly participated in this event. The subject of our conference has been the subject of several reflections and studies that have shown that it has several dimensions that are in some cases more or less complex. They concern issues of yield and allocation of factors of production, the business environment, the informal sector, access to financing, etc. These questions are also at the center of the programs of the meetings we organize with the CGEM and the GPBM. Today's event therefore represents an opportunity for an exchange of ideas and experiences focused on the challenges of developing private investment in Morocco, in the light of the results of the joint EIB-WB survey in the MENA region. The survey is a valuable source of information to better understand the obstacles to the promotion of the private sector, which over time has become central to development policy efforts. Certainly in our country, after independence the authorities opted for the liberalization of the economy and the application of the principles of liberalism, but the State played the role of the strategist, the leader and the main investor and actor in the economic development of the country. From the 90s and with the adoption of the PAS, Morocco and like several developing countries, began a privatization process and undertook a set of reforms to promote initiative and private investment in search of sustainable and inclusive growth. More recently, the authorities have opted for a new way of managing the country's development based on public-private partnerships. As a result, several sectoral strategies have been launched. I quote in particular, the industrial emergence plan, the industrial acceleration plan, the Green Morocco plan, Morocco's energy strategy and the 2020 tourism vision.... Thanks to these reforms, the political stability enjoyed by our country, the macroeconomic management deemed sound by the International Institutions and the choice of openness, the national economy has strengthened its attractiveness. According to the 2017 barometer of attractiveness published by the international firm Ernst & Young, Morocco is at the top of the most attractive countries on the African continent. More generally, the investment effort in Morocco is significant and very high compared to several emerging countries. The investment rate has averaged nearly 34% over the last 10 years compared to, for example, 23.7% in Malaysia and Chile or 28.3% in Turkey. Despite all these efforts, the process of convergence of the national economy remains slow. The slowdown in growth in recent years as well as the decline in its potential which, according to the conclusions of a study by our research department would be limited to 4.5%, highlight the low return on investment as well as the lack of effectiveness of the various reforms undertaken. This also reflects disability. of our economy to take advantage of the various windows of opportunities that are opening up, including the dividend of its demographic transition and the political and social stability it enjoys, to accelerate its economic and social development. Slow growth has been reflected in labour market conditions, which have deteriorated in recent years. The participation rate was recorded in a downward trend, over the last ten years to return to 46% in 2016, a level that remains below those observed in many emerging countries. Similarly, job creation remains low and unemployment affects a significant proportion, of more than 9%, of the active population, and in particular young people and graduates, of whom respectively more than 29% and 18% do not find jobs. Growth in Morocco is also not very inclusive. Inequalities remain significant both between regions and between different social categories. Nearly half of the national wealth is created in two regions "Casablanca-Settat" and "Rabat-Sale-Kenitra", nearly 3 out of 10 young people are unemployed and the majority of women remain inactive, especially in cities or. more than 8 out of ten do not enter the labour market. The national economy therefore continues to suffer from certain structural limitations, and this despite the various sectoral strategies put in place by the government. In this respect, I shall confine myself to three observations which I consider important: 1. Slow process of transformation of the structure of the national economy: the Moroccan economy remains dependent on the achievements of the sector agricultural, itself largely dependent on climatic conditions. This sector has contributed nearly 12% of GDP over the last ten years and represents at the end of 2016 nearly 38% of the employed active population. The industrial sector, for its part, contributes 17% of the value added and employs no more than 11% of the workforce and the added value of the tourism sector remains very volatile and highly dependent on the security situation in some countries of the region. In terms of sectoral strategies, despite the dynamics of the automotive sector and, to a lesser extent, some other global businesses, the desired knock-on effects are still limited. The content of exports in imports remains in general important, reflecting the weak integration of the country's industrial fabric, which has consequences for the trade balance deficit, which also suffers from the strong dependence of the national economy on imports of energy products. In this regard, the establishment of ecosystems with the aim of improving the integration rate of Morocco's global trades, and producing the expected ripple effects of large flows of foreign direct investment is a promising direction that should improve the results of these strategies. These schemes, which today cover several branches of activity, in particular automotive, textile, aeronautics, chemical industry, industry pharmaceutical, agribusiness should also strengthen small and medium-sized enterprises, the backbone of the national economy. Finally, the weight of informal activities in GDP raises questions about the performance of efforts to modernize the productive fabric and the weak capacity of the industrial sector to promote the reallocation of resources. 2. Insufficient supply of skills: On this point, it appears from the various studies carried out by national or international institutions such as the World Bank, that the national education system suffers from a low level of performance and quality that does not allow it to support reforms aimed at improving the productivity of the economy and to play its role in terms of inclusion. Conversely, and if appropriate reforms are not taken, the current system could exacerbate social disparities and unemployment among graduates. 3. Slow improvement of the business climate: Efforts undertaken in this regard have enabled Morocco to significantly improve its ranking in terms of ease of doing business, positioning itself according to the latest Ranking of the World Bank of October 2017 at the 69th place globally and at the 3rd position both on the African continent and in the MENA region. However, significant differences persist mainly in the applicability of laws and procedures. Indeed, and if we refer to the approach of the World Bank, Morocco could significantly improve the business environment by acting in particular on two levers. It is first of all a question of obtaining the loans. And let me make it clear at this point that it is not about the ease of obtaining a loan or a limited supply of credit, but rather about the quality of the legal environment and the extent of the information that allows the protection of lenders and borrowers. Indeed, and according to the latest assessment of the World Bank, Morocco's score is limited to 2 out of 12 with regard to the reliability of legal rights which measures the degree of protection of the rights of borrowers and lenders. On the other hand, it performs relatively better in terms of the coverage and accessibility of credit information available at the public or private registry level. At this level, and thanks to the implementation of the office credit, Morocco obtains a score of 7 out of 8. Similarly, Morocco's score is heavily penalized by the low insolvency settlement score that assesses the laws and procedures used in the insolvency management process. Today, our country has several assets. To fully benefit, Morocco must accelerate ongoing reforms, particularly with regard to the education system, justice, innovation and research. Our meeting today is an opportunity to discuss and debate no only problems but also the challenges to be met and the opportunities that are available to our country and that we must absolutely seize in order to set in motion a virtuous dynamic. which promotes its economic development. The private sector is called upon today to play a central role in the dynamics of reforms that our country is experiencing today, to actively contribute to this positive energy and to assume its role asa driver of growth and wealth creation.

Title: International Conference on Green Finance: Inclusive Green Finance
text: International Conference Under the theme "Inclusive Green Finance" Opening speech by Mr Abdellatif JOUAHRI Wali de Bank Al-Maghrib 30 October 2019 Ladies and Gentlemen, Honourable Assistance, Dear Friends and Colleagues, I am pleased to welcome you to Rabat on the occasion of the conference we are co-organizing with the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI) on green finance. First of all, I would like to thank our partners the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI) and the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for the Greening of the Financial System (NGFS) for their valuable contribution to the organization of this event in Morocco. My thanks also go to all the participants and speakers who made the trip to take part in this conference and I am delighted to see that all continents are now represented across forty countries. This conference was preceded by a 2-day seminar for AFI members that focused on inclusive green finance and benefited about fifty participants. Our meeting today is part of the agenda of events organized by Bank Al-Maghrib as part of the celebration of its sixtieth anniversary and comes a few weeks before the 25th Conference of the Parties on Climate to be held this year in Chile. Recently, the United Nations, the IMF and other international institutions insisted in a report on "Financing for Sustainable Development" on the urgency of aligning the financial systems at the national and international levels with the challenges of sustainable development, otherwise the commitments made for the fight against climate change and the eradication of poverty by 2030 will not be able to be kept. Aware of the challenges of climate change and the benefits of financial inclusion as a factor of economic efficiency and social equity, the AFI has joined its voice to that of international organizations by including this theme among the orientations of its network. Ladies and gentlemen This conference bridges two of the most pressing concerns facing emerging and developing countries: financial inclusion and climate change. Global warming is unequivocal and unprecedented and it is now recognized that our planet and its ecosystems will suffer irreversible consequences if measures are not taken quickly to limit it below the threshold agreed at the level of the Paris Agreement. It is also recognized that this warming further threatens populations already weakened by poverty, limited access to water and electricity and financial exclusion. The magnitude of the threat is even more intense for the African continent, which is most exposed to the effects of climate change and has some of the lowest financial inclusion rates in the world with an average estimated at around 40% by the latest Global Findex. Ladies and gentlemen The risks associated with climate change, whether physical, generated by extreme weather events, or transition, induced by the shift to low-carbon economic models, are complex to understand and measure. This complexity is accentuated by the absence of a common language or taxonomy to distinguish between green and brown assets, a lack of sufficiently granular data and tools for assessing these risks, the nature of which is certain but whose magnitude and impacts on the financial sector remain poorly understood. Understanding the issue of climate change, from the perspective of central banks and supervisors that we are, implies understanding the structural changes that will have to affect the financial system and more broadly the economy and that will challenge us in the conduct of our fundamental missions, both in terms of price stability, financial stability and financial inclusion. Strengthening our capacities in this area, cooperation and knowledge sharing at the national, regional and international levels are essential in this regard. In this regard, the NGFS, a network of central banks and supervisors for the greening of the financial system, created in December 2017 by eight central banks on the occasion of the "One Planet Summit" held in Paris, is an initiative that I would particularly like to welcome. Designed as a platform for global peer exchange, this network, which Bank Al-Maghrib joined early on, aims to facilitate the financial sector's contribution to the achievement of the Paris Agreement and the development by the financial community of appropriate practices for managing climate and environmental risks. Since its creation, the dynamic of membership of this network has continued to accelerate, reflecting a growing awareness of the financial authorities of the urgency of their action. The NGFS now has 46 members who are voluntarily committed to supporting and accompanying green finance. This movement has also attracted the interest of international standard-setting bodies, in particular the Basel Committee which recently joined it and others who have expressed their you can't follow suit. Bank Al-Maghrib took this opportunity to stimulate dialogue with public authorities and other regulators at the national level and with its counterparts at the African level to the effect of to build, together, the contours of an active cooperation on the subject of green finance and climate resilience. I am pleased to see that some of the African central banks we have approached have affirmed their willingness to join the movement and are also counting on the establishment of Moroccan banking groups in 27 African countries for the deployment, at the continental level, of convergent green financial policies. Ladies and gentlemen, In Morocco, initiatives in favour of the greening of the financial system were initially individual and scattered before being federated through the adoption of a roadmap national engaging the public and private actors concerned, 3 years ago, on the occasion of the Cop22 in Marrakech. Among the main achievements that followed, I would like to mention:  the development of some green financing offers by the banking sector, most of which are backed by bilateral and multilateral financing lines,  the issuance of first green bonds or  the establishment by the Casablanca Stock Exchange of a benchmark index measuring the performance of the prices of companies responsible in terms of environmental, social and good governance. To accelerate the banking sector's consideration of climate issues, Bank Al-Maghrib is currently working on a regulatory directive setting out our expectations in this area as a regulator. We are also preparing to launch, with our partners concerned, a national study on climate risks in Morocco with the support of international experts. That said, we are still at the very beginning of a long process and there is still a long way to go to start making significant progress in the transition to a more resilient and low-carbon economy. This year, Morocco adopted a National Climate Plan to 2030 that aims to ensure the adaptation of the most affected sectors, namely water, agriculture and fisheries, as well as the mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions mainly by the electricity generation, transport and agriculture sectors. The implementation of this plan requires considerable investments that require a sharing of funding and risks between the public and private sectors as well as national and international donors. It also requires, in addition to the use of the State budget, an appropriate tax system, guarantee products or innovative financing instruments such as green funds and public-private partnerships. Ladies and gentlemen Finance that is both green and inclusive now makes sense, and it is even existential. Based on this observation, the members of the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI) concluded in 2017, an agreement on Financial Inclusion, Climate Change and Climate Finance in Sharm El Sheikh which was translated into an action plan the following year. Allow me, in this regard, to share with you some initiatives taken in Morocco that combine green finance and financial inclusion. These initiatives are part of a more comprehensive policy of financial inclusion that Bank Al-Maghrib has been conducting for the past fifteen years in coordination with the parties concerned. This policy has worked to develop adapted financial products, increase access points, set up financial information infrastructures, improve the relationship between banks and customers and promote financial education for targeted populations. In this wake, the recent start of Shariaa-compliant finance and mobile payment has broadened the product offering and should help to include a clientele that was previously little or not served. To further boost and federate efforts in this area, a National Strategy for Financial Inclusion was finalized and adopted in early 2019. It plans to accelerate the implementation of numerous reforms relating to digital financial services, microfinance, inclusive insurance and collaborative financing, targeting youth, women and rural areas as a priority. This strategy naturally led to the development of the first financial solutions with a green dimension targeting small farmers and MSMEs. These include the establishment of a financing offer, benefiting from the support of the State, dedicated to small and medium-sized farms that do not have access to bank credit because of their economic fragility. One of the objectives is to enable this population, which represents 70% of the Moroccan agricultural fabric, to adopt agricultural practices that are resilient to climate change. An insurance offer has also been set up to cover losses suffered by farmers as a result of climate-related losses. More broadly, a solidarity fund against catastrophic events is in the operationalization phase, for the compensation of victims of natural disasters. In addition to financial support from the State, it should be fed by a dedicated parafiscal tax. With regard to MSMEs, the public credit guarantee institution has recently integrated the green dimension into its offer by adopting an incentive system consisting in improving its intervention conditions for loans intended for companies operating in the green economy. It has also developed a financing offer targeting green projects. These still limited initiatives need to be strengthened and complemented by other mechanisms to meet the magnitude of the needs. In this, Microfinance has a decisive role to play in guiding the clientele of micro-enterprises and VSEs towards resilient projects and their financing. Digital technology is also an opportunity to accelerate low-cost financial inclusion, contributing to people's resilience, including in the face of the climate. However, care must be taken to ensure that the underlying infrastructure draws the energy they need from clean sources. I would also like to stress the importance of strengthening and broadening the scope of financial education actions to raise awareness on a large scale and promote responsible and resilient behaviour in the face of climate and environmental challenges as well as those of Financial Inclusion. Aware of this imperative, Bank Al-Maghrib has set up a Financial Education Foundation since 2013 which is in its 2nd strategic plan and which must, in particular through the training of trainers, contribute effectively to this objective. Ladies and gentlemen, The programme of this conference will allow a broad sharing of experience. The intervention of quality panelists will not fail to provide insight into the issues facing us and to enrich both the debates and the appropriate responses. Remaining convinced that this conference will be crowned with success, I wish you a pleasant stay in our country.
