Title: At the International Symposium celebrating the 50th anniversary of the Bank
text: Honorable advisors of His Majesty, Honorable ministers, Mr. General Manager of the International Monetary Fund, Mr. President of the Arab Monetary Fund, Mr. President of the African Development Bank, Mr. President of the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development, Mr. President of the European Central Bank, Distinguished governors, Excellencies ambassadors, Secretaries general, Ladies and gentlemen, It is my pleasure to welcome you and to express to you, on behalf of all staff members of Bank Al-Maghrib, my heartfelt thanks and sincerest gratitude for being with us today in this symposium, organized in celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of our institution. Morocco has always been a place for regional and global exchange and dialogue. Among the events that illustrate this, let me mention that Marrakech, a historical city which dates back to the 11th century, hosted in 1989 the signing of the Treaty establishing the Maghreb Arab Union, and then in 1994 the signing of the founding agreement of the World Trade Organization. The history of Bank Al-Maghrib is indeed a reflection of the contemporary history of Morocco. In fact, if we today celebrate the 50th anniversary of Bank Al-Maghrib, the creation of the Moroccan central bank goes back to well before that, exactly to the early 20th century. That was on the occasion of the Algeciras conference, held between January and April 1906 with the participation of thirteen countries to determine the different reforms that would be imposed on Morocco, particularly at the political, economic and financial level. It was then decided, by virtue of an international agreement, to establish the State Bank of Morocco, the broad lines of which were set. Later, in 1911 the bank was granted the privilege of issue. However, the international nature of the bank started to fade after the signing of the Protectorate Treaty in 1912. After the independence, his late Majesty King Mohammed V inaugurated Bank Al-Maghrib in 1959, as the central bank of a sovereign country, with mission to issue currency and conduct monetary policy. At the same time, a number of national banking and financial institutions were set up to accompany Moroccod5s economic and social development. Ladies and gentlemen, If the current crisis is unprecedented in its scale and consequences, the mechanisms and levels of addressing it are exceptional too. In fact, many countries took emergency measures to tackle the crisis by implementing huge stimulus plans and ensure the continued functioning of financial institutions and markets. They then sought to coordinate positions under the international forums, primarily the G-20, and the regional organizations and blocs, the aim being to define the policies able to restore financial stability and provide the appropriate conditions for an economic recovery. Central banks, in turn, injected large amounts of liquidity to restore money marketsd5 stability, and substantially reduced policy rates to levels close to zero in some countries. In the same context, the international organizations took urgent steps to assess the spillovers of the crisis and brought their intervention mechanisms into play. Morocco has managed to resist against the direct effects of the financial crisis, on the back of its solid fundamentals and structural reforms, as well as its sound banking and financial system and efficient exchange rate regime. Nonetheless, given its openness on the global economy, Morocco felt the impact of the economic crisis on the productive sectors linked to foreign demand, particularly from Europe, our first partner. In response, the Government has implemented a number of measures under the 2009 Finance Act to bolster domestic demand and investment, and put in place action plans to support the sectors hit by the crisis, while establishing committees to follow up and evaluate the results of the measures taken. Morocco closely follows the development of the global economic situation, and continues to implement the structural reforms within the framework of a long-run vision that seeks to increase the growth rate, raise the competitiveness of the economy and improve the business climate. Ladies and gentlemen, Despite the positive, but vulnerable, indicators that we observed early 2009, we should carry on action to work our way out of the crisis as soon as possible. In addition, some questions have started to arise about the post-crisis era. We have chosen for this symposium an issue of current concern in order to examine global and regional experiences. I am firmly convinced that our distinguished speakers and discussants will enrich the debates and contribute to analyzing and exchanging the experiences. It will also constitute a value added to the debate currently taking place internationally to make sure that such a crisis does not occur again and lay the foundations for decades of growth on a sound basis. I would like to thank you once again for your presence, and invite you to seize this opportunity to enjoy the rich heritage of this city and feel its historical spirit.

Title: High-Level Regional Symposium on Financial Stability
text: HIGH-LEVEL REGIONAL SYMPOSIUM ON FINANCIAL STABILITY 3rd edition OPENING SPEECH OF THE GOVERNOR Rabat, December 9, 2019 Bank Al-Maghrib Training Centre Governor of the National Bank of Rwanda and Chairman of the Association of African Central Banks (AACB), Vice-Chair of the Financial Stability Board (FSB), Chair of the Macroprudential Committee for the International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS), Representative of the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), Ladies and gentlemen, representatives of African regulators, Honorable audience, It gives me great pleasure to welcome you in Bank Al-Maghribd5s Training Center in Rabat, on the occasion of the third edition of the High-Level Regional Symposium on Financial Stability. On behalf of the Moroccan Committee for Coordination and Surveillance of Systemic Risks, gathering the three regulators, I wish to thank all the participants and speakers for their interest in this meeting. I would also like to welcome our guests from across Africa, convey to them my gratitude for accepting our invitation and agreeing to share their experiences in the panels held as part of this symposium. My warm thanks go, in particular, to Mr. John RWANGOMBWA, Governor of the National Bank of Rwanda and Chairman of the AACB, for honoring us in this symposium. I wish to underline here that the AACB has, to our great delight, kindly accepted to be a regular partner in the organization of this biennial event, thus reflecting the particular importance it grants to financial stability issues. I am also grateful for the presence of eminent experts of the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the World Bank, the International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS), the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the French Prudential Supervisory Authority (ACPR), the French Financial Markets Authority (AMF), the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD) as well as the different representatives of the Moroccan financial sector. The contribution of each and every one throughout this event will undoubtedly provide us with valuable insight into the issues and actions to be undertaken in order to strengthen the financial stability framework in our respective countries and, by corollary, in our continent. Ladies and gentlemen, As you know, Member States of the African Union have decided, in 2018, to create the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). This major step is intended to further integrate African markets for an inclusive and sustainable socio-economic growth and an enhanced competitiveness of African countries, both at the continental and international levels. Thereupon, increasing financial integration in Africa has become a major requirement to accompany this momentum, particularly through facilitating trade and investment opportunities. In the same vein, and in line with the vision of His Majesty the King, Morocco strengthened this financial and economic integration by signing various partnerships and cooperation agreements with African countries. Besides, as part of the financial and the banking sectord5s compliance with such orientation, Moroccan banks strongly expanded their activities in Africa over the last couple of years and are now present in 27 countries of the continent. Despite its undeniable benefits and opportunities, financial integration in Africa is not risk-free with regard to financial stability namely due to the possible contagion and spreading of risks between our countriesd5 financial systems. It has therefore become urgent to adjust the risk management measures, to set up an appropriate stress test system, and to strengthen close cooperation between home and host regulators. Ladies and gentlemen, Today, considering the significant changes in our internal and external environment, our African financial system must be in constant evolution to cope with the emerging risks and vulnerabilities to financial stability. These changes relate, first and foremost, to the disruptive implications and impacts of digital transformation and technological innovations on the African financial sphere. The Fintech and Insurtech impetus, the use of Big Data, the alternative financing methods d2crowdfundingd3, mobile banking development, as well as the use of Blockchain technologies are all examples illustrating the substantial incursion of these innovations in the banking, insurance and capital markets sectors. Hence, considering that these changes are likely to transform our economic and financial environment, we are compelled to pay them considerable importance. In this regard, we had invited financial sector stakeholders to debate these issues, last March, within the regional conference for Africa and the Middle East on the digital transformation and the implementation of the Bali Fintech Agenda, held jointly with the IMF, and more recently during the Africa Blockchain Summit, held last November. The risks arising from these disruptive technologies have increased sharply due to the enhanced and expeditious digitalization of financial services. These particularly include the risks of using IT platforms for money laundering and terrorism financing, consumer protection and the resurgence of cyber-attacks targeting the financial sector. On the latter point, international institutions unanimously acknowledge the need to establish a reference framework for cyber security regulation. In Morocco, financial authorities have, in 2018, elaborated a roadmap to monitor cyber risks in the national financial system, in light of the international standards. In this context, a diagnosis of cyber security maturity at financial institutions is being prepared pursuant to a collaborative approach among the three regulators. On another equally important aspect, climate change, now an almost irreversible reality, is a critical vulnerability area for the financial sector. As such, the physical risks caused by the increasingly repeated climate disasters and those associated with the transition to a low-carbon economy, notably when abrupt and unordered, can lead to important disruptions and financial losses which could hamper the resilience of the financial sector. Consequently, financial regulators are, under their financial stability mandate, called upon to set up climate risks mapping, though still in the making. They are thus required to gradually improve their approaches as to identifying and measuring the financial sectord5s exposure to such risks. Our African continent is more particularly concerned with this issue, as climate change threat is much more acute. Furthermore, the last financial crisis of 2008 revealed the necessity to prevent, manage and regulate risks related to bankruptcy of financial institutions, considered until then c7too big to failc8. Based on these lessons, the main post-crisis reforms concerned identifying financial institutions of systemic importance and setting up a strengthened supervisory framework for them. As such, several countries achieved significant progress in this field, and established a resolution and crisis management framework that would define the powers, instruments and funding mechanisms required to address potential resolution cases in an orderly and controlled manner. Ladies and gentlemen, Throughout the sessions planned for today, we will be able to debate further on the themes related to these different changes. This meetingd5s agenda, marked by speeches of distinguished panelists from the banking and insurance sectors and capital markets, will definitely yield insights into the challenges, lessons and possible tracks for reflection to improve and strengthen our capabilities and mechanisms to further safeguard financial stability in our countries, hence our continent. I am fully confident that this third edition will be crowned with success. I thank you all for your attention and wish you a pleasant stay in Rabat.

Title: Inaugural address at the 5th edition of the seminar on financial infrastructures e...
text: 5TH EDITION OF THE SEMINAR ON FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE AND CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT Rabat, from 22 to 25 September 2014 INAUGURAL ADDRESS BY MONSIEUR LE WALI DE BANK AL-MAGHRIB Rabat, 22 September 2014 Ladies and Gentlemen, I am pleased to welcome you to Morocco and to express my sincere thanks for your participation in the fifth edition of the seminar on financial infrastructure and credit risk management. I would like to thank in particular the International Finance Corporation and the Arab Monetary Fund who are jointly organizing this event with Bank Al-Maghrib. The topics that will be discussed at this seminar are extremely important, especially for the countries of the region, many of which are represented today, that aspire to promote financial inclusion and develop their financial systems. Financial information sharing mechanisms for sound credit risk management will rightly feature prominently in your debates. They are, in fact, an imperative for effective financial intermediation, the development of which is often hampered by the absence or weakness of financial information. These arrangements are of particular importance for all actors in the credit risk management process. First, for borrowers who can take advantage of the quality of their credit reports to reduce their financing costs. Then, for lenders who can have a wealth of information, in real time, supplementing the balance sheet data of borrowers, facilitating risk analysis and the assessment of the creditworthiness of the latter. And finally, for regulators for whom the system is one of the pillars of the stability of the financial system that makes it possible to meet the challenges in terms of consumer education, by instilling in them a financial discipline capable of avoiding their over-indebtedness. Therefore, it is important for all these stakeholders to be at the state of the art in this area, in particular central banks in their capacity as regulators who have an important role to play in creating momentum around the use of credit information registers and more generally for the upgrading of financial infrastructures. These issues must be prioritized, especially in an environment marked by difficult economic conditions and risks of financial instability. In this context, our economies are undergoing significant changes both in the banking industry and in the behaviour of consumers and credit seekers. It is also important to highlight the acceleration, at the regional level, of the development of economic, commercial and financial relations, which present us with new challenges for the convergence of the legal frameworks and banking practices of our countries towards the highest standards. To support these developments, financial infrastructures can only be efficient if they cover, in addition to effective information-sharing arrangements, strong institutions and markets, robust payment and settlement systems and strengthened financial capacities. This seminar is an excellent opportunity to discuss these issues in the presence of eminent experts and whose conclusions and recommendations will be followed, I am convinced, with great interest by the various institutions represented here. For my part, and in order to contribute to these debates, I would like to tell you about Morocco's experience, which is part of a more global strategy for the integrated development of the financial sector by 2020. This strategy, which was adopted at the end of the previous decade, aims to make our country a regional financial hub and confirms our commitment to promote economic partnerships with the countries of the African continent within the framework of win/win cooperation. In addition to the accelerated and controlled development of the capital market, it also aims to deepen the national banking market through action to promote the banking of the population, improve access to finance for companies and strengthen and modernize the financial infrastructure. To achieve our ambitions, we work at the Bank level on the basis of three-year strategic plans and operational objectives, as part of a concerted approach with public and private actors. This is the case with the financial information sharing project, which has been a major challenge for us to increase the financing capacity of the economy and succeed in banking reforms, particularly those related to Bale 2 and Bale 3. Thus, the work that was carried out with the IFC for several years led to the start of the activity of the 1st Credit Bureau in Morocco in 2009. It has made it possible to centralize and improve credit information for individuals and all categories of enterprises, including MSMEs and microcredit beneficiaries. Over the past four years, its activity has grown significantly, with the increase in the number of institutions that feed and consult its database and including in addition to all banks and specialized finance companies, 4 microcredit associations among the largest in the country. Today, this database registers about 5 million customers including about 200,000 companies and more than 10 million credit agreements representing 93% of the total outstanding loans distributed. Similarly, consultations of credit reports have increased significantly, reaching a daily average of 6,000 consultations this year. This increase has been facilitated by the automation of the consultation process in a large number of institutions. Thanks to Credit Bureau, banking institutions, despite a difficult economic situation, marked by rising risks, were able to control the level of their outstanding debts. Similarly, the micro-credit sector, which, following rapid growth, has experienced difficulties due to the significant increase in unpaid receivables, has returned to a healthy situation favoured by the sharing of credit information. In order to consolidate and improve financial reporting, we have included new structuring actions in Bank Al-Maghrib's 2013-2015 three-year strategic plan. Thus, the Bank has awarded a second license to a new Credit Bureau, which will be put into operation in 2015 with the aim of diversifying the range of services and reducing the cost of these services. Similarly, we are currently examining the procedures for opening the activity of Credit Bureau to non-financial data providers. Bank Al-Maghrib is conducting, with the assistance of the IFC, a study to evaluate the current legal and regulatory framework in order to study the feasibility of exchanging data from entities not supervised by the Central Bank, such as telecom operators, water/electricity authorities, etc. etc. On the other hand, the government has initiated, in consultation with the partners concerned and with the assistance of the FMA, the IFC and the EBRD, the project of the overhaul of the law of personal property security which has 2 components: -the first part is to promote a new legal framework allowing SMEs to use movable property as collateral and to facilitate its acceptance by banks and its realization. -the second part concerns the establishment of a collateral registry to centralize information on assets pledged by debtors and to ensure the priority of creditors against competing right holders. Aware of the interest represented by the access, by companies and banking institutions, to the most exhaustive financial and economic information possible, Bank Al Maghrib has taken the initiative to take 3 other measures that seem important to me to highlight. The 1st consisted of setting up, in partnership with public and private partners, the MSME Observatory. Its purpose is to make available to companies and other private and public actors demographic, economic and financial studies and information concerning the productive fabric of the country. The 2nd concerns access by merchants to the Centrale des Cheques Irregulars. This project, which is part of Bank Al-Maghrib's actions to give credibility to the cheque, is likely to allow companies to secure their transactions. Its commissioning is scheduled for 2015. The 3rd measure concerns the provision to the banking system, before the end of this year, of a new tool to help assess the risk relating to unpaid invoices on Standard Bills of Exchange (LCN). In parallel with these actions, we ensure strict compliance with the regulations in force regarding the protection of personal data. In this sense, Bank Al-Maghrib and the National Commission for the Control of the Protection of Personal Data (CNDP) signed in 2013 a memorandum of understanding and cooperation, to allow in particular the promotion of the culture of protection of personal data in the banking and financial sector and the adoption of modalities of application of the legal and regulatory framework more adapted to this sector. In this context, a commission set up with the banking associations has been set up to coordinate the actions and procedures for the implementation of the provisions of the law by credit institutions. I cannot conclude without wishing you every success in your work and thanking the International Finance Corporation, the Arab Monetary Fund and other international financial institutions for their constant support for improving financial information sharing mechanisms. Finally, I like to invite you to take advantage of your stay in Morocco and Rabat, the imperial city of the Kingdom, to discover its heritage and its millennial wealth.

Title: At the Regional Symposium on Financial Stability
text: DSM REGIONAL SYMPOSIUM ON FINANCIAL STABILITY OPENING REMARKS BY MONSIEUR LE WALI Rabat, 12 December 2017 Bank Al-Maghrib Vocational Training Center Ladies and gentlemen, It is an honour and a pleasure for me to welcome you today to the premises of this Bank Al-Maghrib training centre in Rabat, as part of this regional symposium on financial stability. On behalf of the members of the Moroccan Committee for Coordination and Supervision of Systemic Risks present here at my side, I thank all the participants and speakers for the interest which they granted to this meeting. I would also like to welcome our guests from the various countries of Africa, expressing my gratitude for having responded favourably to our invitation. and for some to have agreed to share their experiences within the framework of the panels planned during this symposium. My heartfelt thanks go, in particular, to Mr. RAMESWURLALL BASANT ROI, Governor of the Central Bank of Mauritius, for having honored us with his presence. I would also like to thank the various representatives of the Moroccan financial sector as well as the eminent experts of the Financial Stability Board, the World Bank and the International Association of Insurance Supervisory Bodies. Your contribution throughout this day will undoubtedly provide us with the necessary lessons and clarifications to undertake effective actions to improve and strengthen the financial stability framework in our respective countries. Ladies and gentlemen Since the advent of the last international financial crisis, issues relating to financial stability and macroprudential supervision have been placed at the heart of the concerns of the financial authorities of our countries. In this context, both central banks and other African financial authorities have embarked on structuring projects aimed at extending their prerogatives to include the mission of contributing to financial stability and at implementing a macro-regional policy based on a governance system and systemic risk management mechanisms adapted to their economic and political contexts. In Morocco, anxious to strengthen and consolidate the resilience of our financial system, the Central Bank, ACAPS, AMMC and MEF have been carrying out for more than 5 years now a fundamental work to implement, in a coordinated and concerted manner, the bases of macroprudential supervision, based on an institutional, legal, analytical and operational framework aimed at identifying and regulating systemic risks and managing possible crises. Ladies and gentlemen At present, the internal and external environment of the African financial system is undergoing significant changes that require both regulators and financial institutions to adapt to face the emergence of new risks. These developments mainly concern: . the impact of digital transformation and technological innovations on the financial sphere (crowdfunding, mobile banking, blockchain technologies "virtual currency", etc.). With the increased digitalisation of financial services also promoting financial inclusion, the risk of an upsurge in cyberattacks targeting the financial sector is becoming increasingly critical and should therefore be addressed; . policies to strengthen economic and financial integration in Africa, which have fostered the expansion of the cross-border activities of several African financial institutions. This expansion is not without risks to financial stability in view of the threats of cross-border contagion. During this day, you will debate around very important themes related to these developments. During the first session, you will discuss with Mr. Aktas, member of the secretariat of the Financial Stability Board, the recent activities of the FSB. A focus will also be on the main financial stability issues in sub-Saharan African countries and the MENA1 region. The second session devoted to the institutional, legal and coordination framework for financial stability will be marked by the presentation of the experiences of Morocco, Egypt, BCEAO and Rwanda, which have adopted different organizational models. In this regard, let me stress the importance of this framework, without which we cannot guarantee the optimal functioning of financial stability activities, in a context where financial links have increased, favoured by the development of pan-African financial institutions. This last point brings me to the subject of the third session of this meeting, which focuses on the challenges of regulation, supervision and management of cross-border risks of these institutions. Indeed, the recent expansion of pan-African financial activities, which, alongside the multiple benefits it brings for regional financial integration, poses new challenges for financial authorities in terms of supervision and management of cross-border risks and requires increased cooperation between authorities of host and home countries to mitigate these risks. In Morocco, the banking sector has experienced a strong expansion of its activity in Africa in recent years and is now present in more than 26 countries of the continent. In the area of cross-border cooperation, the central bank has signed several agreements with the financial authorities of the host countries, conducted joint monitoring missions and organized several colleges of supervisors. 1 The last meetings of the FSB regional consultation groups were held on 14 and 15 November in Pretoria, for the Sub-Saharan Africa region and on 20 November for the MENA region, respectively. Furthermore, with regard to international standards for the insurance sector, I am pleased to point out that an IAIS expert present here will share with you the work carried out by this Institution in setting up a framework for assessing systemic risks in relation to the cross-border activity of insurance undertakings. With regard to the last session of this symposium dedicated to the cyber resilience, the increasing digitalization of financial services and the worrying scale of cyber risks.attacks by financial institutions and market infrastructures challenge us in several respects. They call for vigilance and the need to strengthen and adapt the processes of regulation and supervision of these risks, in consultation with the various actors concerned both nationally and internationally. This session will be marked by the presentation of an expert from the World Bank and those of representatives of the AMMC and two financial market infrastructures, namely, Maroclear and the Casablanca Stock Exchange. Ladies and gentlemen I remain convinced that this symposium, given the importance of the planned themes, will provide lessons and avenues for reflection that will enable us to improve and strengthen our capacities and mechanisms to further preserve financial stability within our countries and hence our continent. It also represents an opportunity for networking and sharing of experience. Finally, I would like to stress the interest of renewing this type of meeting in order to continue our exchanges and our reflections in the light of future developments that will not fail to impact us. Wishing your work every success, I thank you for your attention.
